\section{Uniform coefficient tails with a slope below one}\label{col:P:07}

\begin{theorem}\label{P:thm:round2-uniform-tail}
For an integer $n\ge2$, put
\[
 T(n)=\min\left\{n,\frac{19}{20}(n+10),\frac9{10}(n+31)\right\}.
\]
Let $f$ be holomorphic and zero-free in the unit disk, with $|f|\le1$
and $|f(0)|=e^{-t}$. Then
\[
 t\ge T(n)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad |[z^n]f|<2/e.
\]
For every $n\ge3$, the uniform squared bound is
\[
 |[z^n]f|^2<\frac{1353}{2500}<\frac4{e^2}.
\]
Equivalently, the useful threshold is $n$ through degree $190$,
$19(n+10)/20$ for degrees $191$ through $368$, and $9(n+31)/10$
for every degree $n\ge369$.
\end{theorem}

This is an extension of the same signed-measure and Laguerre-energy method.
It uses two additional fixed rational polynomials, not an extrapolation from
numerical tests at selected degrees.  It excludes an entire ray for every
degree and every admissible function, without a stationarity assumption.

\subsection{The exact inputs and the all-real majorants}

Recall the proved transfer and probability identity
\[
 |[z^n]f|^2\le S_n(t)-e^{-2t},\qquad
 S_n(t)=\Pr\{X_n\ge2t\},\qquad
 d\Pr(X_n=x)=e^{-x}L_n(x)^2\,dx.
\]
The polynomial moments $M_k(n)=\mathbb E X_n^k$ are reconstructed by
\[
 xL_j=(2j+1)L_j-(j+1)L_{j+1}-jL_{j-1}.
\]

For ordered rational nodes $a_1<\cdots<a_k<b<c_1<\cdots<c_l$, the unique
polynomial $p$ of degree at most $2(k+l)$ with
\[
 p(a_i)=p'(a_i)=0,\qquad p(b)=1,\qquad p(c_j)=1,\quad p'(c_j)=0
\]
satisfies $p\ge0$ on $\mathbb R$ and $p\ge1$ on $[b,\infty)$.
The proof is the exact Rolle root-count argument proved above:
$p'$ has $k+l$ imposed roots, $k-1$ additional roots between the zero
contacts, and $l$ additional roots between consecutive one contacts,
including $b$.  These exhaust its possible $2(k+l)-1$ roots, so they are
simple.  The derivative is positive between $a_k$ and $b$; its alternating
signs make every zero contact a minimum of value $0$ and every other
double contact a minimum of value $1$.  This proves both global sign claims.
The argument permits negative zero-contact nodes and unequal numbers of
contacts on the two sides.

The exact rational nodes are specified in
\texttt{spectral\_round2\_inputs.json}.  There are two sets:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c}
 b&k&l&\deg p&d&n_0\\ \hline
 19/10&12&12&48&10&191\\
 9/5&30&34&128&31&369
\end{array}
\]
All node values in the second row are rational multiples of $1/10000$;
the first row uses rational multiples of $1/1000000$.
These nodes and the stated contact equations completely determine each
polynomial.  Decimal discovery calculations play no role in verification.

\subsection{One polynomial inequality covers each infinite ray}

For either input row, write $p(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{D}p_jx^j$ and set
\[
 G(n)=\frac{1353}{2500}(n+d)^D
       -\sum_{j=0}^{D}p_jM_j(n)(n+d)^{D-j}.
\]
The exact checker verifies that every coefficient of $G(n_0+s)$ is
strictly positive.  A positive common denominator and a positive common
integer divisor may be removed before this test; they do not change signs.
There are 49 comparisons in the first row and 129 in the second.
Consequently, for every integer $n\ge n_0$,
\[
 \Pr\{X_n\ge b(n+d)\}
 \le\mathbb E\,p\!\left(\frac{X_n}{n+d}\right)
 <\frac{1353}{2500}.
\]
By monotonicity of the probability tail, this proves the desired coefficient
bound whenever $t\ge b(n+d)/2$ in the corresponding infinite range.

The joins to earlier proofs are exact and have no missing integer degree.
For $n\le190$,
\[
 \frac{19}{20}(n+10)\ge n,
\]
so the previous uniform $t\ge n$ theorem supplies the first row's finite
range.  The new polynomial ray begins at $n=191$.
For $n\le368$,
\[
 \frac9{10}(n+31)-\frac{19}{20}(n+10)=\frac{368-n}{20}\ge0,
\]
so the now-established first row supplies the second row's finite range.
The second polynomial ray begins at $n=369$.
Thus no additional per-degree coefficient checks are required in this round.
The case $n=2$ and the rational comparison
$1353/2500<4/e^2$ are inherited from the preceding exact proof.

\subsection{An independent reconstruction of the moment certificate}

There is a second, explicit formula for the moments, which does not use
the tridiagonal walk.  The generating function
\[
 \sum_{m=0}^{\infty}L_m(x)u^m
 =\frac1{1-u}\exp\!\left(-\frac{xu}{1-u}\right)
\]
and integration against $x^k e^{-x}\,dx$ give, for sufficiently small
$u,v$ (or by coefficient differentiation at the origin),
\[
 \sum_{m,l\ge0}u^mv^l\int_0^\infty
       x^ke^{-x}L_m(x)L_l(x)\,dx
 =k!\frac{(1-u)^k(1-v)^k}{(1-uv)^{k+1}}.
\]
Taking the diagonal coefficient $u^nv^n$ yields the polynomial identity
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:independent-laguerre-moments}
 M_k(n)=k!\sum_{j=0}^k\binom{k}{j}^{\!2}
                  \binom{n+k-j}{k}
       =\sum_{j=0}^k\binom{k}{j}^{\!2}
                    \prod_{r=1}^k(n+r-j).
\end{equation}
When $j>n$, the displayed binomial is zero, so the finite formula is
valid for every integer $n\ge0$ without a changed summation limit.
It is also an equality of polynomials in $n$.

The independent audit reconstructs all 129 moment polynomials with
\eqref{P:eq:independent-laguerre-moments}, checks all rational interpolation
contacts, forms the two gap polynomials, and shifts them by a separate
Horner algorithm.  All 49 and 129 shifted coefficients are strictly
positive, and the two primitive gap polynomials agree exactly with the
walk-based verifier.  This checks the same infinite rays by a second
moment construction; it is not an additional finite-index extrapolation.

\subsection{What this scalar method can and cannot exclude}

The stationary mass constraint $t\ge n/N$ and the new theorem confine any
remaining deficient-support extremizer to
\[
 \frac nN\le t<T(n).
\]
The one-atom stratum is excluded.  The new scalar ray does not exclude an
additional entire stratum with $N\ge2$: for example, its leading slope
$9/10$ remains above the two-atom lower mass $n/2$.

There is a precise limitation of this unweighted $H^2$ transfer.
For every fixed nonnegative integer $k$, the leading term of $M_k(n)$ is
$\binom{2k}{k}n^k$.  This follows directly from the tridiagonal walk:
after division by $n$, the limiting recurrence has diagonal $2$ and
off-diagonals $-1$, and its closed-walk count is the constant term of
$(2-z-z^{-1})^k$, namely $\binom{2k}{k}$.
Therefore $X_n/n$ converges in distribution to the arcsine law on $[0,4]$,
with density $1/(\pi\sqrt{x(4-x)})$.
For clarity, moment convergence suffices here: bounded first moments give
tightness, bounded higher moments give uniform integrability, and the limit
moments force support in $[0,4]$ and determine a unique measure there.
For $0<c<2$ and any fixed constant $C$ it follows that
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}S_n(cn+C)
   =\frac2\pi\arccos\sqrt{\frac c2}.
\]
The limiting threshold for the unweighted squared-energy upper bound is
\[
 c_*=
 2\sin^2\!\left[\frac\pi2\left(1-\frac4{e^2}\right)\right]
 =0.8704878209\ldots.
\]
If $c<c_*$, that particular upper bound exceeds $4/e^2$ for all sufficiently
large $n$.  This limits the unweighted $H^2$ estimate, not the original
coefficient problem or every variant of the signed-measure method.
In particular, reaching the lower-mass strata will require additional
structure or a stronger norm estimate.

\subsection{Reproducibility}

Run \texttt{python spectral\_round2\_certificate.py} with its adjacent
helper and input files in the same extracted build directory.
The verifier uses only standard-library exact arithmetic.  It freshly
reruns the preceding all-degree certificate, reconstructs the two Hermite
polynomials from rational nodes, checks all contact conditions, generates
all moments through order 128, verifies all shifted coefficient signs,
and checks both degree-range joins.  The output records exact arithmetic
hashes and counts.  All required files and exact node data are embedded in this source.
\section{An auxiliary-free moment-energy exclusion}\label{col:P:08}
\label{P:sec:energy}

Throughout this section let $n=N+d$, $1\leq N<n$, and suppose that
positive masses and unit-circle support points satisfy the necessary
stationary equations
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:moments}
 S_k:=\sum_{j=1}^N(k\lambda_j-1)\alpha_j^k
 =\frac12\sum_{\ell=1}^d
 \left(\sigma_\ell^k+\overline{\sigma_\ell}^{-k}\right),
 \quad 1\leq k\leq n,\qquad 0<|\sigma_\ell|<1.
\end{equation}
Define $S_0=d$ and $S_{-k}=\overline{S_k}$. The value assigned to $S_0$
is essential: the formula defining $S_k$ from the atoms for positive $k$
must not be used at $k=0$.

\begin{lemma}[Inertia of the moment matrix]\label{P:lem:inertia}
For $0\leq m\leq n$, the Hermitian matrix
$H_m=(S_{i-j})_{i,j=0}^{m}$ has at most $d$ positive and at most $d$
negative eigenvalues, and rank at most $2d$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put $v_m(z)=(1,z,\ldots,z^m)^{\mathsf T}$ and
$u_\ell=1/\overline{\sigma_\ell}$. Directly from \eqref{P:eq:moments},
including the diagonal, we have
\[
 H_m=\frac12\sum_{\ell=1}^d
 \left(v_m(\sigma_\ell)v_m(u_\ell)^*
       +v_m(u_\ell)v_m(\sigma_\ell)^*\right).
\]
Each summand is a congruence of the matrix
$\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1/2\\1/2&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$,
which has one positive and one negative eigenvalue. More explicitly,
the sum is $WJW^*$, where $J$ has positive and negative indices $d$.
Restriction of a Hermitian form cannot increase either index, proving
all three assertions. Repeated auxiliary roots cause no difficulty.
The same conclusion holds on the closed auxiliary boundary
$|\sigma_\ell|=1$: then $u_\ell=\sigma_\ell$ and its summand is
a positive semidefinite rank-one matrix.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Weighted moment-energy cut]\label{P:thm:energy}
For every integer $m$ with $d\leq m\leq n$, a solution of
\eqref{P:eq:moments} satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:energy-cut}
 2\sum_{k=1}^{m}(m+1-k)|S_k|^2
 \ \geq\ (m+1)d(m+1-d).
\end{equation}
In particular, a strict reverse inequality certifies impossibility
without determining any auxiliary roots.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The trace of $H_m$ equals $(m+1)d>0$. If its positive eigenvalues are
$\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_p$, then $p\leq d$ by Lemma~\ref{P:lem:inertia} and
\[
 (\operatorname{tr}H_m)^2
 \leq\left(\sum_{i=1}^p\rho_i\right)^2
 \leq d\sum_{i=1}^p\rho_i^2
 \leq d\|H_m\|_F^2.
\]
But
$\|H_m\|_F^2=(m+1)d^2+
2\sum_{k=1}^m(m+1-k)|S_k|^2$. Substitution proves the result.
\end{proof}

The case $m=d$ requires only the first $d$ atomic moments. The case
$m=n$ has right-hand side $(n+1)d(N+1)$. These are necessary conditions,
not sufficient conditions for extremality.

\section{Uniform neighborhoods of deleted regular polygons}\label{col:P:09}
\label{P:sec:deleted}

The following theorem extends a symmetric configuration exclusion to
closed neighborhoods with nonconstant masses and independently perturbed
support points. It applies to every choice of the deleted vertices.

\begin{theorem}[Robust deleted-polygon certificate]\label{P:thm:deleted}
Let $n\geq2d+1$, $N=n-d$, and $c>0$. Let $Z$ be a rotated regular
$n$-gon on the unit circle, let $D\subset Z$ contain exactly $d$ vertices,
and write $Z\setminus D=\{\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_N\}$. For given atoms
define
\[
 E_\lambda=\sum_{j=1}^N|\lambda_j-c|,\qquad
 E_\alpha=\sum_{j=1}^N|\alpha_j-\zeta_j|,\qquad
 K_d(c)=\sum_{k=1}^{2d}k|kc-1|.
\]
If
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:deleted-budget}
 2d(2d+1)E_\lambda+2K_d(c)E_\alpha<\frac{cd}{2},
\end{equation}
then the atoms cannot satisfy \eqref{P:eq:moments}.
In particular, the entire closed region
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:deleted-box}
 \begin{split}
 |\lambda_j-c|&\leq\frac{c}{16N(2d+1)},\\
 |\alpha_j-\zeta_j|&\leq
 \frac{c}{16N(2d+1)(1+2dc)},\qquad 1\leq j\leq N,
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
is excluded. On a subspace of dimension $d+1$ the associated moment
matrix then has quadratic form at least $cd/4$ times the squared norm.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Set $m=2d<n$ and let $H_m^0$ be the moment matrix for the reference
configuration $\lambda_j=c$, $\alpha_j=\zeta_j$, with diagonal $d$.
The sum of the $k$th powers of all vertices in $Z$ vanishes for
$1\leq k\leq m$. Consequently
\[
 H_m^0=\sum_{\eta\in D}
 U_\eta(J-cD_m)U_\eta^*,\qquad
 U_\eta=\operatorname{diag}(1,\eta,\ldots,\eta^m),
 \quad (D_m)_{ij}=|i-j|,
\]
where $J$ is the matrix with every entry equal to $1$.
Let
$L=\{x:v_m(\eta)^*x=0\text{ for every }\eta\in D\}$.
The deleted vertices are distinct, so $\dim L=m+1-d=d+1$.

For a vector $y=(y_0,\ldots,y_m)$ with $\sum y_i=0$, put
$p_r=\sum_{i=0}^r y_i$ for $0\leq r<m$, and put $p_{-1}=p_m=0$.
An exact summation gives
\[
 -y^*D_my=2\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}|p_r|^2,
 \qquad
 \|y\|^2=\sum_{r=0}^m|p_r-p_{r-1}|^2
 \leq4\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}|p_r|^2.
\]
For $x\in L$, each $y=U_\eta^*x$ has sum zero and the same norm
as $x$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:base-gap}
 x^*H_m^0x\geq\frac{cd}{2}\|x\|^2\qquad(x\in L).
\end{equation}

By telescoping powers on the unit circle,
$|\alpha_j^k-\zeta_j^k|\leq k|\alpha_j-\zeta_j|$.
The difference $e_k=S_k-S_k^0$ therefore satisfies
\[
 |e_k|\leq kE_\lambda+k|kc-1|E_\alpha.
\]
The difference matrix has zero diagonal and operator norm at most
$2\sum_{k=1}^{m}|e_k|$. This is bounded by the left side of
\eqref{P:eq:deleted-budget}. Combining with \eqref{P:eq:base-gap}
gives a positive definite restriction to $L$, so $H_m$ has at least
$d+1$ positive eigenvalues. Lemma~\ref{P:lem:inertia} forbids this.

For the explicit region \eqref{P:eq:deleted-box}, use
$K_d(c)\leq d(2d+1)(1+2dc)$. The mass and angular contributions to
the norm error are each at most $cd/8$, giving total at most $cd/4$.
This is strictly below the reference gap $cd/2$ even on all boundary
faces of the displayed region.
\end{proof}

The theorem allows $c$ to vary continuously. The number of deleted sets,
the number of atoms, and the size of the matrix may grow with $n$;
the displayed proof establishes the whole family at once.
The angular tolerance is a chord distance; an angular displacement in
radians of at most the same number is a sufficient condition.

\begin{remark}[A more general moment-completion form]
The proof only uses closeness of the first $2d$ moments to a deleted
polygon model. Suppose arbitrary $d$ unit points $\eta_\ell$ are chosen
and set
\[
 R_k=\sum_j\alpha_j^k+\sum_\ell\eta_\ell^k,
 \qquad W_k=\sum_j(\lambda_j-c)\alpha_j^k.
\]
Whenever $2d\leq n$ and
\[
 2\sum_{k=1}^{2d}|(kc-1)R_k+kW_k|<cd/2,
\]
the same comparison matrix excludes the configuration. Distinctness of
the $\eta_\ell$ is unnecessary here: its failure only increases the
dimension of $L$. This formulation can certify moment boxes that are
not coordinatewise close to a regular polygon.
\end{remark}
% Proven parameterized exclusions, separate from the published n=8 paper.
% Requires amsmath, amssymb, amsthm.  This is an inclusion fragment.
\section{Three explicit parameterized exclusion families}\label{col:P:10}

Let $n\ge2$, $1\le N<n$, $d=n-N$, and suppose
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r1-moments}
 S_k:=\sum_{j=1}^{N}(k\lambda_j-1)\alpha_j^k
   =\sum_{i=1}^{d}T_k(q_i)e^{ik\phi_i},
 \quad 1\le k\le n,
 \qquad \lambda_j>0,\ |\alpha_j|=1,\ q_i\ge1.
\end{equation}
For $d=1$ rotate the common phase so that $\phi_1=0$; then
$S_k=T_k(q)$, $q\ge1$.  Each theorem below excludes a stated closed
parameter region for every indicated integer $n$.  It does not assert
that the regions cover the entire extremal parameter space.

\subsection{A wider first-moment tube around a deleted regular polygon}

\begin{theorem}[Deleted-$n$-gon tube]\label{P:thm:r1-deleted}
Let $n\ge3$, $N=n-1$, $1\le T\le2$, and $c=T/N$.
Let $\eta\in\mathbb T$ and
$\zeta_j=\eta e^{2\pi i j/n}$, $1\le j\le N$.
There is no solution of \eqref{P:eq:r1-moments} with $d=1$ and
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r1-deleted-box}
 |\lambda_j-c|\le\frac{T}{4N^2},\qquad
 |\alpha_j-\zeta_j|\le\frac{T}{4N^2}
 \quad(1\le j\le N).
\end{equation}
The first real moment has a certified strict gap of at least
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r1-deleted-gap}
 \frac{T}{2N}+\frac{T^2}{4N^2}.
\end{equation}
The conclusion holds for every common rotation and every relabelling
of the matched atoms.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The root-of-unity identity is $\sum_{j=1}^{N}\zeta_j=-\eta$.
Put $E_\lambda=\sum_j|\lambda_j-c|$ and
$E_\alpha=\sum_j|\alpha_j-\zeta_j|$.
Since $0<c\le1$,
\[
 \begin{split}
 \left|S_1-(1-c)\eta\right|
 &\le \sum_j\left|(\lambda_j-c)\alpha_j
                   +(c-1)(\alpha_j-\zeta_j)\right|\\
 &\le E_\lambda+(1-c)E_\alpha\le c/4+(1-c)c/4.
 \end{split}
\]
Consequently
\[
 \Re S_1\le|S_1|\le1-c/2-c^2/4<1\le q,
\]
contrary to the first moment equation.  Multiplication of the gap by
$4N^2$ gives the positive polynomial $2TN+T^2$.  In the coordinates
$N=u+2$, $T=1+v$, $u\ge0$, $0\le v\le1$, this polynomial is
$5+2u+6v+2uv+v^2$, so the positivity is uniform in $n$.
The lower mass face also obeys the necessary cardinal floor:
\[
 \frac{T}{N}-\frac{T}{4N^2}-\frac1{N+1}
 \ge\frac{3N-1}{4N^2(N+1)}>0.
\]
No total-mass or auxiliary-tail cutoff was used.
\end{proof}

More generally, for any common mass $0<c<2$, the same first-moment
argument excludes the complete coupled region
\[
 E_\lambda+|1-c|E_\alpha<1-|1-c|.
\]
The displayed closed boxes are one explicit rational family inside
that larger region.  The multiplier of the first real equation is the
integer $1$; the geometric root sum supplies the common reference term.

\subsection{A uniform clustered light/heavy exclusion}

Set
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r1-cluster-constants}
 \varepsilon=\frac38,\qquad
 a=1-\frac{\varepsilon^2}{2}=\frac{119}{128},\qquad
 b=2a^2-1=\frac{5969}{8192},\qquad
 g=2b^2-1=\frac{2074529}{33554432}>0.
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[First-moment alignment]\label{P:lem:r1-alignment}
Suppose $d=1$, all $\lambda_j\le1$, at least one $\lambda_j<1$,
and there is a unit point $\beta$ such that
$|\alpha_j-\beta|\le3/8$ for every $j$.
The first moment equation forces
\[
 -\Re\beta\ge a,\qquad
 \Re\alpha_j\le-b,\qquad
 \Re(\alpha_j^2)\ge g\quad\hbox{for every }j.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put $\mu_j=1-\lambda_j\ge0$ and $M=\sum_j\mu_j>0$.
The first moment is $\sum_j\mu_j\alpha_j=-q$.
The chord constraints give $\Re(\alpha_j\overline\beta)\ge a$.
Taking the real part after multiplication by $\overline\beta$,
and using $q\le M$, gives
\[
 -q\Re\beta\ge aM,\qquad -\Re\beta\ge aM/q\ge a.
\]
If $x=\Re(\alpha_j\overline\beta)\ge a$ and
$y=-\Re\beta\ge a$, multiplication of these unit complex numbers
gives
\[
 \Re\alpha_j\le-xy+\sqrt{1-x^2}\sqrt{1-y^2}
             \le-a^2+(1-a^2)=-b.
\]
Since $b>0$ and $|\alpha_j|=1$, the square has real part
$2(\Re\alpha_j)^2-1\ge2b^2-1=g$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Parameterized light/heavy cluster]\label{P:thm:r1-cluster}
Let $d=1$, $N=n-1$, $h\ge1$ be an integer, and $A>0$ satisfy
$n>\max(h+1,2A)$.  Suppose $N-h$ designated light masses and $h$
heavy masses obey
\[
 \lambda_j\le A/n\quad\hbox{on the light labels},\qquad
 \lambda_j\le\frac12+\frac1{2h}\quad\hbox{on the heavy labels}.
\]
If all support points have chord distance at most $3/8$ from one
unit center, the first two equations in \eqref{P:eq:r1-moments} are
inconsistent.  A strict gap in the second real equation is
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r1-cluster-gap}
 g\frac{(n-1-h)(n-2A)}{n}>0.
\end{equation}
In particular, for every $n\ge5$, this excludes a clustered hull with
$n-3$ light masses at most $2/n$ and two heavy masses at most $3/4$.
Its gap is $g(n-3)(n-4)/n$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
All masses are at most one and at least one light mass is less than
one, so Lemma~\ref{P:lem:r1-alignment} applies.  A light contribution
to $\Re S_2$ is at most $-g(1-2A/n)$.  A heavy contribution is at
most $1/h$: if $2\lambda_j-1\ge0$, use
$\Re\alpha_j^2\le1$; otherwise the contribution is nonpositive
because $\Re\alpha_j^2\ge g>0$.
It follows that
\[
 \Re S_2\le1-g(n-1-h)(1-2A/n)<1\le T_2(q),
\]
which is the desired contradiction.  All angular and mass faces are
closed; the strictness comes from the positive displayed factors.
The integer multiplier of the second real equation is $1$.
For the two-heavy case, clearing the positive denominator and putting
$n=s+5$ reduces the sign to $s^2+3s+2>0$ for $s\ge0$.
\end{proof}

The result also excludes an all-light cluster with $\lambda_j\le1/2$,
without any $n$-dependent mass cap: the second real summand is then
nonpositive at every label and its target is at least one.

\subsection{A regular-\texorpdfstring{$N$}{N}-gon family for all high-support defects}

We apply Theorem~\ref{P:thm:energy}, including its closed auxiliary
boundary version, to obtain the following explicit family.

\begin{theorem}[Regular-$N$-gon tube]\label{P:thm:r1-regularN}
Let $d=n-N\ge1$, $N>d$, $c>0$, and
$\zeta_j=\eta e^{2\pi i j/N}$, $0\le j<N$, with $|\eta|=1$.
There is no solution of \eqref{P:eq:r1-moments} satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r1-regularN-box}
 |\lambda_j-c|\le\frac1{2N(d+1)},\qquad
 |\alpha_j-\zeta_j|\le
           \frac1{2N(d+1)(1+dc)}.
\end{equation}
The weighted first-$d$-moment energy has a strict certified gap
$d(5d+4)/6$ below its necessary lower bound.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $1\le k\le d<N$, the regular polygon has
$\sum_j\zeta_j^k=0$.  The telescoping factorization of
$\alpha_j^k-\zeta_j^k$ bounds its modulus by
$k|\alpha_j-\zeta_j|$.  Therefore, with
\[
 B=E_\lambda+(1+dc)E_\alpha\le\frac1{d+1},
\]
one has $|S_k|\le kB$ for every $1\le k\le d$.
The exact power-sum identity is
\[
 \sum_{k=1}^{d}(d+1-k)k^2
      =\frac{d(d+1)^2(d+2)}{12}.
\]
Consequently
\[
 2\sum_{k=1}^{d}(d+1-k)|S_k|^2
 \le\frac{B^2d(d+1)^2(d+2)}6
 \le\frac{d(d+2)}6
 <d(d+1),
\]
contradicting Theorem~\ref{P:thm:energy} with $m=d$.
The difference is exactly $d(5d+4)/6>0$.
The mass intervals may be intersected with $\lambda_j\ge1/n$ or any
other valid restriction without changing the proof.
\end{proof}

These are explicit parameterized regions and certificates.  Their
common rotations, choices of deleted vertex, and label permutations
are included in the quantifiers.  The proof uses no finite-degree
search to infer an infinite pattern.  The accompanying audit checks
the rational constants, polynomial identities, and positive cleared
numerators symbolically.  A complete all-degree proof would still need
a covering and exclusion of the complementary regions.
% New regional certificates; no earlier artifact is changed.
% Inclusion fragment, requiring amsmath, amssymb, amsthm, booktabs.
\section{Light-atom harmonic concentration with unrestricted heavy angles}\label{col:P:11}

We work in the one-defect stratum $N=n-1$.  Let $L=n-3$ of the atoms
be designated light and the other two heavy.  Throughout this section,
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r2-mass-hull}
 n\ge8,\qquad
 \frac1n\le\lambda_j\le\frac2n\quad(j\in\mathcal L),
 \qquad
 \frac25\le\lambda_j\le\frac34\quad(j\in\mathcal H),
 \quad |\mathcal L|=L,\quad |\mathcal H|=2.
\end{equation}
All support points have modulus one.  The necessary moment equations
are
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r2-moments}
 S_k=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(k\lambda_j-1)\alpha_j^k
       =T_k(q)e^{ik\phi},\qquad 1\le k\le n,\quad q\ge1.
\end{equation}
The conclusions below exclude only the regions that are stated.  They
do not assert a cover of the complementary one-defect domain.
The heavy angles are unrestricted in every result in this section.

\subsection{An exact rational envelope for low harmonics}

\begin{lemma}[Two auxiliary-free harmonic upper bounds]
\label{P:lem:r2-harmonic-envelope}
Every solution of \eqref{P:eq:r2-mass-hull}--\eqref{P:eq:r2-moments}
satisfies $q<11/10$.  Moreover, for $1\le k\le n$,
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r2-harmonic-upper}
 T_k(q)\le U_k(n):=1+\frac{5k^2}{2n}-\frac{6k^2}{n^2},
 \qquad T_k(q)<T_k(11/10).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The total mass obeys
\[
 t\le\frac{2(n-3)}n+\frac32=\frac72-\frac6n.
\]
Since every mass is at least $1/n$, the $n$th moment gives
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r2-top-moment}
 T_n(q)=|S_n|\le\sum_j(n\lambda_j-1)
       =nt-(n-1)\le\frac{5n}{2}-5.
\end{equation}
For $q=\cosh s$, $s\ge0$, positivity of the power series of $\cosh$
gives, for $1\le k\le n$,
\[
 T_k(q)-1
 =\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\frac{(ks)^{2r}}{(2r)!}
 \le\frac{k^2}{n^2}
       \sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\frac{(ns)^{2r}}{(2r)!}
 =\frac{k^2}{n^2}(T_n(q)-1).
\]
This proves the rational bound in \eqref{P:eq:r2-harmonic-upper}.

For the constant cutoff, the coefficients of $T_n(1+x)$ are
nonnegative.  More explicitly, the Chebyshev differential equation
gives the recurrence
\[
 c_0=1,\qquad
 c_{j+1}=\frac{n^2-j^2}{(j+1)(2j+1)}c_j,
 \qquad T_n(1+x)=\sum_{j=0}^n c_jx^j.
\]
At $x=1/10$, retain the terms through $j=3$ to obtain
\[
 T_n(11/10)\ge
 1+\frac{n^2}{10}+\frac{n^2(n^2-1)}{600}
    +\frac{n^2(n^2-1)(n^2-4)}{90000}.
\]
After subtracting $5n/2-5$ and multiplying by $90000$, the right
side is
\[
 P(n)=n^6+145n^4+8854n^2-225000n+540000.
\]
The complete exact shifted expansion is
\[
 P(8+s)=s^6+48s^5+1105s^4+14880s^3
          +125974s^2+410232s+162720,
\]
which has strictly positive coefficients, including its constant term,
for $s\ge0$.  The accompanying standard-library auditor independently
reconstructs this expansion.
Thus $T_n(11/10)>5n/2-5$ for every $n\ge8$.
Monotonicity of $T_n$ on $[1,\infty)$ and
\eqref{P:eq:r2-top-moment} imply $q<11/10$.  This also implies the
second bound in \eqref{P:eq:r2-harmonic-upper}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A projection certificate with angular outliers}

Define the heavy contribution bounds
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r2-heavy-bound}
 H_1=\frac65,\qquad H_k=\frac{3k}{2}-2\quad(k\ge2).
\end{equation}
They satisfy
\[
 \sum_{j\in\mathcal H}|k\lambda_j-1|\le H_k.
\]
For $k=1$ use $1-\lambda_j\le3/5$.  For $k\ge2$, the endpoint
comparison $3k/4-1\ge1-2k/5$ gives
$|k\lambda_j-1|\le3k/4-1$.

\begin{theorem}[Harmonic concentration with outliers]
\label{P:thm:r2-projection}
Assume \eqref{P:eq:r2-mass-hull}, let $1\le k<n/2$, and let
$0<a\le1$.  Suppose that for some unit complex number $\beta$,
at least $L-r$ light atoms obey
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r2-harmonic-cap}
 \Re(\overline\beta\alpha_j^k)\ge a,
\end{equation}
where the other $r$ light angles are unrestricted.
Put
\[
 D(n,k,a,r)=a(L-r)(1-2k/n)-r(1-k/n).
\]
There can be no solution of \eqref{P:eq:r2-moments} if either
\begin{align}
 D(n,k,a,r)&>H_k+U_k(n),\label{P:eq:r2-project-rational}\\
 \text{or}\qquad
 D(n,k,a,r)&\ge H_k+T_k(11/10).
 \label{P:eq:r2-project-constant}
\end{align}
Every mass face and every angular face in these hypotheses is included.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For a light atom set $\mu_j=1-k\lambda_j$.  Then
\[
 0<1-2k/n\le\mu_j\le1-k/n.
\]
Consequently the projection of the light sum obeys
\[
 \Re\left(\overline\beta
             \sum_{j\in\mathcal L}\mu_j\alpha_j^k\right)
 \ge a(L-r)(1-2k/n)-r(1-k/n)=D(n,k,a,r).
\]
The moment equation also gives
\[
 \sum_{j\in\mathcal L}\mu_j\alpha_j^k
 =\sum_{j\in\mathcal H}(k\lambda_j-1)\alpha_j^k-S_k.
\]
Its modulus is at most $H_k+T_k(q)$.  Apply either bound in
Lemma~\ref{P:lem:r2-harmonic-envelope}.  The strictness in the constant
cutoff permits equality in \eqref{P:eq:r2-project-constant}.
\end{proof}

Condition \eqref{P:eq:r2-harmonic-cap} is a union of $k$ closed arcs.
If $\beta=e^{i\gamma}$, they are centered at
$(\gamma+2\pi j)/k$, $0\le j<k$, and each has angular half-width
$\arccos(a)/k$.  No distribution among the arcs is prescribed, and
no heavy atom is required to lie in any of them.
The proof uses the full weighted light sum and allows the stated
outliers; it does not replace the support by an independent mass measure.
Each exclusion uses the $k$th moment together with the $n$th moment
that supplied the harmonic envelope.  No assertion is made that the
first $k$ moments alone suffice for these exclusions.

\subsection{Explicit low-harmonic families}

For $a=5/8$, the following table records closed excluded families.
The gap is the light projection lower bound minus
$H_k+T_k(11/10)$.  A quarter of the light atoms may be outliers in
the last three rows; the integer requirement is
$r\le\lfloor(n-3)/4\rfloor$.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{cccl}
\toprule
$k$ & Outliers & Index range & Certified gap\\
\midrule
$1$ & $0$ & $n\ge8$ &
 $(25n^2-217n+150)/(40n)$\\
$2$ & $0$ & $n\ge10$ &
 $(125n^2-1359n+1500)/(200n)$\\
$3$ & $0$ & $n\ge16$ &
 $(625n^2-10149n+11250)/(1000n)$\\
$1$ & $\le(n-3)/4$ & $n\ge17$ &
 $(35n^2-583n+330)/(160n)$\\
$2$ & $\le(n-3)/4$ & $n\ge20$ &
 $(175n^2-3561n+3300)/(800n)$\\
$3$ & $\le(n-3)/4$ & $n\ge33$ &
 $(875n^2-28971n+24750)/(4000n)$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Each numerator has strictly positive coefficients after writing
$n=n_0+s$, where $n_0$ is the first index in its row and $s\ge0$.
These are symbolic all-index certificates, not sampled checks.
The cases $k=2,3$ allow genuine two-arc and three-arc configurations.

There is also a two-arc family already at every $n\ge8$: take
$k=2$, no light outliers, and $a=49/50$.  Its gap is
\[
 \frac{49n^2-464n+588}{50n}>0,
\]
whose cleared numerator becomes $49s^2+320s+12$ at $n=8+s$.
Thus the $n=8$ member is nonempty as a parameter region and has exact
gap $3/100$, even with arbitrary heavy angles.

\subsection{The number of allowed arcs may grow with the index}

\begin{corollary}[Growing multi-arc families]
\label{P:cor:r2-growing}
Under \eqref{P:eq:r2-mass-hull}, choose any integer $k$ with
$2\le k\le n/6$.  If all light atoms satisfy
\eqref{P:eq:r2-harmonic-cap} with $a=5/8$, the moment equations are
inconsistent, with a projection gap of at least
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r2-growing-all-gap}
 \frac{7n-18}{72}>0.
\end{equation}
Alternatively, choose $2\le k\le n/12$ and require the cap for only
at least three quarters of the light atoms.  The remaining light
angles and both heavy angles may be arbitrary.  This family is
excluded with gap at least
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r2-growing-outlier-gap}
 \frac{11n+297}{576}>0.
\end{equation}
In the first family necessarily $n\ge12$; in the second necessarily
$n\ge24$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For the first case,
\[
 D(n,k,5/8,0)\ge\frac5{12}(n-3),\qquad
 H_k+U_k(n)\le\frac{23n}{72}-1,
\]
where the negative term $-6k^2/n^2$ was discarded to obtain an upper
bound.  Subtraction gives \eqref{P:eq:r2-growing-all-gap}.

For the second case, $D$ decreases with $r$.  At $r\le L/4$,
\[
 D(n,k,5/8,r)\ge\frac{(n-3)(7n-22k)}{32n}
 \ge\frac{31(n-3)}{192}.
\]
Meanwhile $H_k+U_k(n)\le41n/288-1$.  Their difference is
\eqref{P:eq:r2-growing-outlier-gap}.  Both are strictly positive on
the stated ranges, so Theorem~\ref{P:thm:r2-projection} applies.
\end{proof}

These families remove phases not covered by a single short common arc:
the light atoms may occupy several separated arcs, some light atoms may
be arbitrary, and the heavy atoms may be arbitrarily far from them.
The number of permitted arcs is itself an unbounded integer parameter.
The remaining complement, including sufficiently diffuse light-angle
configurations, still requires additional exclusions.
% Standalone fragment for the general-n stationary reduction.
\section{Cardinal Gram inequalities for simultaneous support nodes}\label{col:P:12}

The hypotheses in this section are those of a positive stationary
coefficient candidate with nonnegative stationary trigonometric polynomial
$h$.  We use the already-proved spectral-factor cardinal identity: the
distinct support points $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_N$ lie on $\mathbb T$,
$N\le n$, and there are polynomials $u_j$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:gram-cardinal-hypothesis}
 \deg u_j\le n-1,\qquad u_j(\alpha_k)=\delta_{jk},\qquad
 \|u_j\|_{H^2}^{2}=\lambda_j>0.
\end{equation}
These conclusions do not follow merely from assigning positive masses
and imposing a selected list of moment equations.  The cardinal norm
identity is an essential hypothesis of every cut below.

\begin{lemma}[A simultaneous Gram cut]\label{P:lem:cardinal-gram-cut}
For a nonempty subset $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$, define
\[
 (G_J)_{jk}=K_n(\alpha_j,\alpha_k),\qquad
 K_n(z,w)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1}(z\overline w)^\ell,
 \qquad j,k\in J.
\]
The matrix $G_J$ is positive definite, and
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:gram-diagonal-and-trace}
 \lambda_j\ge(G_J^{-1})_{jj}\quad(j\in J),\qquad
 \sum_{j\in J}\lambda_j\ge\operatorname{tr}(G_J^{-1}).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The space of polynomials of degree at most $n-1$, with coefficient
$\ell^2$ norm, has reproducing kernel $K_n$.  Evaluation kernels at
distinct points are linearly independent when $|J|\le n$: their first
$|J|$ coefficients form a nonsingular Vandermonde matrix.  Thus their
Gram matrix $G_J$ is positive definite.

For a fixed $j\in J$, the polynomial of least norm with values
$v(\alpha_k)=\delta_{jk}$ for $k\in J$ lies in the span of these
evaluation kernels.  Its coefficient vector in that span is
$G_J^{-1}e_j$, and its squared norm is
$e_j^*G_J^{-1}e_j=(G_J^{-1})_{jj}$.
The difference between $u_j$ and this minimizer vanishes at all points
of $J$, so it is orthogonal to the kernel span.  Pythagoras and
\eqref{P:eq:gram-cardinal-hypothesis} prove the individual bound.
Summing gives the trace bound.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The exact two-node bound and its chord consequence}

For distinct nodes $\alpha_j,\alpha_k$, write
$K_{jk}=K_n(\alpha_j,\alpha_k)$.  The two-node matrix has diagonal
$n$ and determinant $n^2-|K_{jk}|^2>0$.  Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:exact-pair-gram-cut}
 \min(\lambda_j,\lambda_k)
 \ge\frac{n}{n^2-|K_{jk}|^2}.
\end{equation}
This exact oscillatory inequality is stronger than the following useful
angle-independent chord estimate:
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:pair-chord-cut}
 \boxed{\quad
 |\alpha_j-\alpha_k|^2
 \ge\frac{12}{n(n^2-1)\min(\lambda_j,\lambda_k)}.
 \quad}
\end{equation}
Indeed,
\begin{align*}
 n^2-|K_{jk}|^2
 &=\sum_{d=1}^{n-1}(n-d)|\alpha_j^d-\alpha_k^d|^2\\
 &\le |\alpha_j-\alpha_k|^2\sum_{d=1}^{n-1}(n-d)d^2\\
 &=\frac{n^2(n^2-1)}{12}|\alpha_j-\alpha_k|^2.
\end{align*}
The middle inequality follows by factoring
$\alpha_j^d-\alpha_k^d$ into $\alpha_j-\alpha_k$ times a sum of $d$
unit-modulus terms.  Combining this with
\eqref{P:eq:exact-pair-gram-cut} proves \eqref{P:eq:pair-chord-cut}.

In particular, whenever at least one of the two masses is at most $2/n$,
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:light-pair-spacing}
 |\alpha_j-\alpha_k|\ge\sqrt{\frac6{n^2-1}}.
\end{equation}
Only one light mass is needed, because the estimate uses the smaller mass.

\subsection{The new tail gives a strict separation for every surviving pair}

For a competitive stationary candidate, meaning $|a_n|\ge2/e$, the
uniform tail theorem implies
\[
 t=\sum_{j=1}^N\lambda_j<T(n),\qquad
 T(n)=\min\left\{n,\frac{19}{20}(n+10),\frac9{10}(n+31)\right\}.
\]
For any two support indices,
$\min(\lambda_j,\lambda_k)\le(\lambda_j+\lambda_k)/2\le t/2<T(n)/2$.
Thus \eqref{P:eq:pair-chord-cut} improves to the strict universal separation
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:surviving-pair-spacing}
 \boxed{\quad
 |\alpha_j-\alpha_k|>
 \sqrt{\frac{24}{n(n^2-1)T(n)}}.
 \quad}
\end{equation}
The factor $24$ uses the bound on the smaller mass by half the total;
using only $\lambda_j<t$ would lose a factor of two in the squared estimate.

\subsection{The three-node determinant and trace cuts}

For three distinct support points, put
\[
 s=|K_{12}|^2+|K_{23}|^2+|K_{31}|^2.
\]
The positive determinant of their Gram matrix is
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:triple-gram-determinant}
 \Delta=n^3-ns+2\Re(K_{12}K_{23}K_{31})>0.
\end{equation}
The cofactor formula gives
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:triple-gram-cuts}
 \lambda_1\ge\frac{n^2-|K_{23}|^2}{\Delta},\qquad
 \lambda_2\ge\frac{n^2-|K_{31}|^2}{\Delta},\qquad
 \lambda_3\ge\frac{n^2-|K_{12}|^2}{\Delta},
\end{equation}
and, in particular,
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:triple-gram-trace}
 \lambda_1+\lambda_2+\lambda_3
 \ge\frac{3n^2-s}{\Delta}.
\end{equation}
Unlike the pair conditions, this retains the phase of the cyclic kernel
product and measures simultaneous interpolation at all three nodes.

\subsection{An exact example separating pair and triple conditions}

The following is only a Gram-feasibility example.  It is not claimed to
satisfy the stationary moment system or to define a coefficient extremizer.
Take $n=3$, nodes $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)=(1,i,-i)$, and assigned
masses $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=\lambda_3=2/5$.
Then
\[
 G=\begin{pmatrix}
 3&-i&i\\ i&3&1\\ -i&1&3
 \end{pmatrix},\qquad
 G^{-1}=\frac14\begin{pmatrix}
 2&i&-i\\ -i&2&-1\\ i&-1&2
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Every off-diagonal kernel has modulus $1$.  Consequently every exact
pair bound is satisfied, since
\[
 \frac{3}{3^2-1}=\frac38\le\frac25.
\]
The chord bounds also hold: the three squared distances are $2,2,4$,
whereas their common required lower bound is $5/4$.
The separate mass bounds $\lambda_j\ge1/3$ and
$t=6/5\ge n/N=1$ hold as well.

Nevertheless $s=3$, the cyclic product is $-1$, and $\Delta=16$.
The triple trace condition requires
\[
 \lambda_1+\lambda_2+\lambda_3\ge\frac{27-3}{16}=\frac32,
\]
which fails because the assigned total is $6/5$.
Each triple diagonal condition likewise requires $\lambda_j\ge1/2$.
Thus the simultaneous Gram constraints exclude data that pass all exact
pair constraints and these basic mass constraints.  The failed triple
condition prevents these assigned masses from being stationary cardinal
norms; the example makes no assertion about an actual stationary candidate.
\subsection{Conditioning on the auxiliary roots determines the masses}

The simultaneous cuts can retain the non-support roots of the spectral
factor as well.  Write
\[
 Q(z)=cA(z)\prod_{j=1}^N(z-\alpha_j),\qquad
 \deg A=d=n-N,\quad c\ne0,
\]
where $A$ has no unit-circle zeros.  Multiplicities among its roots
are allowed.  Every stationary cardinal polynomial $u_j$ belongs to
\[
 \mathcal V_A=\{A(z)p(z):\deg p\le N-1\},
 \qquad \dim\mathcal V_A=N.
\]
Let $B$ be the $n$-by-$N$ matrix that maps the coefficient vector of
$p$ to that of $Ap$, and set
\[
 H_A=B^*B,\qquad
 E_{jr}=A(\alpha_j)\alpha_j^r\quad
 (1\le j\le N,\ 0\le r\le N-1).
\]
Multiplication by the nonzero polynomial $A$ is injective, so $H_A$
is positive definite.  The matrix $E$ is a nonzero diagonal matrix
times a Vandermonde matrix, so it is invertible.  The cardinal values
uniquely determine the coefficient vector $E^{-1}e_j$ of $p_j=u_j/A$.
Consequently the masses obey the exact equalities
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:conditioned-mass-equality}
 \boxed{\quad
 \lambda_j=(E^{-*}H_AE^{-1})_{jj}=(G_A^{-1})_{jj},
 \qquad t=\operatorname{tr}(G_A^{-1}),\qquad
 G_A=EH_A^{-1}E^*.
 \quad}
\end{equation}
Here $G_A$ is the evaluation-kernel matrix of the subspace
$\mathcal V_A$ with the inherited coefficient norm.  Orthogonal
projection of the full evaluation kernels onto this subspace proves
$0<G_A\le G$ as Hermitian matrices.  Thus its inverse is at least
$G^{-1}$, strengthening the unconditioned individual and trace bounds.
For a proper subset of the support, least-norm interpolation in
$\mathcal V_A$ gives the corresponding inequalities using the
principal submatrix of $G_A$.

Equation~\eqref{P:eq:conditioned-mass-equality} is a necessary reduction:
once the support and auxiliary polynomial are specified, the masses
are determined.  It does not assert that arbitrary choices of that
geometry satisfy the other stationary equations or attain the target
coefficient.  In particular it supplies no unproved covering claim for
the remaining geometry.

% Chebyshev interpolation, weighted mass cuts, and the consequences below
% are derived here, rather than attributed as statements already in [149].

\section{Chebyshev interpolation and quantitative cardinal Gram exclusions}\label{col:P:13}
\label{P:sec:r3-analytic-clusters}

The finite Taylor spectral argument in corpus manuscript~\cite{P:Corpus149} motivates the transfer; the Chebyshev and divided-difference consequences below are derived here.

Throughout this section, $n$ is the coefficient index.  A candidate has
$N\le n$ distinct support points $\alpha_j$ on the unit circle and positive
masses $\lambda_j$.  We use the previously proved cardinal Gram condition:
for every subset $J$ of $s\le n$ points,
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-analytic-cardinal-input}
 G_J=\left(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\alpha_i^k\overline{\alpha_j}^{\,k}
       \right)_{i,j\in J},\qquad
 \lambda_j\ge(G_J^{-1})_{jj}\quad(j\in J).
\end{equation}
Distinct points make this Gram matrix positive definite.  The coefficient
tail theorem separately gives $t:=\sum_j\lambda_j<T(n)\le n$ for a
competitive candidate.  The local Gram inequalities below do not require
this last bound; the global exclusions invoke it explicitly.
No assertion here concerns arbitrary positive atomic functions without
the cardinal Gram hypothesis.

Set
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-centered-K}
 \omega_k=k-\frac{n-1}{2},\qquad
 K_{n,r}=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}|\omega_k|^{2r}\quad(r\ge1).
\end{equation}
For chosen real arguments $\alpha_j=e^{i\theta_j}$, the matrix
$V_{kj}=e^{-ik\theta_j}$ has Gram matrix $G_J$.
Multiplying column $j$ by $e^{i(n-1)\theta_j/2}$ changes its entries to
$e^{-i\omega_k\theta_j}$ and changes its Gram matrix by diagonal-unitary
conjugation.  Inverse diagonal entries are therefore unchanged.  In even
degree the half-integer frequencies use the chosen real arguments only;
no single-valued fractional power on the whole circle is assumed.

\subsection{A weighted cluster certificate}

\begin{theorem}[Chebyshev rank certificate]\label{P:thm:r3-chebyshev-gram}
Suppose $s$ support points in $J$ lie in an arc of half-width $\rho>0$.
For every integer $1\le r<s$,
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-rootmass}
 \left(\sum_{j\in J}\sqrt{\lambda_j}\right)^2
 >\frac{(s-r)^2\,4^{r-1}(r!)^2}{K_{n,r}\rho^{2r}}.
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-chebyshev-mass}
 \sum_{j\in J}\lambda_j
 >\frac{(s-r)^2\,4^{r-1}(r!)^2}
         {sK_{n,r}\rho^{2r}}.
\end{equation}
If only upper bounds $\lambda_j\le U_j$ are known, the necessary condition is
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-mass-box}
 K_{n,r}\rho^{2r}\left(\sum_{j\in J}\sqrt{U_j}\right)^2
 >(s-r)^2\,4^{r-1}(r!)^2.
\end{equation}
Failure of any one of these strict necessary inequalities excludes the
entire closed parameter region on which its opposite weak inequality is
certified.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Choose arguments with $\theta_j=\theta_0+\delta_j$ and
$|\delta_j|\le\rho$.  Interpolate each scalar function
$\delta\mapsto e^{-i\omega_k\delta}$ at the $r$ roots
$\xi_l=\rho\cos((2l-1)\pi/(2r))$ of $T_r(\delta/\rho)$.
The vector interpolant has rank at most $r$ as a matrix whose columns are
evaluated at the $\delta_j$.  Its scalar error is bounded by
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-interpolation-error}
 \frac{|\omega_k|^r}{r!}\left|\prod_{l=1}^r(\delta-\xi_l)\right|
 \le\frac{|\omega_k|^r\rho^r}{2^{r-1}r!}.
\end{equation}
This estimate holds for complex-valued exponentials: the
Hermite--Genocchi formula represents their order-$r$ divided difference
as the integral of the $r$th derivative over a simplex of volume $1/r!$.
Taking absolute values gives the first bound, and the monic Chebyshev
identity gives the second.  The derivative formula also handles repeated
nodes by continuity.  For $\omega_k\ne0$ and an evaluation point distinct
from the interpolation nodes, the first bound is strict: the phase in
that simplex integral is not constant on a set of full measure.

Let $a_j>0$ be arbitrary and divide column $j$ of the centered matrix and
its interpolant by $\sqrt{a_j}$.  The squared Frobenius error is strictly
less than
\[
 E^2=\frac{K_{n,r}\rho^{2r}}{4^{r-1}(r!)^2}
                  \sum_{j\in J}a_j^{-1}.
\]
Strictness holds because $s>r$ distinct points cannot all be interpolation
nodes, and at least one frequency is nonzero.
Write $D=\operatorname{diag}(a_j)$.  The scaled Gram matrix is a
diagonal-unitary conjugate of $D^{-1/2}G_JD^{-1/2}$.
If its positive eigenvalues are $\mu_1\ge\cdots\ge\mu_s$, the best-rank-$r$
approximation inequality gives $\sum_{i>r}\mu_i<E^2$.
Consequently
\[
 \sum_j a_j\lambda_j
 \ge\operatorname{tr}(DG_J^{-1})
 =\sum_i\mu_i^{-1}
 \ge\frac{(s-r)^2}{\sum_{i>r}\mu_i}
 >\frac{(s-r)^2}{E^2}.
\]
Taking $a_j=\lambda_j^{-1/2}$ proves \eqref{P:eq:r3-rootmass}.
Cauchy--Schwarz gives \eqref{P:eq:r3-chebyshev-mass}; alternatively take
all $a_j=1$.  Monotonicity in the upper mass bounds proves
\eqref{P:eq:r3-mass-box}.
\end{proof}

For a known cluster mass upper bound $M$, a useful explicit exclusion
radius is
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-radius-optimization}
 \rho\le
 \max_{1\le r<s}
 \left(\frac{(s-r)^2 4^{r-1}(r!)^2}{sM K_{n,r}}\right)^{1/(2r)}.
\end{equation}
One need not evaluate a root numerically: for each integer $r$, compare
$sM K_{n,r}\rho^{2r}$ with the exact numerator.
If a whole-candidate box gives $t\le\tau$ and every outside mass is
greater than $1/n$, then
$\sum_{j\in J}\lambda_j<\tau-(N-s)/n$.
This bound can be combined with $\sum_{j\in J}U_j$ by taking the smaller
available upper bound.

There is also a useful explicit light/heavy budget.  Suppose $q=s-h$
of the selected masses are at most $L$, the remaining $h\ge1$ are
unrestricted individually, and their total is at most $M$, where
$L\le M/s$.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-waterfill}
 \sum_{j\in J}\sqrt{\lambda_j}
 \le q\sqrt L+\sqrt{h(M-qL)}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, for light total $x\le qL$, Cauchy--Schwarz bounds the two groups
by $\sqrt{qx}+\sqrt{h(M-x)}$; this is increasing up to $x=qM/s$.
Substitution into \eqref{P:eq:r3-rootmass} supplies a mass-pattern-dependent
exclusion without assigning any extra phases or auxiliary roots.

\subsection{An all-index bound at every eligible arc scale}

The frequencies in \eqref{P:eq:r3-centered-K} are the midpoints of the $n$
unit intervals partitioning $[-n/2,n/2]$.  Strict convexity therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-midpoint-K}
 K_{n,r}<\int_{-n/2}^{n/2}|x|^{2r}\,dx
       =\frac{n^{2r+1}}{4^r(2r+1)}.
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform arc occupancy]\label{P:thm:r3-uniform-occupancy}
Let $n\ge8$ and let a competitive stationary candidate satisfy
\eqref{P:eq:r3-analytic-cardinal-input} and $t<T(n)\le n$.
For every integer
\[
 \left\lceil2\log_2 n\right\rceil\le r\le N-1,
\]
an arc of full angular width $2r/n$ contains at most $r$ support points.
The assertion holds for every support deficiency $d=n-N$ and every
positive mass pattern.  When $N\le\lceil2\log_2n\rceil$ the indicated
range is empty; no support stratum is excluded on that account.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $s=r+1$ points lie in such an arc and put $\rho=r/n$.
We record the factorial constant explicitly.  Since $\log x$ increases,
\[
 \log(r!)\ge\int_1^r\log x\,dx=r\log r-r+1,
 \qquad r!\ge e(r/e)^r>2(r/\sqrt8)^r.
\]
The last strict inequality uses $2<e<11/4<\sqrt8$.  For a rational
verification of the upper estimate, the exponential series gives
\[
 e<\frac{65}{24}+\frac1{100}=\frac{1631}{600}<\frac{11}{4},
\]
where the terms starting with $1/5!$ are bounded by a geometric series
with ratio $1/6$; $(11/4)^2=121/16<8$.
Combining \eqref{P:eq:r3-chebyshev-mass} and
\eqref{P:eq:r3-midpoint-K} now gives
\[
 \sum_{j\in J}\lambda_j
 >\frac{(2r+1)2^r}{(r+1)n}
 \ge\frac{2r+1}{r+1}\,n>n,
\]
because $r\ge2\log_2 n$.  This contradicts $t<n$.

For completeness, the smallest permitted subset size is compatible with
deficient support whenever the theorem is nonvacuous.  At $n=8$ it is
$\lceil2\log_2 8\rceil+1=7=n-1$.
For real $x\ge9$, $x-2\log_2x-2$ is positive: it is positive at $9$
because $9^2<2^7$, and its derivative is
$1-2/(x\log2)>1-4/x>0$.
Thus $\lceil2\log_2 n\rceil+1\le n-1$ for all integers $n\ge8$.
\end{proof}

In particular the preceding $\lceil3\log_2n\rceil$ scale remains a valid
choice whenever it is at most $N-1$; the theorem supplies additional
smaller scales rather than deleting the larger-scale constraints.
If a union of arcs covers the support and arc $a$ has width at most
$2r_a/n$, with each $r_a$ in the applicable range, then
$N\le\sum_a r_a$.  Overlap cannot invalidate this upper bound.

More generally, disjoint selected clusters $J_a$ consume additive mass
budgets.  For any choices $1\le r_a<|J_a|$,
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-additive-clusters}
 t>\sum_a
 \frac{(|J_a|-r_a)^2 4^{r_a-1}(r_a!)^2}
 {|J_a|K_{n,r_a}\rho_a^{2r_a}}.
\end{equation}
If this lower bound reaches an available total-mass upper bound, the
whole multi-arc configuration is excluded.  Each atom must be counted
only once in this mass-budget statement.

\subsection{Individual masses from angular divided differences}

\begin{theorem}[Individual divided-difference cut]\label{P:thm:r3-individual-dd}
Let $s=r+1$ selected support points have distinct chosen real arguments
$\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_s$.  For each $j$,
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-individual-dd}
 \lambda_j>
 \frac{(r!)^2}
 {K_{n,r}\prod_{i\ne j}|\theta_j-\theta_i|^2}.
\end{equation}
The weak version remains available if strictness is not needed.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put $b_j=\prod_{i\ne j}(\theta_j-\theta_i)^{-1}$ and let $\widetilde G$
be the centered-frequency Gram matrix.  The standard dual norm inequality
gives
\[
 (\widetilde G^{-1})_{jj}\ge\frac{|b_j|^2}{b^*\widetilde G b}.
\]
Its denominator is
\[
 b^*\widetilde G b
 =\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}
       \left|\sum_{j=1}^s b_je^{-i\omega_k\theta_j}\right|^2.
\]
The inner sum is the order-$r$ divided difference of
$e^{-i\omega_k\theta}$, and has modulus at most $|\omega_k|^r/r!$.
For every nonzero frequency the inequality is strict, since the
Hermite--Genocchi simplex phase varies continuously over a nondegenerate
interval when the arguments are distinct.  Hence the denominator is
strictly less than $K_{n,r}/(r!)^2$.
Apply \eqref{P:eq:r3-analytic-cardinal-input} and diagonal-unitary invariance to
obtain \eqref{P:eq:r3-individual-dd}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A light middle point]\label{P:cor:r3-middle-light}
Suppose three points occur in the order
$\theta_1<\theta_2<\theta_3$ in an arc of full width at most $2\rho$.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-middle-light}
 \lambda_2>
 \frac{4}{K_{n,2}\rho^4},\qquad
 K_{n,2}=\frac{n(n^2-1)(3n^2-7)}{240}<\frac{n^5}{80}.
\end{equation}
In particular, for every $n\ge3$, if $c,R>0$ satisfy $cR^4\le5120$,
the simultaneous conditions
\[
 \lambda_2\le\frac cn,
 \qquad \theta_3-\theta_1\le\frac Rn
\]
are impossible.  Two simple rational choices are
\[
 (c,R)=(5/4,8),\qquad (c,R)=(2,7).
\]
The two endpoint masses and all other support points are unrestricted.
The statement is about the middle point in angular order, not an
arbitrary light endpoint of a triple.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Let $a=\theta_2-\theta_1$ and $b=\theta_3-\theta_2$.
Then $ab\le((a+b)/2)^2\le\rho^2$.
The $r=2$ case of \eqref{P:eq:r3-individual-dd} proves the first bound.
Taking $\rho=R/(2n)$ and using \eqref{P:eq:r3-midpoint-K} gives
$\lambda_2>5120/(R^4n)\ge c/n$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Explicit three-, four-, and five-point mass budgets}

The central power sums needed below are
\begin{align}
 K_{n,1}&=\frac{n(n^2-1)}{12},\nonumber\\
 K_{n,2}&=\frac{n(n^2-1)(3n^2-7)}{240},\nonumber\\
 K_{n,3}&=\frac{n(n^2-1)(3n^4-18n^2+31)}{1344},\nonumber\\
 K_{n,4}&=\frac{n(n^2-1)(5n^6-55n^4+239n^2-381)}{11520}.
 \label{P:eq:r3-small-K}
\end{align}

\begin{proposition}[Small clusters]\label{P:prop:r3-small-clusters}
Let $s\in\{3,4,5\}$ points lie in an arc of half-width $\rho>0$, and
write $M_J=\sum_{j\in J}\lambda_j$.  Then
\begin{align}
 s=3:&\quad M_J>\frac{6}{K_{n,2}\rho^4},\label{P:eq:r3-three-mass}\\
 s=4:&\quad M_J>
 \frac{9(71+17\sqrt{17})}{8K_{n,3}\rho^6}
 >\frac{1269}{8K_{n,3}\rho^6},\label{P:eq:r3-four-mass}\\
 s=5:&\quad M_J>\frac{576C_5}{K_{n,4}\rho^8}
 >\frac{7992}{K_{n,4}\rho^8}.\label{P:eq:r3-five-mass}
\end{align}
Here $y_5$ is the unique root in $(0,1)$ of
$3y^3-6y^2+8y-3=0$, and
\[
 C_5=\frac{3y_5^2-4y_5+3}{2y_5^2(1-y_5)^2}>\frac{111}{8}.
\]
These constants optimize the barycentric squared-weight minimization
used in this proof.  No optimality claim is made for the actual Gram
inverse over all configurations.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Put $r=s-1$.  Summing \eqref{P:eq:r3-individual-dd} reduces the problem to
minimizing
\[
 F_s(x_1,\ldots,x_s)=
 \sum_j\prod_{i\ne j}|x_j-x_i|^{-2}
\]
over distinct ordered points in $[-1,1]$.  Expansion of the span decreases
$F_s$, so its minimum has $x_1=-1$ and $x_s=1$.
Write the remaining coordinates as cumulative positive gaps with total
two.  For each summand, its logarithm is a sum of negative logarithms of
positive linear gap sums, hence is convex.  Exponentiation preserves
convexity here.  Reflection of the gaps preserves $F_s$, so averaging a
gap vector with its reflection cannot increase $F_s$ and gives a
symmetric configuration.  Boundary collisions make $F_s$ diverge, so a
minimum exists in the interior of the gap simplex.

For $s=3$ the symmetric nodes are $-1,0,1$, giving $C_3=3/2$.
For $s=4$ they are $-1,-\sqrt y,\sqrt y,1$, and
\[
 F_4(y)=\frac{1+y}{2y(1-y)^2},\qquad
 F_4'(y)=\frac{2y^2+3y-1}{2y^2(1-y)^3}.
\]
Its unique minimum is at $y=(\sqrt{17}-3)/4$, with value
$C_4=(71+17\sqrt{17})/32>141/32$.
The final strict inequality follows from $17^3=4913>4900=70^2$.

For $s=5$ the symmetric nodes are
$-1,-\sqrt y,0,\sqrt y,1$, and
\[
 F_5(y)=\frac{3y^2-4y+3}{2y^2(1-y)^2},\qquad
 F_5'(y)=\frac{3y^3-6y^2+8y-3}{y^3(1-y)^3}.
\]
The derivative numerator is strictly increasing, since its derivative is
$9(y-2/3)^2+4$, and changes sign between zero and one.  This proves the
claimed unique minimizer and expression for $C_5$.

Here is a rational proof of the convenient lower bound $C_5>111/8$.
The numerator of $F_5(y)-111/8$, with positive denominator
$8y^2(1-y)^2$, is
\[
 P(y)=12-16y-99y^2+222y^3-111y^4.
\]
Writing $x=y-1/2$ gives
$P=-111x^4+(135/2)x^2-4x+1/16$.
For $|x|\le1/10$ this is at least
$(6639/100)x^2-4x+1/16$, whose discriminant is $-239/400<0$.
For $1/10\le|x|\le1/2$ it is at least
$Q=(159/4)x^2-4x+1/16$.
For $x\le0$ this is positive.  For $x\ge1/10$ it increases and
$Q(1/10)=3/50>0$.  Thus $P>0$ throughout $[0,1]$.
Finally multiply $C_s$ by $(r!)^2/(K_{n,r}\rho^{2r})$.
\end{proof}

For example, if a cluster has mass at most $A/n$ and full arc width at
most $R/n$, the following entirely rational parameter regions are excluded:
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-small-normalized}
 \begin{array}{c|c}
 s&\hbox{sufficient condition for exclusion}\\ \hline
 3&A R^4\le7680\\
 4&A R^6\le4548096\\
 5&A R^8\le4713873408.
 \end{array}
\end{equation}
These follow from \eqref{P:eq:r3-midpoint-K} and the rational lower bounds
above.  They are sufficient regions, not a complete classification.

\subsection{Scope, comparison, and verification}

The midpoint and Chebyshev improvements are analytic inequalities valid
at every indicated degree.  Their role is to make previously implicit
full-Gram constraints into explicit exclusions with small descriptions.
They do not add an independent assumption to the full Gram system.
The light-middle condition with $(c,R)=(5/4,8)$ is a particularly simple
corollary; no claim is made that every listed constant improves every
available exact pair cut.  The $(2,7)$ middle certificate does detect
local configurations that pass all exact pair cuts.  One verified
example has $n=8$, arguments $-7/16,0,7/16$, and the three masses $1/4$:
the pair Gram inequalities hold, while the middle certificate fails.
This is a comparison of local relaxations, not a proposed full critical
candidate satisfying all moment equations.

The standard-library checker \texttt{analytic\_cluster\_audit.py}
verifies the four central-power formulas by exact polynomial recurrence
identities in both parities; the derivative identities and rational
constant certificates; the exponential bound; the normalized family
constants; and the local pair-versus-triple example using rational sine
enclosures.  Infinite validity follows from the proofs above, not from
testing finitely many $n$ or finitely many configurations.  The remaining
general Krzyz domain includes diffuse configurations, other mass budgets,
and the unsolved full stationary moment compatibility problem.

\section{Regular support polygons without a mass-equality hypothesis}\label{col:P:14}
\label{P:sec:r3-regular-free-masses}

This section treats one auxiliary root, so $N=n-1$ and
\[
 S_k=\sum_{j=1}^{N}(k\lambda_j-1)\alpha_j^k
     =T_k(q)e^{ik\phi},\qquad 1\le k\le n,
 \quad q\ge1,\quad \lambda_j>0.
\]
Here $T_k$ is the Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind; it is
unrelated to the total-mass cutoff $T(n)$.  Unlike the earlier
regular-support tube, the result below imposes no closeness of the
individual masses to a common value.

\begin{lemma}[A uniform three-index convexity gap]
\label{P:lem:r3-cheb-convex-gap}
For $n\ge4$ and $q\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-cheb-convex-gap}
 \frac{2q}{n-1}
 +\frac{n-3}{n(n-1)}T_n(q)
 -\frac{T_{n-2}(q)}{n-2}
 \ge \delta_n:=\frac{2(n-3)}{n(n-2)}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $q=\cosh u$, $u\ge0$, and put $f_u(x)=\cosh(ux)/x$ for
$x>0$.  The series
\[
 f_u(x)-\frac1x
 =\frac{u^2x}{2}+\sum_{j=2}^{\infty}
       \frac{u^{2j}x^{2j-1}}{(2j)!}
\]
is a locally uniform sum of a linear function and convex functions.
It is convex.  Apply Jensen's inequality to the indices $1,n$, with
weights $2/(n-1)$ and $(n-3)/(n-1)$, whose weighted mean is $n-2$.
The same Jensen difference for $1/x$ is
\[
 \frac2{n-1}+\frac{n-3}{n(n-1)}-\frac1{n-2}
 =\frac3n-\frac1{n-2}=\delta_n.
\]
Since $f_u(k)=T_k(q)/k$, this proves the claim, including $u=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[A regular-support tube with arbitrary positive masses]
\label{P:thm:r3-regular-free-masses}
Let $n\ge4$, $N=n-1$, and let the positive masses have total
$t=\sum_j\lambda_j$.  Suppose the one-root moment equations above
hold and the support can be bijectively matched to a rotated regular
$N$-gon $(\zeta_j)$ with
\[
 \max_j|\alpha_j-\zeta_j|\le\epsilon.
\]
Then necessarily
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-regular-error-budget}
 \delta_n\le C_n(t)\epsilon,
 \qquad
 C_n(t)=2(n-2)t+\frac{2(n-1)(2n-3)}{n}.
\end{equation}
Consequently:
\begin{enumerate}
\item if $t<n$, the closed tube $\epsilon\le1/(2n^3)$ is excluded;
\item if $t\le7/2$, the larger closed tube $\epsilon\le1/(6n^2)$
      is excluded;
\item more generally, if $t<\tau$, every closed tube with
      $\epsilon\le\delta_n/C_n(\tau)$ is excluded.
\end{enumerate}
These assertions allow arbitrary auxiliary phase and all $q\ge1$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A common rotation permits $\zeta_j^N=1$.  Define
\[
 p_k=\sum_j\alpha_j^k,\qquad
 m_k=\sum_j\lambda_j\alpha_j^k.
\]
The regular polygon has first power sum zero, so
$|p_1|\le N\epsilon$.  Factoring the difference of powers gives
$|\alpha_j^N-1|\le N\epsilon$.  Since $n=N+1$,
\[
 |m_n-m_1|\le Nt\epsilon,\qquad
 |p_n-p_1|\le N^2\epsilon.
\]
It follows that
\[
 \begin{split}
 |S_n-nS_1|
 &=|n(m_n-m_1)+Np_1-(p_n-p_1)|\\
 &\le E_n:=N(nt+2N)\epsilon.
 \end{split}
\]
The identity
$\alpha_j^{N-1}-\overline{\alpha_j}
 =\overline{\alpha_j}(\alpha_j^N-1)$ similarly gives
\[
 |m_{n-2}-\overline{m_1}|\le Nt\epsilon,\qquad
 |p_{n-2}-\overline{p_1}|\le N^2\epsilon,
\]
and therefore
\[
 |S_{n-2}-(n-2)\overline{S_1}|
 \le E_-:=N(n-2)(t+2)\epsilon.
\]
Taking absolute values and using the reverse triangle inequality,
\[
 |T_n(q)-nq|\le E_n,\qquad
 |T_{n-2}(q)-(n-2)q|\le E_-.
\]
Substitution into Lemma~\ref{P:lem:r3-cheb-convex-gap} yields
\[
 \delta_n
 \le\frac{n-3}{n(n-1)}E_n+\frac{E_-}{n-2}
 = C_n(t)\epsilon.
\]
This proves the error budget and its general-$\tau$ consequence.

For the first explicit tube,
$C_n(t)<C_n(n)=2n^2-10+6/n<2n^2$, while
$\delta_n\ge1/n$ for $n\ge4$.  Thus
$\epsilon\le1/(2n^3)$ contradicts the error budget, even at its
closed boundary.
For the second tube,
\[
 6n^2\delta_n-C_n(7/2)
 =n+12-\frac{24}{n-2}-\frac6n>0.
\]
After multiplication by $n(n-2)$ and substitution $n=v+4$, the
numerator is $v^3+22v^2+74v+20$, strictly positive for $v\ge0$.
Hence $\epsilon\le1/(6n^2)$ also contradicts the error budget.
\end{proof}

In the two-heavy hull, $n-3$ light masses at most $2/n$ and two
other masses at most $3/4$ imply
$t\le7/2-6/n<7/2$.  The second tube therefore applies without
requiring the individual masses to approach a common value.

\subsection{A coefficient-energy exclusion with arbitrary masses}

For completeness we include the quantitative root-matching lemma used
in corpus manuscript~\cite{P:Corpus059}, S10.  Only this elementary
lemma is used, not its special rank-two permanent identity.

\begin{lemma}[Root matching from coefficient energy]
\label{P:lem:r3-root-matching}
Let $p(z)=z^M+c_0+\sum_{k=1}^{M-1}c_kz^k$, $M\ge2$, have all
roots on the unit circle.  Put
\[
 \eta=\sqrt{(M-1)\sum_{k=1}^{M-1}|c_k|^2}.
\]
If $\eta\le1/(8M)$, the roots can be bijectively matched to a
rotated regular $M$-gon with chord error at most $4\eta/M$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The case $\eta=0$ is immediate.  The constant coefficient satisfies
$|c_0|=1$.  Let $q_0(z)=z^M+c_0$, whose roots $\zeta_i$ have mutual
distances at least $4/M$, and put
$\rho=4\eta/M\le1/(2M^2)$.  On $|z-\zeta_i|=\rho$,
\[
 |q_0(z)|
 \ge M\rho\prod_{j\ne i}
          \left(1-\frac\rho{|\zeta_i-\zeta_j|}\right)
 \ge M\rho(1-M^2\rho/4)
 \ge\frac78M\rho=\frac72\eta.
\]
Meanwhile Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 |p(z)-q_0(z)|
 \le\eta(1+\rho)^{M-1}
 \le\eta e^{M\rho}<2\eta.
\]
The disks are disjoint, and Rouche's theorem places one root of $p$
in each disk.  This proves the matching.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A necessary support-energy floor]
\label{P:cor:r3-support-energy-floor}
Let $n\ge4$, $N=n-1$, and suppose the one-root moment equations
hold for positive masses with $t<n$.  Write
\[
 B(z)=\prod_{j=1}^{N}(z-\alpha_j)
 =z^N+b_0+\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}b_kz^k,
 \qquad E_B=\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}|b_k|^2.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-support-energy-floor}
 \boxed{\quad
 E_B>\frac{(n-1)^2}{64n^6(n-2)}.
 \quad}
\end{equation}
If also $t\le7/2$, the stronger necessary bound is
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-support-energy-floor-hull}
 \boxed{\quad
 E_B>\frac{(n-1)^2}{576n^4(n-2)}.
 \quad}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
If the first strict inequality fails, then
$\eta=\sqrt{(N-1)E_B}\le N/(8n^3)\le1/(8N)$.
Lemma~\ref{P:lem:r3-root-matching} gives chord error
$4\eta/N\le1/(2n^3)$, contradicting
Theorem~\ref{P:thm:r3-regular-free-masses}.
The second follows in the same way from
$\eta\le N/(24n^2)\le1/(8N)$, which gives error at most
$1/(6n^2)$.  No comparison between distinct individual masses is
used in either argument.
\end{proof}

The energy floor is a rotation- and permutation-invariant exclusion.
It extends the earlier use of coefficient energy, which additionally
required the masses to be nearly equal.  It does not upper-bound the
energy on the complementary candidate domain.

% New round-3 results.  This fragment does not edit an earlier publication.
% The proof is self-contained given the explicitly stated moment/mass premises.
% VMRC [193] motivates the last nonnegative-deficit step; the inequalities
% below are newly derived here, not claims quoted from that manuscript.

\section{A deleted-polygon tube with unrestricted mass distribution}\label{col:P:15}

The former deleted-polygon exclusions required the masses to be close
to a common value.  The following exclusion needs no such condition.
It uses the first two moments together with their complementary
moments and the top moment.

\begin{theorem}[An angle-only deleted-polygon exclusion]
\label{P:thm:arbitrary-mass-deleted-tube}
Let $n\ge5$ be an integer, let $N=n-1$, and suppose that
\[
 \alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_N\in\mathbb T,\qquad
 \lambda_j\ge\frac1n,\qquad
 \frac n{n-1}\le t:=\sum_j\lambda_j<n.
\]
Let $q\ge1$ and $z\in\mathbb T$.  Assume the complete one-defect
moment equations
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:round3-one-defect-moments}
 S_k:=\sum_{j=1}^N(k\lambda_j-1)\alpha_j^k
       =T_k(q)z^k,\qquad 1\le k\le n,
\end{equation}
where $T_k(\cosh s)=\cosh(ks)$.
There is no rotation of a regular $n$-gon, with one vertex omitted,
that admits a bijective matching $j\mapsto\zeta_j$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:round3-angle-only-radius}
 \boxed{\quad |\alpha_j-\zeta_j|\le\rho_{\mathrm{del}}(n):=\frac1{1000n^2}
          \quad(1\le j\le n-1).\quad}
\end{equation}
The boundary of this tube is included.  The conclusion also includes
the closed auxiliary boundary $q=1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose such a matching exists.  A common rotation allows the omitted
reference vertex to be $1$, so $\zeta_j$ are exactly the other $n$th
roots of unity.  The same rotation replaces $z$ in
\eqref{P:eq:round3-one-defect-moments}, preserving all equations.
Write $\delta=\rho_{\mathrm{del}}(n)$ and
\[
 p_k=\sum_j\alpha_j^k,\qquad m_k=\sum_j\lambda_j\alpha_j^k,
 \qquad W=nt-N,\qquad u=z^n.
\]
The mass bounds give
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:round3-W-bounds}
 2<W<n^2-n+1,\qquad n\delta\le\frac1{5000}<\frac1{10}.
\end{equation}
For $1\le k<n$, factoring differences of powers gives
\[
 |p_k+1|\le Nk\delta,\qquad
 |m_{n-k}-\overline{m_k}|
 =\left|\sum_j\lambda_j\overline{\alpha_j}^k
                     (\alpha_j^n-1)\right|
 \le nt\delta.
\]
Since $S_k=km_k-p_k$, these inequalities yield
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:round3-complement-residual}
 \left|kS_{n-k}-(n-k)\overline{S_k}-(2k-n)\right|
 \le k(n-k)(nt+2N)\delta.
\end{equation}

The top moment is especially well conditioned because
$w_j=n\lambda_j-1\ge0$.  Its comparison with the reference top
moment gives
\[
 |T_n(q)u-W|
 =\left|\sum_jw_j(\alpha_j^n-1)\right|\le Wn\delta,
 \qquad T_n(q)\le\sum_jw_j=W.
\]
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:round3-top-phase}
 W(1-n\delta)\le T_n(q)\le W,\qquad
 |u-1|\le\frac{2n\delta}{1-n\delta}\le4n\delta.
\end{equation}
In particular $T_n(q)>9/5$, so $q>1$ even if the hypotheses allowed
$q=1$.

Put $D_k=kT_{n-k}(q)-(n-k)T_k(q)$, which is real.  Multiply
\eqref{P:eq:round3-complement-residual} by $z^k$, use
\eqref{P:eq:round3-top-phase}, and note that
$T_{n-k}(q)\le T_n(q)\le W$.  This proves
\[
 |D_k-(2k-n)z^k|\le E_k',\qquad
 E_k'=k(n-k)(W+3N)\delta+4knW\delta.
\]
In particular,
\[
 E_1'\le(5nW+3nN)\delta,
 \qquad E_2'\le(10nW+6nN)\delta.
\]
The imaginary part of the $k=1$ relation gives
$(n-2)|\operatorname{Im}z|\le E_1'$.  Thus
$|z^2-1|=2|\operatorname{Im}z|\le2E_1'/(n-2)$, and the $k=2$
relation implies
\begin{align}
 H_n(q)&:=2\bigl(T_{n-2}(q)-1\bigr)
                -(n-2)\bigl(T_2(q)-1\bigr)\notag\\
 &\le |H_n(q)|
 \le E_2'+\frac{2(n-4)}{n-2}E_1'
 \le(20nW+12nN)\delta
 \le\frac W{100}.\label{P:eq:round3-H-upper}
\end{align}
For the last inequality, use $W>2$, $N<n$, and
$(20/n+6)/1000\le1/100$ for every $n\ge5$.

We next prove a uniform lower bound for this same positive Chebyshev
combination.  Taylor coefficients of $T_n(1+x)$ are nonnegative.
For completeness, the Chebyshev differential equation gives the
recurrence
\[
 c_0=1,\qquad
 c_j=\frac{n^2-(j-1)^2}{j(2j-1)}c_{j-1}
 \quad(1\le j\le n),\qquad T_n(1+x)=\sum_{j=0}^n c_jx^j.
\]
Therefore
\[
 T_n(3/2)\ge1+\frac{n^2}{2}
                   +\frac{n^2(n^2-1)}{24}>n^2-n+1.
\]
The last difference, multiplied by $24$, is
$n^4-13n^2+24n$.  On writing $n=5+v$, this polynomial becomes
\[
 420+394v+137v^2+20v^3+v^4>0\qquad(v\ge0).
\]
It follows from \eqref{P:eq:round3-W-bounds} and
\eqref{P:eq:round3-top-phase} that $q<3/2$.

Write $q=\cosh s$ with $s>0$, and put $m=n-2\ge3$.
Comparison of the positive power series of $\cosh(2s)-1$ and
$\cosh(ms)-1$ gives
\[
 T_2(q)-1\le\frac4{m^2}\bigl(T_m(q)-1\bigr).
\]
Also the function
$e^{-x}\sinh(x)/x=\int_0^1e^{-2xv}\,dv$ is decreasing for $x>0$.
Apply this fact at $ms/2$ and $ns/2$ to obtain
\[
 \frac{T_m(q)-1}{T_n(q)-1}
 =\left(\frac{\sinh(ms/2)}{\sinh(ns/2)}\right)^2
 \ge\frac{m^2}{n^2}e^{-2s}>
       \frac{m^2}{9n^2}.
\]
Here $e^s=q+\sqrt{q^2-1}<2q<3$.
Combining the last two inequalities yields
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:round3-H-lower}
 H_n(q)>
 \frac{2(n-2)(n-4)}{9n^2}\bigl(T_n(q)-1\bigr)
 \ge\frac2{75}\bigl(T_n(q)-1\bigr)
 >\frac4{375}W.
\end{equation}
The middle inequality uses
$25(n-2)(n-4)-3n^2=22(n-5)^2+70(n-5)\ge0$.
For the last one, \eqref{P:eq:round3-top-phase}, $W>2$, and
$n\delta<1/10$ give $T_n(q)-1>(2/5)W$.
Finally $4/375-1/100=1/1500>0$ contradicts
\eqref{P:eq:round3-H-upper}.  The strict margin is greater than
$W/1500$ although all tube faces in
\eqref{P:eq:round3-angle-only-radius} are closed.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{An explicit lower auxiliary gap.}
Under the hypothetical tube assumptions one also obtains
\[
 q>1+\frac1{4n^2}.
\]
Indeed the displayed coefficient recurrence implies
$c_j\le2^j n^{2j}/(2j)!$.  Hence
\[
 T_n\!\left(1+\frac1{4n^2}\right)
 \le\sum_{j=0}^n\frac{1}{2^j(2j)!}
 \le\sum_{j=0}^n4^{-j}<\frac43<\frac95<T_n(q).
\]
This lower gap is not needed for the stronger relative estimate
\eqref{P:eq:round3-H-lower}; it records explicitly why a near-boundary
auxiliary root cannot evade the tube proof.

\subsection{The exact small polygons and the spurious four-point branch}

For an exact deleted regular $n$-gon, normalize the omitted vertex
to $1$.  Then $p_k=-1$ for $1\le k<n$ and $p_n=N$.  The top
moment gives $T_n(q)z^n=W>0$, so $z^n=1$ and $T_n(q)=W$.
Complementary moments give the exact relations
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:round3-exact-complement}
 kT_{n-k}(q)-(n-k)T_k(q)=(2k-n)z^k.
\end{equation}
For $n\ge5$, the argument above with zero errors already excludes
these configurations.  The cases $n=3,4$ have simple separate
algebraic proofs under the same mass lower bound and $q\ge1$.

For $n=3$, the $k=1$ relation makes $z$ real.  Since $z^3=1$,
$z=1$, and $T_2(q)-2q=-1$ becomes $2q(q-1)=0$.
Thus $q=1$, whereas $T_3(q)=W>2$, a contradiction.

For $n=4$, again $z\in\{1,-1\}$.  The choice $z=1$ gives
\[
 T_3(q)-3q+2
 =2(q-1)(2q^2+2q-1)=0,
\]
so $q=1$, contradicting $T_4(q)=W>2$.
The choice $z=-1$ instead gives
\[
 T_3(q)-3q-2
 =2(q+1)(2q^2-2q-1)=0.
\]
There is an apparent branch $q=(1+\sqrt3)/2>1$ with $q^2=q+1/2$.
It does not satisfy the full moment system.  Write the support as
$(i,-1,-i)$.  The first and second weighted moments are
\[
 m_1=-q-1,\qquad m_2=q^2-1.
\]
They force the masses at $i$ and $-i$ to be $3/4$, and the mass at
$-1$ to be $q+1$.  Thus $t=q+5/2$ and $W=4q+7$.
But reduction modulo $q^2-q-1/2$ gives $T_4(q)=8q+3$, so the
top equation would require $q=1$.  This contradiction removes the
apparent branch.  We claim an explicit robust radius here only for
$n\ge5$; the exact $n=3,4$ calculations are separate statements.

\section{A certified top-moment deficit exclusion without angle boxes}\label{col:P:16}

Corpus manuscript~\cite{P:Corpus193} uses exact sums of nonnegative
defects to turn near equality into localization.  The following
application has its own explicit identity, constants, and matching
proof; it does not import a stability exponent from that manuscript.

\begin{corollary}[A strict top-deficit cut]
\label{P:cor:round3-top-deficit-cut}
Let $n\ge5$, $N=n-1$, and suppose the one-defect moments
\eqref{P:eq:round3-one-defect-moments} hold with
\[
 \lambda_j>1/n,\qquad n/(n-1)\le t<n.
\]
Assume in addition the cardinal pair separation for competitive
stationary candidates,
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:round3-pair-premise}
 |\alpha_i-\alpha_j|>
 \sqrt{\frac{24}{n(n^2-1)T(n)}},\qquad T(n)\le n.
\end{equation}
Define
\[
 \gamma=\min_j(n\lambda_j-1)>0,\qquad
 \Delta=nt-(n-1)-T_n(q).
\]
Then every such candidate satisfies the strict inequality
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:round3-deficit-cut}
 \boxed{\quad
 \Delta>\frac{\gamma}{8\,000\,000\,n^2}.
 \quad}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Set $w_j=n\lambda_j-1>0$, $W=\sum_jw_j$, and
$\beta=S_n/|S_n|=z^n$.  Since $|S_n|=T_n(q)\ge1$, this
phase is defined.  There is an exact nonnegative identity
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:round3-deficit-identity}
 \sum_jw_j|\alpha_j^n-\beta|^2
 =2W-2\operatorname{Re}(\overline\beta S_n)
 =2\Delta.
\end{equation}
Suppose contrary to \eqref{P:eq:round3-deficit-cut} that
$\Delta\le\gamma/(8\,000\,000n^2)$.  Then every support point
satisfies
\[
 |\alpha_j^n-\beta|\le R:=\sqrt{2\Delta/\gamma}
 \le\frac1{2000n}<1.
\]
Choose a nearest $n$th root $\zeta$ of $\beta$.  Write
$\alpha_j/\zeta=e^{i\theta}$ with $|\theta|\le\pi/n$.
Since $2\sin(n|\theta|/2)\le R$ and
$\arcsin(R/2)\le R$ for $0\le R\le1$,
\[
 |\alpha_j-\zeta|\le|\theta|\le\frac{2R}{n}
 \le\frac1{1000n^2}=\rho_{\mathrm{del}}(n).
\]
The separation premise is strictly greater than $4/n^2$:
\[
 \frac{24}{n^2(n^2-1)}-\frac{16}{n^4}
 =\frac{8n^2+16}{n^4(n^2-1)}>0.
\]
Two support points assigned to the same root would have distance
at most $2\rho_{\mathrm{del}}(n)=1/(500n^2)<4/n^2$, a contradiction.
Thus the $n-1$ support points use distinct vertices of a regular
$n$-gon, leaving exactly one unused vertex.  Theorem
\ref{P:thm:arbitrary-mass-deleted-tube} excludes precisely this closed
tube, proving the strict deficit inequality.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Use on rational parameter boxes.}
If a certified mass box has lower endpoints $\ell_j>1/n$, put
$\gamma_0=\min_j(n\ell_j-1)>0$.  Any box satisfying all the other
candidate premises and
\[
 n t_{\max}-(n-1)-T_n(q_{\min})
 \le\frac{\gamma_0}{8\,000\,000n^2}
\]
is excluded by the corollary.  The quantities in this test are
rational whenever the box endpoints are rational: $T_n$ can be
evaluated by its exact integer recurrence.  Dependencies can be
retained to improve this sufficient box test.
Strict $\lambda_j>1/n$ does not furnish a common positive lower
bound for $\gamma$ over the entire remaining domain.  The
pointwise inequality \eqref{P:eq:round3-deficit-cut} is still valid,
but it becomes weak as a mass tends to $1/n$.

\paragraph{Scope.}
The angle-only theorem needs the stated positive mass, total mass,
and complete one-defect moment premises.  The deficit corollary
also needs the stationary cardinal pair constraint; that constraint
does not follow merely from a subset of moment equations.
These results remove new infinite families of the parameter domain.
They do not cover all angular configurations, all auxiliary defects,
or all surviving positive mass vectors, and do not assert a global
all-degree coefficient theorem.

% Standalone fragment. Existing delivered manuscripts are not modified.
% The standing input is the stationary spectral cardinal norm identity.
\section{Conditioned Gram matrices and exclusions near a regular light polygon}\label{col:P:17}
\label{P:sec:r3-spectral}

The Schur-complement and inverse-trace methods in corpus manuscripts~\cite{P:Corpus043,P:Corpus034} motivate this application. We use only the elementary identities proved below, not the special permanent or graph hypotheses of those manuscripts.

We assume the stationary spectral cardinal identity.  Namely, let
\(n\ge2\), let \(N=n-d\) distinct support points lie on the unit circle,
and write
\[
 Q(z)=cA(z)\prod_{j=1}^N(z-\alpha_j),\qquad \deg A=d,
 \qquad A(\alpha_j)\ne0.
\]
The masses of a stationary candidate satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-cardinal-input}
 \lambda_j=\left\|\frac{Q(z)}{(z-\alpha_j)Q'(\alpha_j)}\right\|_{H^2}^2.
\end{equation}
Every norm below is the Euclidean norm of the coefficient vector, or
equivalently the normalized circle \(H^2\) norm.  The conclusions are
necessary for such stationary data, not for arbitrary solutions of only
the truncated critical moment equations.

\paragraph{Conjugation convention.}
The points \(\alpha_j\) in this section are zeros of the spectral factor
\(Q\).  Choose a consistent spectral-factor and moment convention when
identifying them with the Herglotz parameters.  Every conclusion below
is invariant under simultaneous conjugation of all support and
auxiliary points.  Reflecting an auxiliary root across the circle does
not change the normalized cardinal norm; hence the interior choice is
permitted when \(d=1\).

\subsection{An explicit rank-one conditioned kernel}

For \(d=1\), put \(A(z)=z-s\), \(r=|s|<1\), and \(N=n-1\).
In the coefficient basis \(1,z,\ldots,z^{N-1}\), multiplication by
\(z-s\) has Gram matrix
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-tridiagonal}
 (H_A)_{jj}=1+r^2,\qquad (H_A)_{j,j+1}=-s,
 \qquad (H_A)_{j+1,j}=-\overline s.
\end{equation}
All other entries vanish.  For \(0\le j\le k\le N-1\),
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-tridiagonal-inverse}
 (H_A^{-1})_{jk}=
 \frac{s^{k-j}(1-r^{2(j+1)})(1-r^{2(N-k)})}
 {(1-r^2)(1-r^{2(N+1)})},
\end{equation}
and the lower triangle is the conjugate transpose.  At \(s=0\) this
means the identity matrix.  The determinant recurrence
\(D_j=(1+r^2)D_{j-1}-r^2D_{j-2}\), with \(D_0=1\), gives
\(D_j=(1-r^{2(j+1)})/(1-r^2)\); the cofactor formula proves
\eqref{P:eq:r3-tridiagonal-inverse}.

There is a simpler kernel expression.  Define
\[
 K_n(z,w)=\sum_{q=0}^{n-1}(z\overline w)^q,
 \qquad \kappa_n(s)=\sum_{q=0}^{n-1}r^{2q}.
\]
The subspace \((z-s)\mathcal P_{n-2}\) is the orthogonal complement
of the evaluation kernel at \(s\) inside \(\mathcal P_{n-1}\).
Therefore its evaluation Gram matrix is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-kernel-rank-one}
 (G_A)_{jk}=K_n(\alpha_j,\alpha_k)
 -\frac{K_n(\alpha_j,s)K_n(s,\alpha_k)}{\kappa_n(s)}.
\end{equation}
In particular, \(\lambda_j=(G_A^{-1})_{jj}\) and
\(t=\operatorname{tr}(G_A^{-1})\).

Partition the support into a light block and two remaining points:
\[
 G_A=\begin{pmatrix}L&U\\U^*&C\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad S=C-U^*L^{-1}U.
\]
Both \(L\) and \(S\) are positive definite.  The block inverse gives
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-schur-masses}
 \lambda_{\rm heavy,1}=(S^{-1})_{11},\quad
 \lambda_{\rm heavy,2}=(S^{-1})_{22},\quad
 t=\operatorname{tr}L^{-1}
 +\operatorname{tr}\!\left[S^{-1}(I_2+U^*L^{-2}U)\right].
\end{equation}
For \(S=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&z\\\overline z&b\end{smallmatrix}\right)\),
the two heavy masses are \(b/(ab-|z|^2)\) and
\(a/(ab-|z|^2)\).  Thus this reduction retains their interaction
with every light point and with the auxiliary root.
For any Hermitian matrix \(X\), a further exact certificate is
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-affine-inverse}
 \operatorname{tr}G_A^{-1}\ge
 2\operatorname{tr}X-\operatorname{tr}(XG_AX),
\end{equation}
because the difference is
\(\|G_A^{1/2}X-G_A^{-1/2}\|_F^2\).
The exclusions below evaluate the same inverse-Gram diagonal norms
through their cardinal polynomials, which avoids matrix inversion.

\subsection{A polynomially sized perturbation of a regular light polygon}

Let \(m\ge3\), let \(\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_m\) be the roots of
\(z^m-1\), and suppose the distinct unit-circle light points satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-light-tube}
 |\beta_j-\zeta_j|\le\varepsilon,
 \qquad \varepsilon\le\frac1{64m^2}.
\end{equation}
An arbitrary common rotation is permitted.  Put
\[
 P(z)=\prod_{j=1}^m(z-\beta_j),\quad P_0(z)=z^m-1,
 \quad R=P-P_0.
\]

\begin{lemma}[Exact polynomial perturbation bounds]
\label{P:lem:r3-light-polynomial}
Under \eqref{P:eq:r3-light-tube},
\begin{align}
 \|R\|_2&\le\frac4{255m}<\frac1{32m},
 &\sup_{|z|=1}|R(z)|&<\frac1{96},
 \label{P:eq:r3-poly-perturb}\\
 |P'(\beta_j)|&\le\frac{128m}{127},
 &\left\|\frac{P(z)}{z-\beta_j}\right\|_2
 &\le\sqrt m+\frac3{64}.
 \label{P:eq:r3-poly-derivative}
\end{align}
Every unit-circle point \(\alpha\) is within distance
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-nearest-light}
 \delta=|\alpha-\beta_j|\le\frac{13}{4m}
\end{equation}
of some light point.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Distinct regular roots are separated by at least \(4/m\), and
\(\prod_{k\ne j}|\zeta_j-\zeta_k|=m\).  For nonnegative \(x_k\)
with \(\sum x_k<1\), expansion of the product gives
\(\prod(1+x_k)\le(1-\sum x_k)^{-1}\).  Hence
\[
 |P(\zeta_j)|\le
 m\varepsilon\prod_{k\ne j}
 \left(1+\frac{\varepsilon}{|\zeta_j-\zeta_k|}\right)
 \le\frac{m\varepsilon}{1-m^2\varepsilon/4}
 \le\frac4{255m}.
\]
The polynomial \(R\) has degree at most \(m-1\).  The finite Fourier
Parseval identity gives
\(\|R\|_2^2=m^{-1}\sum_j|R(\zeta_j)|^2\), proving its norm bound.
The coefficient Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives
\(\|R\|_\infty\le4/(255\sqrt m)\le4/(255\sqrt3)<1/96\);
the last comparison follows by squaring, since
\(384^2<3\cdot255^2\).

At a perturbed light root,
\[
 |P'(\beta_j)|
 \le m\prod_{k\ne j}
