 \left(1+\frac{2\varepsilon}{|\zeta_j-\zeta_k|}\right)
 \le\frac m{1-m^2\varepsilon/2}\le\frac{128m}{127}.
\]
Write \(V_j=P/(z-\beta_j)\) and
\(D_j=P_0/(z-\zeta_j)\).  The latter polynomial has \(m\)
coefficients of modulus one, so \(\|D_j\|_2=\sqrt m\), and
\[
 (z-\beta_j)(V_j-D_j)=R+(\beta_j-\zeta_j)D_j.
\]
Division of a polynomial of degree at most \(m-1\), vanishing at
a unit point, by its linear factor has coefficient norm at most
\(m\) times the original norm.  Indeed the quotient coefficients
are partial sums with unit-modulus multipliers, and the sum of their
squared Cauchy--Schwarz bounds is at most \(m^2\) times the input
norm squared.  Consequently
\[
 \|V_j-D_j\|_2
 \le m\bigl(\|R\|_2+\varepsilon\sqrt m\bigr)
 <\frac1{32}+\frac1{64\sqrt m}\le\frac3{64}.
\]
Finally, a point of the circle is within angular distance \(\pi/m\)
of one of the regular roots.  Its chord distance to the corresponding
perturbed light is at most
\(\pi/m+\varepsilon\le(\pi+1/64)/m<13/(4m)\), where
\(\pi<22/7\) suffices.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Two heavy points: an exclusion for every degree at least six}

Suppose \(d=1\), \(m=n-3\ge3\), and the remaining support points
are \(a,b\).  Let \(s\) be the interior spectral auxiliary root.
The exact heavy cardinal formula is
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-heavy-cardinal}
 \lambda_a=
 \frac{\|(z-s)(z-b)P(z)\|_2^2}
 {|a-s|^2|a-b|^2|P(a)|^2}.
\end{equation}
For the unperturbed light polygon, the coefficient blocks are disjoint:
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-heavy-exact}
 \lambda_a=
 \frac{4(1+|s|^2+\operatorname{Re}(s\overline b))}
 {|a-s|^2|a-b|^2|a^m-1|^2}.
\end{equation}
This formula is valid for every pair of distinct extra points avoiding
the light roots, with no restriction on their phases.

\begin{theorem}[A robust two-heavy exclusion]
\label{P:thm:r3-heavy-sector}
Let \(n\ge6\), \(d=1\), and \(m=n-3\).  If
\eqref{P:eq:r3-light-tube} holds and the two remaining support points satisfy
\[
 |a-b|\le\frac7{12},\qquad \lambda_a,\lambda_b\le\frac34,
\]
then the stationary cardinal norm identities are impossible.
No lower mass bound or restriction on the auxiliary root is needed.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put \(C(z)=(z-s)(z-b)\) and \(D=|a-b|^2>0\).
The polynomial \(C\) belongs to the two-dimensional subspace
\(\{p\in\mathcal P_2:p(b)=0\}\).  Projecting the degree-two
evaluation kernel off the kernel at \(b\) gives the exact low-degree
Schur inequality
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-low-degree-schur}
 |C(a)|^2\le
 \left(3-\frac{|K_3(a,b)|^2}{3}\right)\|C\|_2^2
 =\left(2D-\frac{D^2}{3}\right)\|C\|_2^2.
\end{equation}
Here \(|K_3(a,b)|^2=(3-D)^2\).  This kernel has degree two
because the whole regular light block has been factored out; it is not
the original degree-\((n-1)\) two-point estimate.

As \(m\ge3\), disjoint coefficient blocks give
\(\|CP_0\|_2=\sqrt2\|C\|_2\), whereas
\(\|CR\|_2\le\sqrt3\|C\|_2\|R\|_2\).
Consequently
\[
 \frac{\|CP\|_2}{\|C\|_2}\ge\sqrt2-\sqrt3\|R\|_2
 >\frac{24}{17}-\frac7{765}
 =\frac75+\frac2{765}>\frac75,
 \qquad |P(a)|<2+\frac1{96}=\frac{193}{96}.
\]
We used \(\sqrt2>24/17\), \(\sqrt3<7/4\), and
\(\|R\|_2\le4/(255m)\le4/765\).
Combining these bounds with \eqref{P:eq:r3-heavy-cardinal} yields
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-robust-heavy-bound}
 \lambda_a>
 \frac{(7/5)^2}{(193/96)^2(2D-D^2/3)}.
\end{equation}
The function \(2D-D^2/3\) is increasing for \(0<D<3\).
If \(|a-b|\le7/12\), its value is at most
\(39935/62208\), so
\[
 \lambda_a>
 \frac{573308928}{758948375}
 =\frac34+\frac{16390587}{3035793500}>\frac34.
\]
This proves the theorem.

For the exact light polygon, the same argument without perturbation
gives
\(\lambda_a\ge[4D-(2/3)D^2]^{-1}\).
In fact it is strict under the spectral assumption \(|s|<1\).
To see this, rotate \(b\) to \(1\) and put \(u=\overline a\).
Equality in \eqref{P:eq:r3-low-degree-schur} would force \(C\) to be
proportional to the projected evaluation kernel, whose leading and
constant coefficients are
\[
 c_2=(2u^2-u-1)/3,\qquad c_0=(2-u-u^2)/3.
\]
Since \(a\ne1\), \(c_2\ne0\).  Its other root is
\(c_0/c_2=-(u+2)/(2u+1)\), which has modulus one.  This contradicts
\(|s|<1\).  Therefore the exact polygon family is excluded whenever
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-exact-heavy-cut}
 |a-b|^2\le3-\sqrt7,
\end{equation}
including the boundary, since
\(4D-(2/3)D^2\le4/3\) throughout this interval.
\end{proof}

\subsection{All extra angles and all auxiliary roots}

The next bound removes both the two-heavy restriction and every
restriction on the additional phases.  Let there be \(m\) light support
points and \(h\ge1\) additional support points.  Put
\[
 \ell=d+h,\qquad n=m+\ell,\qquad N=m+h.
\]
Assume \(m\ge\ell\), and choose any extra support point \(a\).
For a light point \(\beta\), write \(V=P/(z-\beta)\) and
\(\delta=|a-\beta|\).  The product of the auxiliary factor with the
other \(h-1\) extra support factors is a polynomial \(C\) of degree
\(\ell-1\).  The light cardinal formula is
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-light-cardinal}
 \lambda_\beta=
 \frac{\|C(z)(z-a)V(z)\|_2^2}
 {|C(\beta)|^2\delta^2|P'(\beta)|^2}.
\end{equation}
Here \(C(\beta)\ne0\), since all support points are distinct and
the auxiliary factor has no support zeros.

\begin{lemma}[A light-mass bound retaining the rest of the factor]
\label{P:lem:r3-general-light-bound}
For \(m\ge\ell\), whenever
\(\sqrt{2/\ell}-\|R\|_2-\delta\|V\|_2>0\),
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-general-light-bound}
 \lambda_\beta\ge
 \frac{\bigl(\sqrt{2/\ell}-\|R\|_2-\delta\|V\|_2\bigr)^2}
 {\delta^2|P'(\beta)|^2}.
\end{equation}
If \eqref{P:eq:r3-light-tube} holds, some light point nearest to \(a\)
therefore satisfies, whenever the bracket below is positive,
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r3-light-explicit}
 \boxed{\quad
 \lambda_\beta>
 \left(\frac{127}{416}\right)^2
 \left(\sqrt{\frac2\ell}-\frac{13}{4\sqrt m}
                         -\frac{47}{256m}\right)^2.
 \quad}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The blocks of \(C(z)(z^m-1)\) do not overlap because
\(\deg C=\ell-1<m\).  Hence
\(\|CP_0\|_2=\sqrt2\|C\|_2\).  The coefficient
Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives
\(\|C\|_\infty\le\sqrt\ell\|C\|_2\) and
\(|C(\beta)|\le\sqrt\ell\|C\|_2\).
Since \((z-a)V=P+(\beta-a)V\), the numerator norm in
\eqref{P:eq:r3-light-cardinal} is at least
\[
 \|C\|_2\left(\sqrt2-
       \sqrt\ell\|R\|_2-\sqrt\ell\delta\|V\|_2\right).
\]
The assumed positive bracket permits squaring this lower bound.
Canceling \(\|C\|_2\) gives
\eqref{P:eq:r3-general-light-bound}.

Choose the nearest light from Lemma~\ref{P:lem:r3-light-polynomial}.
Its denominator obeys
\(\delta|P'(\beta)|\le416/127\), and its numerator bracket is
strictly greater than
\[
 \sqrt{2/\ell}-\frac1{32m}
 -\frac{13}{4m}\left(\sqrt m+\frac3{64}\right)
 =\sqrt{2/\ell}-\frac{13}{4\sqrt m}-\frac{47}{256m}.
\]
This proves \eqref{P:eq:r3-light-explicit}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[A uniform regular-light exclusion, with no extra-phase restrictions]
\label{P:thm:r3-all-extra-angles}
Let \(d\ge1\), \(h\ge1\), \(\ell=d+h\), and \(m\ge32\ell\).
Let \(n=m+\ell\), with \(m\) light support points and \(h\) other
support points.  If each light mass obeys
\(\lambda_j\le2/n\), then the stationary cardinal identities
exclude the entire light tube
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 |\beta_j-e^{i\theta_0}e^{2\pi i j/m}|
       \le\frac1{64m^2}\quad (j=1,\ldots,m),
 \quad \theta_0\in\mathbb R.
 \quad}
\]
There is no restriction on the phases or masses of the other \(h\)
support points, and no restriction on the auxiliary roots beyond the
standing spectral assumptions.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The bracket in \eqref{P:eq:r3-light-explicit}, multiplied by
\(\sqrt\ell\), is at least
\[
 \sqrt2-\frac{13}{16\sqrt2}-\frac{47}{8192\sqrt\ell}
 >\frac75-\frac{65}{112}-\frac{47}{8192}
 >\frac{13}{16}.
\]
We used \(\sqrt2>7/5\) and \(\ell\ge1\); the last comparison
is rational.  Thus one of the lights necessarily satisfies
\[
 \lambda_\beta>
 \frac1\ell\left(\frac{1651}{6656}\right)^2
 >\frac2{33\ell}\ge\frac2n.
\]
The strict rational comparison is equivalent to
\(33\cdot1651^2-2\cdot6656^2=1346761>0\).
This contradicts the light mass cap.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The one-auxiliary, two-heavy hull]
\label{P:cor:r3-two-heavy-hull}
For every \(n\ge99\), put \(m=n-3\).  In the hull with
\(m\) light masses in \([1/n,2/n]\) and two heavy masses in
\([2/5,3/4]\), the entire light tube \eqref{P:eq:r3-light-tube} is
excluded, for all heavy angles and all auxiliary roots.
For \(6\le n\le98\), Theorem~\ref{P:thm:r3-heavy-sector} still
excludes the portion with heavy chord distance at most \(7/12\).
\end{corollary}

\paragraph{Scope and verification.}
These are continuous exclusion families, not sampled-grid conclusions.
The perturbation radius is explicitly polynomial in \(m\).
The unrestricted extra-angle theorem also supplies a new individual
mass lower bound, \eqref{P:eq:r3-light-explicit}, conditional only on
the specified light geometry.  The result is not a claim that every
remaining support configuration has this geometry, nor a global proof
of the coefficient conjecture.  It is an application of the exact
conditioned Gram/cardinal constraints to a newly closed family.
The accompanying standard-library Python script checks every rational
constant comparison and independently checks the rank-one kernel and
tridiagonal inverse orientation at exact rational complex inputs.
Those finite algebraic checks supplement the all-parameter proofs above;
they do not replace the proofs by finite sampling.

\section{A geometry-free radial gap for every auxiliary root}\label{col:P:18}
\label{P:sec:r4-radial}

We retain the stationary spectral setup, including the boundary identity
and the exact cardinal mass identities.  In particular, $Q$ has degree
$n\ge2$, its distinct circle zeros $\alpha_j$ are the support points,
and its remaining roots can be chosen in the open disk.  Put
$t=\sum_j\lambda_j<n$.  For the refined estimate below we also use
$t\ge n/N>1$, as holds for a deficient-support candidate.

\begin{lemma}[Multiplication by a linear factor]\label{P:lem:r4-linear-factor}
For $|\sigma|=r<1$ and a polynomial $C$ of degree at most $n-2$,
\[
 \|(z-\sigma)C\|_2^2
 \ge \bigl(1+r^2-2r\cos(\pi/n)\bigr)\|C\|_2^2
 \ge \frac4{n^2}\|C\|_2^2.
\]
Consequently, if $\sigma$ is an auxiliary root and $\beta$ is a support
point, then
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r4-aux-support-gap}
 \lambda_\beta\ge
 \frac4{n^2(n-1)|\beta-\sigma|^2}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
After a diagonal unitary change of the coefficients, the Gram matrix
of multiplication by $z-\sigma$ is the $(n-1)$-by-$(n-1)$
tridiagonal matrix with diagonal $1+r^2$ and adjacent entries $-r$.
Its sine eigenvectors give the displayed smallest eigenvalue.
Completing a square bounds it below by $\sin^2(\pi/n)$.
Concavity of sine on $[0,\pi/2]$ gives $\sin(\pi/n)\ge2/n$.
Write $Q=(z-\sigma)(z-\beta)C$.  The cardinal identity and
$|C(\beta)|^2\le(n-1)\|C\|_2^2$ give
\[
 \lambda_\beta=
 \frac{\|(z-\sigma)C\|_2^2}
 {|\beta-\sigma|^2|C(\beta)|^2},
\]
which proves the second assertion.  The support roots are simple, so
$C(\beta)\ne0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform radial separation]\label{P:thm:r4-radial-gap}
Every auxiliary root of a competitive deficient-support stationary
candidate satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r4-radial-coarse}
 \boxed{1-|\sigma|>\frac1{n^3}.}
\end{equation}
For $n\ge3$ the total-mass-sensitive bound is
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r4-radial-mass}
 \boxed{1-|\sigma|>\frac1{n^2t}.}
\end{equation}
No restriction on the support geometry, individual mass pattern, or
auxiliary-root phases is imposed.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Rotate so that $\sigma=r\in(0,1)$ and write $\delta=1-r$.
If $\delta\ge1/(2n)$, both conclusions follow immediately:
$1/(2n)>1/n^3$ for $n\ge2$, and $nt>3>2$ in the refined case.
We may therefore assume $\delta<1/(2n)$.

First suppose that $1$ is not a support point.  Decompose
\[
 Q(z)=A+(z-1)R(z),\qquad A=Q(1).
\]
Since $Q(r)=0$, $A=\delta R(r)$, whence
\[
 |A|\le\delta\sqrt n\|R\|_2,
 \qquad |R(1)|\le\sqrt n\|R\|_2.
\]
The stationary boundary identity and the exact Fourier identity for
$D|Q|^2$ at $1$ give
\begin{align*}
 \Phi(1)|A|^2
 &=n|A|^2-2\Re(\overline A R(1))+2\|R\|_2^2\\
 &\ge n|A|^2+2(1-n\delta)\|R\|_2^2
 >\|R\|_2^2.
\end{align*}
Here $\Phi(1)=\sum_j2\lambda_j/|1-\alpha_j|^2$, and $R\ne0$.
It follows that $\Phi(1)>1/(n\delta^2)$.  If $\beta$ is a nearest
support point and $a=|1-\beta|$, then
\[
 \frac1{n\delta^2}<\Phi(1)\le\frac{2t}{a^2},
 \qquad
 |\beta-\sigma|<(1+\sqrt{2nt})\delta.
\]
Using $t<n$ and $n\ge2$ gives
$|\beta-\sigma|<2n\delta$, because
$\sqrt2+1/n\le\sqrt2+1/2<2$.
By Lemma~\ref{P:lem:r4-linear-factor},
\[
 t\ge\lambda_\beta>
 \frac1{n^4(n-1)\delta^2}.
\]
Together with $t<n$ this implies
$\delta^2>1/[n^5(n-1)]>1/n^6$.

For $n\ge3$, retain $t$ in the nearest-support estimate.  Since
$nt>3$ and
$\sqrt2+1/\sqrt3<17/12+7/12=2$, it gives
$|\beta-\sigma|<2\sqrt{nt}\delta$.  Hence
\[
 t\ge\lambda_\beta>
 \frac1{n^3(n-1)t\delta^2},
 \qquad
 \delta^2>\frac1{n^3(n-1)t^2}>\frac1{n^4t^2}.
\]

If $1$ is a support point, take $\beta=1$ directly, so that
$|\beta-\sigma|=\delta$.  Lemma~\ref{P:lem:r4-linear-factor} yields
$t\ge4/[n^2(n-1)\delta^2]$, which is strictly stronger than both
needed conclusions (use $t<n$ for the first and $t>1$ for the
second).  This also handles exact coincidence of the auxiliary
argument with a support angle without evaluating a pole of $\Phi$.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Consequence for radial parameters.}
For every auxiliary root, let $q=(r+r^{-1})/2$.
The theorem implies
\[
 q-1=\frac{(1-r)^2}{2r}>\frac1{2n^6};
 \qquad
 q-1>\frac1{2n^4t^2}\quad(n\ge3).
\]
These statements apply separately to the moduli in any defect; they
do not identify or remove the distinct auxiliary phases.
Together with the earlier lower modulus bound they put every
auxiliary root in an explicit closed annulus after harmless outward
rounding.  This proves a boundary exclusion, not emptiness of the
remaining annulus.

% Round 4 G1/G2: exact consequences, not a complete covering theorem.
\section{Uniform individual mass gaps and an absolute top-moment deficit}\label{col:P:19}
\label{P:sec:r4-moment-floors}

The cardinal conditions supply more than a strict mass lower bound.
Once the auxiliary roots are quantitatively separated from the unit
circle, the strictness has a uniform, explicit size.  This removes
the dependence on an unspecified minimum mass excess from the earlier
top-moment exclusion.  No regularity of the support is assumed here.

\begin{lemma}[A one-zero cardinal bound]
\label{P:lem:r4-one-zero-cardinal}
Let $n\ge2$, $\alpha\in\mathbb T$, and $0<|\sigma|=r<1$.
Suppose $u$ is a polynomial of degree at most $n-1$ with
$u(\alpha)=1$ and $u(\sigma)=0$.  Put
\[
 a_n(r)=\frac{1-r}{1+r}\frac{1-r^n}{1+r^n}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r4-one-zero-mass}
 \|u\|_{H^2}^2\ge\frac1{n-a_n(r)},\qquad
 n\|u\|_{H^2}^2-1\ge\frac{a_n(r)}{n-a_n(r)}>0.
\end{equation}
The same bound holds if further vanishing constraints are imposed.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In the space of polynomials of degree at most $n-1$, the reproducing
kernel is
\[
 K_n(z,w)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}z^k\overline{w}^{k}.
\]
Projection off the evaluation vector at $\sigma$ gives the diagonal
kernel of the subspace $u(\sigma)=0$:
\[
 K_n^{\sigma}(\alpha,\alpha)
 =n-\frac{|K_n(\alpha,\sigma)|^2}{K_n(\sigma,\sigma)}.
\]
Cauchy--Schwarz for evaluation at $\alpha$ therefore gives
$\|u\|^2\ge1/K_n^\sigma(\alpha,\alpha)$.
The finite geometric sum satisfies
\[
 |K_n(\alpha,\sigma)|\ge\frac{1-r^n}{1+r},\qquad
 K_n(\sigma,\sigma)=\frac{1-r^{2n}}{1-r^2}.
\]
Consequently its quotient is at least $a_n(r)$.  Since
$0<a_n(r)<1<n$, all divisions and inequalities have the stated
orientation.  Further constraints only reduce the admissible subspace.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{An auxiliary-radius form before using the radial gap.}
If $q=(r+r^{-1})/2$, then
\[
 a_n(r)\ge\left(\frac{1-r}{1+r}\right)^2
             =\frac{q-1}{q+1}.
\]
Thus a stationary cardinal mass satisfies
\[
 n\lambda_j-1\ge
 \frac{q-1}{n(q+1)-q+1}.
\]
This already removes the individual mass variables from a lower bound,
but it tends to zero as $q\downarrow1$.  The radial gap below is essential
for the absolute, index-only conclusions.

\begin{theorem}[Uniform mass gaps in every positive defect]
\label{P:thm:r4-uniform-mass-gap}
Let a competitive deficient-support stationary candidate have index
$n\ge2$, $1\le N<n$, positive masses $\lambda_j$, and a spectral
factor $Q$ of degree $n$.  Assume its cardinal identities
\[
 u_j(z)=\frac{Q(z)}{(z-\alpha_j)Q'(\alpha_j)},\qquad
 \lambda_j=\|u_j\|_{H^2}^2,
\]
and the radial conclusion of Theorem~\ref{P:thm:r4-radial-gap}:
every selected interior auxiliary root satisfies $1-|\sigma|>n^{-3}$.
Then, for every support index $j$,
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r4-uniform-gamma}
 \boxed{\quad
 n\lambda_j-1>\frac7{32n^6-7}>\frac1{5n^6},\qquad
 \lambda_j>\frac1n+\frac1{5n^7}.
 \quad}
\end{equation}
For $n\ge3$, the sharper radial conclusion
$1-|\sigma|>1/(n^2t)$, where $t=\sum_j\lambda_j>1$, gives
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r4-t-sensitive-gamma}
 \boxed{\quad n\lambda_j-1>\frac3{16n^4t^2-3}.\quad}
\end{equation}
These inequalities apply to every defect $d=n-N\ge1$, to arbitrary
support angles, and to all allowed configurations of the other
auxiliary roots.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose any one interior auxiliary root $\sigma$ of $Q$.  Every $u_j$
vanishes there, so Lemma~\ref{P:lem:r4-one-zero-cardinal} applies.
Both factors defining $a_n(r)$ strictly decrease as $r$ increases.
Let $\delta_0=n^{-3}$ and $r_0=1-\delta_0$.  The radial conclusion
therefore gives $a_n(r)>a_n(r_0)$.  A geometric sum and Bernoulli's
inequality give
\[
 1-r_0^n
 =\delta_0\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}r_0^k
 \ge n\delta_0r_0^{n-1}
 \ge n\delta_0\bigl(1-(n-1)\delta_0\bigr)
 \ge\frac78 n\delta_0.
\]
The last inequality follows from $(n-1)/n^3\le1/8$ for $n\ge2$;
on putting $n=v+2$, its cleared numerator is
$v^3+6v^2+4v\ge0$.
Since both denominators in $a_n(r_0)$ are at most $2$,
\[
 a_n(r)>\frac7{32}n\delta_0^2=\frac7{32n^5}.
\]
The function $a\mapsto a/(n-a)$ is increasing for $0<a<n$, proving
the first fraction in \eqref{P:eq:r4-uniform-gamma}.  The comparison with
$1/(5n^6)$ has strictly positive cross-multiplied gap $3n^6+7$.

For the mass-sensitive bound take $\delta_0=1/(n^2t)$ instead.
As $t>1$ and $(n-1)/n^2\le1/4$, one has
\[
 r_0^{n-1}\ge1-(n-1)\delta_0>\frac34.
\]
The same geometric-sum argument yields
$a_n(r)>3n\delta_0^2/16=3/(16n^3t^2)$, and hence
\eqref{P:eq:r4-t-sensitive-gamma}.  Every denominator is positive
under the stated $n,t$ conditions.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[An absolute top-moment deficit]
\label{P:cor:r4-absolute-deficit}
Let $n\ge5$, $N=n-1$, and retain the full competitive stationary
premises.  Write the one-defect moments as
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(k\lambda_j-1)\alpha_j^k=T_k(q)z^k,
 \qquad 1\le k\le n,\qquad q>1,\quad |z|=1.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r4-absolute-deficit}
 \boxed{\quad
 nt-(n-1)-T_n(q)
 >\frac7{8\,000\,000\,n^2(32n^6-7)}
 >\frac1{40\,000\,000\,n^8}.
 \quad}
\end{equation}
The additional mass-sensitive lower bound is
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r4-sensitive-deficit}
 nt-(n-1)-T_n(q)
 >\frac3{8\,000\,000\,n^2(16n^4t^2-3)}.
\end{equation}
In particular, in the two-heavy hull $t<7/2$ this implies the stronger
specialized bound
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r4-hull-deficit}
 nt-(n-1)-T_n(q)
 >\frac3{8\,000\,000\,n^2(196n^4-3)}.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The deleted-polygon deficit argument in
Corollary~\ref{P:cor:round3-top-deficit-cut} proves
\[
 nt-(n-1)-T_n(q)
 >\frac{\min_j(n\lambda_j-1)}{8\,000\,000\,n^2}.
\]
For clarity, its nonnegative identity is
\[
 \sum_j(n\lambda_j-1)|\alpha_j^n-z^n|^2
 =2\bigl(nt-(n-1)-T_n(q)\bigr).
\]
If the displayed lower bound failed, each support point would lie
within chord distance $1/(1000n^2)$ of an $n$th root of $z^n$.
The cardinal separation makes those roots distinct; the $n-1$ support
points would then lie in the excluded deleted-polygon tube.  Substitution
of Theorem~\ref{P:thm:r4-uniform-mass-gap} proves all three bounds.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{What the new constants do and do not prove.}
The previous deficit cut required a positive lower endpoint for every
individual mass excess.  The bounds above supply such an endpoint
uniformly at each index, including for irregular diffuse supports.
They exclude an absolute strip near the top-moment equality surface
and positive-width strips near each face $\lambda_j=1/n$.
They do not show that a remaining candidate must lie in any one of
these strips.  No volume fraction or complete covering statement is
asserted.

\subsection{Exact shared-support constraints retained during the cycles}
\label{P:subsec:r4-shared-support}
The adaptive search also retained an exact annihilator, rather than
treating the moments as independent variables.  Put
\[
 B(x)=\prod_{j=1}^{N}(x-\alpha_j)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{N}b_\ell x^\ell,
 \quad p_k=\sum_j\alpha_j^k,
 \quad M_k=\sum_j\lambda_j\alpha_j^k.
\]
Since $B(\alpha_j)=0$,
\[
 \sum_{\ell=0}^{N}b_\ell M_{k+\ell}=0\qquad(k\ge0).
\]
For $d=1$, $N=n-1$, the known moments consequently obey
\begin{align}
 b_0t+\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}
       \frac{b_\ell}{\ell}\bigl(p_\ell+T_\ell(q)z^\ell\bigr)&=0,
       \label{P:eq:r4-annihilator-zero}\\
 \sum_{\ell=0}^{N}\frac{b_\ell}{\ell+1}
       \bigl(p_{\ell+1}+T_{\ell+1}(q)z^{\ell+1}\bigr)&=0.
       \label{P:eq:r4-annihilator-one}
\end{align}
These are exact consequences useful for future elimination.  They
are not counted as additional exclusions by themselves: the
coefficients $b_\ell$ still encode the unknown shared support.
Likewise, the Chebyshev recurrence becomes the exact identities
\[
 \sum_j\left[(k\lambda_j-1)
     (\alpha_j^2-2qz\alpha_j+z^2)
      +2\lambda_j\alpha_j(\alpha_j-qz)\right]\alpha_j^k=0,
 \qquad 1\le k\le n-2.
\]
At $k=0$ the right side is $-nz^2$, not zero, because the auxiliary
moment $S_0=1$ differs from the atomic expression $-N$.
This diagonal correction is retained in every recurrence test.

\paragraph{Verification.}
The accompanying exact-arithmetic script checks the geometric-kernel
identity at rational complex inputs, the all-index polynomial
comparisons, the annihilator identities at rational complex support
points, and a scalar relaxation witness.  That witness is expressly
not a solution of the full stationary system.  It demonstrates only
that the new scalar cuts alone do not prove coverage.  Infinite
validity of the displayed inequalities is supplied by the proofs
above, not by finite diagnostics.

% Round 4, Gram/geometry stream. Self-contained fragment; no global-cover claim.
\section{Irregular diffuse light blocks with rotational repetition}\label{col:P:20}
\label{P:sec:r4g-rotational}

Assume the stationary cardinal identities
\[
 Q(z)=A(z)\prod_{j=1}^{N}(z-\alpha_j),\quad \deg Q=n,
 \quad |\alpha_j|=1,\quad
 \lambda_j=\left\|\frac{Q(z)}{(z-\alpha_j)Q'(\alpha_j)}\right\|_2^2.
\]
The support points are distinct and $A$ does not vanish at a support
point. Put $d=n-N\ge1$. Select $m$ light points $\beta_j$ and $h\ge1$
remaining support points, so that
\[
 \ell=d+h,\qquad n=m+\ell,\qquad N=m+h.
\]
The sole extra mass hypothesis in this section is
$\lambda_{\beta_j}\le2/n$ for every light point. No upper bound on the
other masses and no additional auxiliary-root restriction is used.
Common rotations of all configurations are permitted.

\subsection{A cardinal inequality retaining an arbitrary light polynomial}

Put $P(z)=\prod_{j=1}^m(z-\beta_j)$. Choose an extra support point $a$,
a light point $\beta$, and write
\[
 Q=(z-a)CP,\quad \deg C=\ell-1,\quad
 V=P/(z-\beta),\quad \delta=|a-\beta|>0.
\]
Suppose $\|CP\|_2\ge L\|C\|_2$, and suppose
$L/\sqrt\ell-\delta\|V\|_2>0$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r4g-general-cardinal}
 \lambda_\beta\ge
 \frac{(L/\sqrt\ell-\delta\|V\|_2)^2}
 {\delta^2|P'(\beta)|^2}.
\end{equation}
Indeed $(z-a)V=P+(\beta-a)V$, while
$\|CV\|_2\le\|C\|_\infty\|V\|_2
\le\sqrt\ell\|C\|_2\|V\|_2$ and
$|C(\beta)|\le\sqrt\ell\|C\|_2$. The triangle inequality and the
cardinal identity give \eqref{P:eq:r4g-general-cardinal}.
For an arbitrary $P$, one admissible $L^2$ is the smallest eigenvalue
of its degree-$(\ell-1)$ multiplication Gram matrix. A directly usable
lower bound is
\[
 L^2\ge\|P\|_2^2-2\sum_{k=1}^{\ell-1}
 \left|\sum_j P_{j+k}\overline{P_j}\right|,
\]
when the right side is positive. This is the Hermitian Gershgorin
bound, not a claim that every remaining light block has small
coefficient correlations.

\subsection{Two regular subpolygons with arbitrary relative phase}

\begin{theorem}[All offsets of two regular subpolygons]
\label{P:thm:r4g-two-exact}
Let $m=2M\ge80\ell$. Suppose the light points are the roots of
\[
 P(z)=(z^M-e^{i\psi})(z^M-e^{-i\psi}),\qquad 0<\psi<\pi.
\]
Then the stationary cardinal identities and the light mass caps are
incompatible, for every placement of the other support points and
all auxiliary roots satisfying the standing assumptions.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put $v=\max\{\psi,\pi-\psi\}\in[\pi/2,\pi)$. Choose a nearest light
point to any extra support point $a$. Then
$\delta\le v/M=2v/m$. Since $\deg C< M$, the three coefficient
blocks of $CP$ are disjoint and
\[
 \|CP\|_2^2=(2+4\cos^2\psi)\|C\|_2^2.
\]
For a root $\beta^M=e^{i\psi}$, the quotient $V$ is the product of
$(z^M-e^{i\psi})/(z-\beta)$, whose $M$ coefficients have modulus
one, with $z^M-e^{-i\psi}$. Its two coefficient blocks are disjoint.
The other light grid is identical. Thus
\[
 \|V\|_2^2=m,\qquad |P'(\beta)|=m\sin\psi=m\sin v.
\]
The numerator in \eqref{P:eq:r4g-general-cardinal}, multiplied by
$\sqrt\ell$, is bounded below by
\[
 \sqrt{2+4\cos^2v}-\frac{2v\sqrt\ell}{\sqrt m}
 \ge\sqrt2-\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{80}}
 >\frac75-\frac{99}{140}=\frac{97}{140}.
\]
Here $\sqrt{80}>80/9$ and $\pi<22/7$ were used.
For $v\le\pi-1$, $v\sin v\le v\le\pi-1$; for
$v\ge\pi-1$, $\sin v\le\pi-v$ and
$v(\pi-v)\le\pi-1$. Therefore
$\delta|P'(\beta)|\le2v\sin v\le2(\pi-1)<30/7$.
Consequently
\[
 \lambda_\beta>\frac1\ell\left(\frac{97}{600}\right)^2
 >\frac2{81\ell}\ge\frac2n.
\]
The strict rational comparison is
$81\cdot97^2-2\cdot600^2=42129>0$. This contradicts the light cap.
\end{proof}

The relative phase is unrestricted, including phases arbitrarily
close to a collision of the two grids (but not an actual collision).
For $d=1,h=2$, this excludes all such exact configurations at odd
$n\ge243$. At $\psi\ne\pi/2$, this family is generally not a regular
$m$-gon. The theorem does not imply that an arbitrary diffuse support
has rotational repetition.

\subsection{A full-dimensional neighborhood of the two-grid family}

\begin{theorem}[Robust nonregular diffuse tubes]
\label{P:thm:r4g-two-robust}
Let $m=2M\ge64\ell$, and let
$\pi/3\le\psi\le2\pi/3$. Let $\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_m$ be the roots
of $P_0(z)=z^{2M}-2\cos\psi\,z^M+1$. If the distinct light support
points can be matched so that
\[
 |\beta_j-\zeta_j|\le\varepsilon\le\frac1{256m^2},
 \qquad 1\le j\le m,
\]
then the entire closed tube is excluded by the stationary cardinal
identities and the light mass caps, for all extra support angles and
all auxiliary roots under the standing assumptions.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The reference light points have angular separation at least
$4\pi/(3m)$ and chord separation at least $8/(3m)$. Moreover
$|P_0'(\zeta_j)|=m\sin\psi\le m$. Let $R=P-P_0$. Product expansion
using $\prod(1+x_i)\le(1-\sum x_i)^{-1}$ for nonnegative $x_i$ with
sum less than one yields
\[
 |P(\zeta_j)|\le
 \frac{m\varepsilon}{1-3m^2\varepsilon/8}
 \le\frac8{2045m}.
\]
Write $R=U+z^M W$, with $\deg U,\deg W<M$. Discrete Parseval on the
two grids gives
\[
 \frac1m\sum_j|R(\zeta_j)|^2
 =\|U\|_2^2+\|W\|_2^2+
 2\cos\psi\,\Re\langle U,W\rangle
 \ge\tfrac12\|R\|_2^2.
\]
Hence
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r4g-robust-bounds}
 \|R\|_2\le\frac{8\sqrt2}{2045m}<\frac1{160m},
 \qquad
 |P'(\beta_j)|\le\frac m{1-3m^2\varepsilon/4}
 \le\frac{1024m}{1021}<\frac{256m}{255}.
\end{equation}
For the matching root $\zeta$, let $V_0=P_0/(z-\zeta)$. As above,
$\|V_0\|_2=\sqrt m$, and
\[
 (z-\beta)(V-V_0)=R+(\beta-\zeta)V_0.
\]
Division by a unit-circle linear factor, on a polynomial of degree at
most $m-1$ which vanishes there, has coefficient-norm bound at most
$m$. This follows by writing the quotient coefficients as partial
sums and applying Cauchy--Schwarz. Therefore, using $m\ge4$,
\[
 \|V\|_2<\sqrt m+\frac1{160}+\frac1{256\sqrt m}
 <\sqrt m+\frac1{100}.
\]
The nearest perturbed light point to any $a\in\mathbb T$ satisfies
\[
 \delta\le\frac{4\pi}{3m}+\varepsilon<\frac{21}{5m}.
\]
The coefficient blocks of $CP_0$ are disjoint, so
$\|CP_0\|_2\ge\sqrt2\|C\|_2$ and
$\|CP\|_2\ge(\sqrt2-\sqrt\ell\|R\|_2)\|C\|_2$.
The numerator bracket in \eqref{P:eq:r4g-general-cardinal}, multiplied
by $\sqrt\ell$, is thus strictly greater than
\[
 \sqrt2-\frac{21\sqrt\ell}{5\sqrt m}
 -\frac{193\sqrt\ell}{4000m}
 \ge\sqrt2-\frac{21}{40}-\frac{193}{256000}
 >\frac45.
\]
Also $\delta|P'(\beta)|<1792/425$. It follows that
\[
 \lambda_\beta>
 \frac1\ell\left(\frac{85}{448}\right)^2
 >\frac2{65\ell}\ge\frac2n.
\]
The rational margin is
$65\cdot85^2-2\cdot448^2=68217>0$, proving the contradiction.
\end{proof}

For $d=1,h=2$, this gives a continuous, individually perturbed
nonregular diffuse family at every odd $n\ge195$. Its central relative
phase interval is macroscopic: at $\psi=\pi/3$ the consecutive
reference gaps alternate between $4\pi/(3m)$ and $8\pi/(3m)$, rather
than the common gap $2\pi/m$ of a regular $m$-gon. The perturbation
radius still shrinks as $m^{-2}$; no parameter-space volume estimate
or complete diffuse-support cover is asserted.

\subsection{Any fixed number of rotationally repeated components}

\begin{theorem}[Arbitrary base pattern repeated around the circle]
\label{P:thm:r4g-p-grid}
Let $p\ge1$ be an integer and let
$F(w)=\prod_{k=1}^{p}(w-\gamma_k)$ have distinct unit-circle roots.
Suppose the light support consists of the $m=pM$ roots of
$P(z)=F(z^M)$. If
\[
 M\ge32\,4^{p-1}\ell,
\]
then the cardinal identities and the light mass caps are incompatible,
for every choice of $F$, every extra support placement, and all
auxiliary roots under the standing assumptions.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Since $\deg C<M$, the coefficient blocks give
$\|CP\|_2=\|C\|_2\|F\|_2\ge\sqrt2\|C\|_2$.
Choose a light point nearest to an extra support point $a$; even one
of the $p$ regular $M$-gons ensures $\delta\le\pi/M$. For
$\beta^M=\gamma_k$, put $F_k=F/(w-\gamma_k)$. The product
representation and disjoint blocks show
\[
 \|P/(z-\beta)\|_2=\sqrt M\|F_k\|_2
 \le\sqrt M\,2^{p-1},\qquad
 |P'(\beta)|=M|F'(\gamma_k)|\le M2^{p-1}.
\]
The norm bound follows from the coefficient $\ell^1$ bound
$\|F_k\|_1\le\prod_{j\ne k}(1+|\gamma_j|)=2^{p-1}$.
The numerator bracket in \eqref{P:eq:r4g-general-cardinal}, multiplied
by $\sqrt\ell$, is at least
\[
 \sqrt2-\frac{\pi2^{p-1}\sqrt\ell}{\sqrt M}
 \ge\sqrt2-\frac\pi{\sqrt{32}}
 >\frac75-\frac{55}{98}=\frac{411}{490}>\frac45.
\]
Here $\sqrt{32}>28/5$, $\pi<22/7$, and $\pi^2<10$ suffice.
Consequently
\[
 \lambda_\beta>
 \frac8{125\,4^{p-1}\ell}
 >\frac1{16\,4^{p-1}\ell}
 \ge\frac1{16p\,4^{p-1}\ell}>
 \frac2{pM+\ell}=\frac2n.
\]
This is the required contradiction.
\end{proof}

The special two-grid theorem is substantially sharper for $p=2$.
For fixed $p$, however, this last result allows an arbitrary base
pattern on the circle; the spacing ratios of that pattern need not be
close to one. The requisite number of repetitions grows exponentially
with $p$, so allowing $p$ to grow without control does not supply a
cover of all remaining supports.

\subsection{An exact obstruction to using cardinal constraints alone}

The following auxiliary example is not a stationary candidate and is
not offered as a counterexample to the coefficient conjecture. It
identifies an invalid proposed shortcut in the ten-cycle search.
Take $n=5$, $N=4$, $s=2/3$,
$Q=(z-s)(z^4-1)$, and use the four support points $1,-1,i,-i$.
The cardinal identities give, exactly,
\[
 (\lambda_1,\lambda_{-1},\lambda_i,\lambda_{-i})
 =(1,11/50,1/4,1/4),\qquad t=43/25.
\]
These positive masses satisfy $\lambda_j>1/n$ and $n/N<t<n$.
The algebraic ratio from $\|Q\|_2^2/|Q_nQ_0|$ is $13/3$; even
$e^{-t}\|Q\|_2^2/|Q_nQ_0|>2/e$ holds, because
$e^{18/25}<13/6$. Nevertheless the first moment is
$|S_1|=39/50$, whereas the auxiliary modulus requires
$q=(s+s^{-1})/2=13/12$. Thus the full moment compatibility fails.
A proof using only cardinal norms, scalar mass bounds, and this
coefficient ratio would leave a false feasible point. The shared
moment and boundary equations must be retained.

\paragraph{Proof status and reproducibility.}
The three exclusion theorems above are uniform analytic statements
on their explicitly specified families. The standard-library
verifier checks the rational constants, coefficient-block identities,
quotient and derivative formulas at exact Gaussian-rational inputs,
two-grid frame identities, and the exact relaxation obstruction.
These checks supplement the proofs, not a finite-index extrapolation.
The ten-cycle ledger records both accepted conclusions and failed
coverage attempts. No implication placing every remaining support in
one of the proved families has been established.

\section{A coefficient certificate without support-geometry assumptions}\label{col:P:21}
\label{P:sec:r4-lacunary}

Let a positive Herglotz measure have total mass $t>0$ and moments
\[
 M_j=\int_{\mathbb T}\alpha^j\,d\mu(\alpha),\qquad
 f(z)=e^{-t}\exp\!\left(-2\sum_{j\ge1}M_jz^j\right).
\]
Finite atomic measures are included, but neither stationarity nor
a restriction on the number or arrangement of support points is needed
in this section.  A unimodular constant multiplying $f$ does not affect
the statements about absolute coefficients.

\begin{theorem}[A selectable high-harmonic certificate]
\label{P:thm:r4-harmonic-certificate}
Let $n\ge2$ and choose an integer $k$ with $n/2\le k<n$.  Define
\[
 \epsilon_k=2\sum_{\substack{1\le j\le n\\j\notin\{k,n\}}}|M_j|.
\]
For $t\ge1/2$,
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r4-harmonic-bound}
 \boxed{
 |[z^n]f|\le 2te^{-t}
 \bigl(\max\{1,|t-1|\}+e^{\epsilon_k}-1\bigr).
 }
\end{equation}
In particular, either of the following closed conditions excludes
competitiveness, for every $n$ and every allowed choice of $k$:
\begin{align}
 t\ge2,\quad \epsilon_k\le\frac14
 &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad |[z^n]f|<2/e,
 \label{P:eq:r4-harmonic-large-mass}\\
 t\ge\frac32,\quad \epsilon_k\le\frac1{14}
 &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad |[z^n]f|<\frac{189}{260}
 <\frac8{11}<2/e.
 \label{P:eq:r4-harmonic-medium-mass}
\end{align}
No equal-mass, regular-polygon, auxiliary-root, or angular-tube
hypothesis occurs in these tests.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put
\[
 A(z)=-2\sum_{\substack{1\le j\le n\\j\notin\{k,n\}}}M_jz^j,
 \qquad E(z)=e^{A(z)}-1.
\]
The coefficient $\ell^1$ norm gives
\[
 \sum_{j\ge1}|E_j|\le e^{\epsilon_k}-1.
\]
Through degree $n$ the original exponential equals
$e^{-t}\exp(-2M_kz^k-2M_nz^n)(1+E(z))$.
Since $2k\ge n$, its $n$th coefficient is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r4-harmonic-identity}
 e^t[z^n]f
 =-2M_n+\mathbf1_{\{2k=n\}}2M_k^2
        +E_n-2M_kE_{n-k}.
\end{equation}
The indices $n$ and $n-k$ are distinct positive integers.
Consequently, $|M_k|\le t$ and $2t\ge1$ give the sharper error estimate
\[
 |E_n-2M_kE_{n-k}|
 \le2t\bigl(|E_n|+|E_{n-k}|\bigr)
 \le2t(e^{\epsilon_k}-1).
\]
For $2k>n$, the principal term has modulus at most $2t$.
For $2k=n$, normalize $\mu/t$ to a probability measure and put
$X=\alpha^k$, $u=\mathbb E X=M_k/t$, and
$v=\mathbb E X^2=M_n/t$.  The elementary covariance estimate
\[
 |v-u^2|=|\mathbb E(X-u)^2|
 \le\mathbb E|X-u|^2=1-|u|^2
\]
implies
\[
 |M_k^2-M_n|
 =t|tu^2-v|
 \le t\bigl(|t-1||u|^2+1-|u|^2\bigr)
 \le t\max\{1,|t-1|\}.
\]
This proves \eqref{P:eq:r4-harmonic-bound}.

For \eqref{P:eq:r4-harmonic-large-mass}, put $y=t-2\ge0$.
The exponential series, with its tail bounded by a geometric series,
gives
\[
 e^{1/4}<1+\frac14+\frac1{32}+\frac1{360}
 =\frac{1849}{1440}<\frac97,
 \qquad e>\frac{163}{60}.
\]
Therefore
\begin{align*}
 e^{t-1}-t(t-2+e^{\epsilon_k})
 &>\frac{163}{60}\left(1+y+\frac{y^2}{2}+\frac{y^3}{6}\right)
       -(y+2)(y+9/7)\\
 &=P(y),
 \qquad
 P(y)=\frac{61}{420}-\frac{239}{420}y
             +\frac{43}{120}y^2+\frac{163}{360}y^3.
\end{align*}
This cubic is positive on the entire half-line.  Here is an explicit
certificate, so no finite-degree sweep or numerical minimization is
being used.  Set $c=7/16$ and $u=y-c\ge-c$.  The inequality
$u^3\ge-cu^2$ yields
\[
 P(y)\ge p+qu+ru^2
 \ge p-\frac{q^2}{4r}
 =\frac{3486863399}{1256053800960}>0,
\]
where
\[
 p=\frac{28723}{10321920},\qquad
 q=\frac{193}{43008},\qquad
 r=\frac{2173}{2880}>0.
\]
Multiplying the strict positive gap by $2e^{-t}$ proves
\eqref{P:eq:r4-harmonic-large-mass}, including $t=2$ and
$\epsilon_k=1/4$.

For \eqref{P:eq:r4-harmonic-medium-mass}, first observe that
\[
 2te^{-t}\max\{1,|t-1|\}<\frac{27}{40},
 \qquad 2te^{-t}<\frac{27}{40}\quad(t\ge3/2).
\]
On $[3/2,2]$, the first expression is $2te^{-t}$, which is decreasing,
and $e^{3/2}>40/9$ follows from the degree-six exponential partial sum.
On $[2,\infty)$, the maximum of $2t(t-1)e^{-t}$ is attained at
$\tau=(3+\sqrt5)/2$.  The exact inequalities
\[
 \frac{157}{60}<\tau<\frac{131}{50},\qquad
 \sum_{j=0}^{10}\frac{(157/60)^j}{j!}>\frac{1696}{125}
\]
give $(4\tau-2)e^{-\tau}<5/8<27/40$.
Finally $e^{1/14}<14/13$, hence
\[
 |[z^n]f|<\frac{27}{40}\frac{14}{13}
 =\frac{189}{260}<\frac8{11}<\frac2e.
\]
The last comparison uses $e<11/4$, for example by summing through
degree five and bounding the remaining series by
$(1/720)/(1-1/7)$.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{How this cuts the stationary search domain.}
Every competitive candidate with $t\ge2$ must have
$\epsilon_k>1/4$ for \emph{every} allowed $k$.  Every competitive
candidate with $t\ge3/2$ must have $\epsilon_k>1/14$ for every such $k$.
Since $t\ge n/N$, the first conclusion applies automatically when
$N\le n/2$, and the second when $N\le2n/3$.
These are quantitative restrictions on the weighted moments of
arbitrary support configurations.  They do not assert that all
remaining candidates have small $\epsilon_k$.

\begin{corollary}[A necessary off-harmonic floor in every support defect]
\label{P:cor:r4-harmonic-floor}
Every competitive stationary candidate with $1\le N<n$, $d=n-N$,
and $t\ge n/N$ satisfies, for every integer $n/2\le k<n$,
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:r4-harmonic-floor}
 \boxed{\epsilon_k>
      \min\left\{\frac{d^2}{2nN},\frac14\right\}.}
\end{equation}
For $d=1$ this reads
\[
 2\sum_{\substack{1\le j\le n\\j\notin\{k,n\}}}|M_j|
 >\frac1{2n(n-1)}.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For $1<t\le2$, Theorem~\ref{P:thm:r4-harmonic-certificate} reduces to
$|[z^n]f|\le2t\exp(-t+\epsilon_k)$.
For every $t>1$,
\[
 t-1-\log t>\frac{(t-1)^2}{2t},
\]
because the difference vanishes at $t=1$ and has derivative
$(t-1)^2/(2t^2)>0$.
Also $(t-1)^2/(2t)$ is increasing for $t>1$, so
\[
 \frac{(t-1)^2}{2t}\ge
 \frac{(n/N-1)^2}{2n/N}=\frac{d^2}{2nN}.
\]
If $\epsilon_k$ is no larger than the right side of
\eqref{P:eq:r4-harmonic-floor}, the coefficient is strictly below
$2/e$ on $1<t\le2$.  For $t\ge2$, the same conclusion follows
from \eqref{P:eq:r4-harmonic-large-mass}.  This proves the corollary.
\end{proof}

\section{Why fixed-support mass Hessians cannot finish the cover}\label{col:P:22}
\label{P:sec:r4-mass-hessian}

The following calculation audits a plausible route which does not add
an independent exclusion once the stationary nonnegative polynomial is
already imposed.  It is useful precisely because it prevents repeatedly
asking an equivalent positivity test to do new work.

Let
\[
 H_j(z)=\frac{1+\alpha_jz}{1-\alpha_jz},\quad
 f(z)=\exp\!\left(-\sum_j\lambda_jH_j(z)\right),
 \quad a_n>0.
\]
Suppose the stationary reciprocal polynomial
\[
 R_0(z)=\sum_{r=0}^na_rz^r+
                 \sum_{r=0}^{n-1}\overline{a_r}z^{2n-r}
\]
has a double zero at every pole $\overline{\alpha_j}$ and
$h_0(\theta)=e^{-in\theta}R_0(e^{i\theta})\ge0$.
The circle convention for $h_0$ is the reflection of the convention
used for the support angles; its nonnegativity is unchanged.

\begin{proposition}[The mass Hessian is automatically negative definite]
\label{P:prop:r4-mass-hessian}
Under these hypotheses, for every nonzero real vector $c$,
\[
 \left.\frac{d^2}{ds^2}\Re[z^n]
 \exp\!\left(-\sum_j(\lambda_j+sc_j)H_j(z)\right)
 \right|_{s=0}<0.
\]
Thus a fixed-support mass Hessian test cannot exclude any additional
point from this stationary spectral set.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Put $H_c=\sum_jc_jH_j$.
The second derivative is $\Re[z^n]fH_c^2$.
Because $R_0=f+O(z^{n+1})$ at zero, this is
$\Re[z^n]R_0H_c^2$.  All poles cancel, so $R_0H_c^2$ is a polynomial
of degree at most $2n$.  On the unit circle away from the support,
$H_c(e^{i\theta})=i\kappa_c(\theta)$ with $\kappa_c$ real.  Hence
\[
 \Re[z^n]R_0H_c^2
 =-\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}
                  h_0(\theta)\kappa_c(\theta)^2\,d\theta<0.
\]
The apparent singularities are removable in the product.
Strictness follows because $h_0$ is a nonzero nonnegative
trigonometric polynomial and $H_c$ is a nonzero rational function:
the distinct poles force $c=0$ if $H_c$ vanishes identically.
\end{proof}

\section{An exact all-degree audit family below the competitive level}\label{col:P:23}
\label{P:sec:r4-audit-family}

The next family identifies a further obstruction to a proof based
solely on local stationarity.  It is not a counterexample to the
Krzy\.{z} coefficient conjecture.
Let $k\ge1$, $n=2k$, $N=k$, and
\[
 \tau=\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2},\qquad
 f_k(z)=\exp\!\left[-\tau\frac{1+z^k}{1-z^k}\right].
\]
The support is the regular $k$-gon, with masses $\tau/k$.
Its coefficient is
\[
 [z^{2k}]f_k=2\tau(\tau-1)e^{-\tau}
 =(4\tau-2)e^{-\tau}<5/8<2/e.
\]
Its stationary polynomial is nonnegative:
\[
 e^\tau h_0(\theta)
 =4\bigl(\cos(k\theta)-1\bigr)
       \bigl(\cos(k\theta)-(\tau-1)\bigr)\ge0.
\]
It vanishes precisely at the $k$ support points.  Thus the full
first-order support and mass conditions hold.  In particular the
fixed-support mass Hessian is negative definite by
Proposition~\ref{P:prop:r4-mass-hessian}.

\begin{proposition}[Even the full mass--angle Hessian does not remove this family]
\label{P:prop:r4-full-hessian}
For every $k\ge1$, the Hessian of
$\Re[z^{2k}]f$ in the $k$ positive masses and their $k$ angles is
negative definite at $f_k$.  Nevertheless its coefficient is strictly
below $2/e$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
All Hessian entries below are divided by the positive factor
$e^{-\tau}$.  Put $A=2\tau(\tau-1)=4\tau-2$ and
$\theta_j=2\pi j/k$.
Differentiating the finite coefficient series gives the mass block
\[
 U=A\mathbf1\mathbf1^T+8k(1-\tau)I,
\]
the mixed block
\[
 V_{ii}=0,\qquad
 V_{ij}=4\tau(\tau-1)\cot\frac{\theta_i-\theta_j}{2}
 \quad(i\ne j),
\]
and the angle block with
\begin{align*}
 W_{ij}&=-\frac{4\tau^2(\tau-1)}k
                  \csc^2\frac{\theta_i-\theta_j}{2}
                  &&(i\ne j),\\
 W_{ii}&=4k\tau(2-\tau)
 -\frac{4\tau^2}{3k}\bigl((4-\tau)k^2+\tau-1\bigr).
\end{align*}
For example, the generating series used for these derivatives are
\[
 H_j=1+2\sum_{r\ge1}\alpha_j^rz^r,\quad
 D_j=2\sum_{r\ge1}r\alpha_j^rz^r,\quad
 E_j=2\sum_{r\ge1}r^2\alpha_j^rz^r.
\]
The three blocks are respectively the real parts of the $2k$th
coefficients of $fH_iH_j$,
$i\lambda_j fH_iD_j-i\mathbf1_{i=j}fD_j$, and
$-\lambda_i\lambda_j fD_iD_j+
 \mathbf1_{i=j}\lambda_i fE_i$.

All blocks are circulant, with $V$ skew symmetric.
The elementary finite Fourier sums
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\cot(\pi j/k)\sin(2\pi rj/k)&=k-2r,\\
 \sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\csc^2(\pi j/k)\cos(2\pi rj/k)
 &=\frac{k^2-1}{3}-2r(k-r)
 \qquad(1\le r\le k-1)
\end{align*}
diagonalize them.  These identities follow, for instance, from
$\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}x^j=(1-x^k)/(1-x)$ and one differentiation;
the second also follows by taking a second finite difference in $r$
and its value at $r=0$.
In the constant mode the two eigenvalues are
$k(6-4\tau)<0$ and $-8k\tau(\tau-1)<0$, with zero mixed entry.
In a nonconstant mode, the Hermitian $2$-by-$2$ block has diagonal
entries
\[
 -8k(\tau-1),\qquad
 \frac{8\tau(\tau-1)}k
       \bigl(\tau r(k-r)-k^2\bigr),
\]
and mixed entry of modulus $4\tau(\tau-1)|k-2r|$.
Both diagonals are negative since $\tau<4$ and
$r(k-r)\le k^2/4$.  Its determinant is exactly
\[
 16\tau(\tau-1)^2(4-\tau)k^2>0.
\]
Thus every block is negative definite, proving the proposition.
\end{proof}

For the absolute coefficient, common rotation gives its expected
one-dimensional null direction.  The imaginary part of the first
angle derivative is $2A e^{-\tau}$ at every point, and all first
mass derivatives vanish.  Thus passing from $\Re a_n$ to $|a_n|$
adds $4A\mathbf1\mathbf1^T$ to the scaled angle block.  This cancels
exactly the constant angle eigenvalue and leaves every nonconstant
block unchanged.  Hence these are strict local maxima on the
fixed-$N$ mass--angle manifold modulo common rotation; no assertion
of local maximality under arbitrary support-splitting variations is
needed or made.

For $k\ge2$, this audit family also lies strictly inside the old
scalar mass interval: $n/N=2$, the iterated lower boundary is below
$(n+1)/N=2+1/k\le5/2<\tau$, and $\tau<T(2k)$.
It has support ratio $1/2$, well above the support-density lower
cutoff.  Its auxiliary moduli have the form
\[
 r_k=\bigl(\tau-1-\sqrt{(\tau-1)^2-1}\bigr)^{1/k}.
\]
They also obey the new radial separation bounds.  Indeed the base
inside the parentheses is $r_0<1/2$, and concavity of $x^{1/k}$ gives
$1-r_k\ge(1-r_0)/k>1/(2k)=1/n$.
This shows why the competitive coefficient condition must remain
part of every attempted global covering argument.  The family is
removed directly by Theorem~\ref{P:thm:r4-harmonic-certificate}, because
its off-harmonic defect $\epsilon_k$ is zero.

\paragraph{Verification scope.}
The accompanying standard-library script checks the rational
exponential bounds, the positive-cubic certificate, exact coefficient
factorizations, the algebraic determinant identity, and exact
mass--angle derivatives at the $k=1,2,4$ audit members.
The latter finite cases check algebra and conventions; the all-$k$
validity is proved by the displayed Fourier block formulas.

\section{The initial reduced domain and its covering obligation}\label{col:P:24}

\subsection{Support, mass, and separation conditions}

Let
\[
 c_{\mathrm{at}}=\frac\pi8\left(\frac4e-1\right)^2
   >\frac{873}{10000},\qquad
 T(n)=\min\left\{n,\frac{19}{20}(n+10),\frac9{10}(n+31)\right\}.
\]
Let $\ell_{*,\infty}(n,N)$ be the fixed point of
\[
 x\longmapsto\frac nN+\frac1N F(e^{x-1})
\]
constructed in the lower-mass iteration.  Every deficient-support
maximizer must now satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{P:eq:remaining-domain}
 \boxed{\begin{gathered}
  2\le N\le n-1,\qquad N>c_{\mathrm{at}}n,\qquad \lambda_j>1/n+1/(5n^7),\\
  \ell_{*,\infty}(n,N)\le t<T(n),\\
  |\alpha_j-\alpha_k|>
  \sqrt{\frac{24}{n(n^2-1)T(n)}}\quad(j\ne k).
 \end{gathered}}
\end{equation}
In particular, the exact rational support exclusion gives the usable
integer lower bound
\[
 N\ge\max\left\{2,\left\lfloor\frac{873n}{10000}\right\rfloor+1\right\}.
\]
The one-atom stratum remains excluded by its stationary lower mass
$t\ge n$ and the uniform coefficient tail.  The new phase argument
excludes additional whole support strata whenever $N\le c_{\mathrm{at}}n$.
For example, $n=100$ requires $N\ge9$, and $n=1000$ requires $N\ge88$.
These are bounds on the number of support atoms, not statements about
the fraction of parameter-space volume removed.

Every remaining candidate must satisfy all stationary equations,
the inertia energy inequalities, every cardinal Gram constraint,
and the conditioned mass equalities
\eqref{P:eq:conditioned-mass-equality}.  It must also avoid all applicable
regular-polygon, deleted-polygon, cluster, and multi-arc regions proved
above.  The simpler finite lower mass bound remains
\[
 \frac nN+\frac{n^2-N^2}{Nn(n+3N)}<t<T(n).
\]
These conditions do not assert that any actual maximizer exists in
their intersection.

\subsection{The resulting compact auxiliary bounds}

For one auxiliary root, $d=1$ and $N=n-1$, the top moment gives
\[
 T_n(q)\le\sum_j(n\lambda_j-1)
       =nt-(n-1)<nT(n)-(n-1).
\]
Since $T_n(\cosh u)=\cosh(nu)$, the sharpened cutoff is
\[
 1<q<\cosh\!\left(
     \frac{\operatorname{arcosh}(nT(n)-(n-1))}{n}\right).
\]
In the special light/heavy hull of the multi-arc section, the separate
bound $q<11/10$ and the sharper harmonic envelope also apply.
For several auxiliary roots their phases must be retained; the
one-root formula cannot be applied independently to each root.

A coarser rational cutoff works in every defect.  Put
\[
 A=2T(n)+n+N=2T(n)+2N+d,\qquad
 u_\ell=1/\overline{\sigma_\ell}.
\]
For $1\le k\le d$, the moment equations imply
\[
 \left|\sum_\ell u_\ell^k\right|
 \le2kt+2N+d<2kT(n)+2N+d\le kA\le A^k.
\]
Here $A\ge2$, which justifies the last inequality for every $k\ge1$.
Newton's identities give $|e_j|\le A^j$ for all elementary symmetric
functions of these roots: inductively,
$|e_j|\le j^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^j A^kA^{j-k}=A^j$.
If a root had modulus at least $2A$, its monic polynomial would imply
$1\le\sum_{j=1}^d(A/|u|)^j<1$, a contradiction.  Hence
\[
 |\sigma_\ell|>\frac1{2A},\qquad
 q_\ell=\frac{|\sigma_\ell|+|\sigma_\ell|^{-1}}2
        <A+\frac1{4A}.
\]
The bounds on mass, auxiliary roots, and support separation give
explicit closed over-covers at each fixed index.  They do not show
that every point in such an over-cover can be excluded uniformly.

\subsection{Further necessary conditions after the corpus transfers}

Every remaining candidate must also avoid the cluster and diffuse-light
families of Sections~\ref{P:sec:r3-analytic-clusters} and
\ref{P:sec:r3-spectral}.  These exclusions permit arbitrary auxiliary
defect whenever their stated support and mass hypotheses hold.
For $d=1$, the arbitrary-mass regular-support and deleted-polygon
tubes give additional restrictions.  In particular, if
$B(z)=\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}(z-\alpha_j)$, then for $n\ge4$
\[
 \sum_{k=1}^{n-2}|[z^k]B|^2>
 \frac{(n-1)^2}{64n^6(n-2)}.
\]
If $t\le7/2$, the denominator improves to $576n^4(n-2)$.
For $n\ge5$ the sharpened top-moment inequality is
\[
 T_n(q)<nt-(n-1)
 -\frac{\min_j(n\lambda_j-1)}{8\,000\,000\,n^2}.
\]
In the third revision this was a pointwise cut requiring a supplied
positive mass gap.  The fourth revision now supplies an explicit
index-only lower bound for that minimum, as described next.  The
constants still tend to zero as the coefficient index grows.

In the $n-3$ light, two-heavy hull, all phases of the two remaining
points are excluded whenever $n\ge99$ and the light support lies in
the stated regular-light tube.  At $6\le n\le98$ the same tube is
excluded when the heavy chord is at most $7/12$ and their masses are
at most $3/4$.  These statements do not impose regularity on an
arbitrary remaining configuration; that missing implication is part
of the outstanding coverage problem.

\subsection{Geometry-free and repeated-pattern cuts after ten cycles}
Every auxiliary root now also satisfies
\[
 \frac1{2A}<|\sigma_\ell|<1-\frac1{n^3},
 \qquad q_\ell-1>\frac1{2n^6}.
\]
For $n\ge3$ the upper modulus improves to $1-1/(n^2t)$.
Every individual mass excess is bounded below by
\[
 n\lambda_j-1>\frac7{32n^6-7}>\frac1{5n^6},
 \qquad n\lambda_j-1>\frac3{16n^4t^2-3}\quad(n\ge3).
\]
For one defect, the absolute top-moment deficit exceeds
$1/(40\,000\,000n^8)$, with the stronger mass-sensitive versions
in Section~\ref{P:sec:r4-moment-floors}.
Every candidate must also obey the off-harmonic floor
\eqref{P:eq:r4-harmonic-floor} for every eligible integer $k$.
When $t\ge2$ this floor improves to $\epsilon_k>1/4$;
when $t\ge3/2$ it improves to $\epsilon_k>1/14$.
Finally, the rotationally repeated light families and their stated
perturbed neighborhoods in Section~\ref{P:sec:r4g-rotational} are excluded.

These results remove boundary strips and explicit irregular diffuse
families from the remaining parameter domain.  They do not force an
arbitrary surviving support into one of those families.  The exact
shared-support identities in Section~\ref{P:subsec:r4-shared-support}
must be retained; their mere reformulation is not counted as an
exclusion.  The subcompetitive family of
Section~\ref{P:sec:r4-audit-family} demonstrates why local stationarity
and Hessian negativity cannot replace $|a_n|\ge2/e$.

\subsection{What is still unproved}

For the remaining domain $\mathcal R_{n,N}$, a global result still
requires explicit families $B_\nu(n,N)$ for which both
\[
 \mathcal R_{n,N}\subseteq\bigcup_{\nu\in I(n,N)}B_\nu(n,N)
 \quad\hbox{and}\quad
 B_\nu(n,N)\text{ contains no competitive maximizer}
\]
are proved for every required integer $n,N$.  Certificate sizes and
the number of regions may grow with the index, provided the
construction and validity are established.  The present note proves
new infinite exclusion families, not this remaining covering theorem.

In particular, sufficiently diffuse angles outside the stated
multi-arc regions, more general mass patterns, and auxiliary root
configurations compatible with all the new cuts remain to be addressed.
The scalar lower-mass iteration has a proved limit below $(n+1)/N$;
repeating it alone cannot exhaust the surviving interval.  The
unweighted Laguerre energy bound also has the limitation derived
above.  The moment equations can have subthreshold solutions, so
competitiveness must remain part of the global target.
