\section{The exact target and the meaning of a closed region}\label{col:F:01}
The Krzy\.{z} problem asks whether
\[
 |a_n|\le 2/e\qquad(n\ge1)
\]
for every holomorphic function $f(z)=\sum_{j\ge0}a_jz^j$ with
$0<|f(z)|\le1$ in the unit disk.  A strict upper bound below $2/e$
on a specified parameter set excludes that entire set from the
competitive extremizers.  The number of inequalities, parameter
intervals or checking cases is not a count of possible counterexamples.

The starting source for the continuation recorded in this part is the uploaded archive
\emph{Krzyz Revision 4 Residual Rounds 01--10} (the uploaded ZIP).
Its sixty submissions extend the earlier fourth revision; they are
not the earlier eight-dimensional catalogue of 384 boxes at degree
eight.  The supplied cumulative audit reports complete deficient
support strata $N=2$ and $N=3$, and the $N=4$ strata at $n=9,10$
and $n\ge27$.  It leaves the degree-$26$ four-atom mass window
$(46/5,39/4)$ after its particular phase and Fourier tests.
These are the baseline scopes used here.  The separate earlier
eighth-degree manuscript was neither replaced nor fully re-audited
by this continuation.  Its four-atom component is identified separately
in the provenance material when used.

\subsection{This revision and its proof scope}
The additional uploaded archive \emph{Krzyz Revision4 Residual Rounds
11--30} contains 120 main manuscripts, six per round.  Their source
texts and screening ledgers are embedded for provenance.  New adopted
proofs begin at Section~\ref{F:sec:r6groundstate}; the cumulative remaining
scope is updated in Section~\ref{F:sec:r6-ledger}.  Earlier finite results
are retained with their original certificates and are not counted again
as new closures.  In particular, the all-degree four-support completion
below belongs to the preceding version of this continuation.

\subsection{Positive measures and stationary candidates}
For a positive finite measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb T$, write
\[
 t=\mu(\mathbb T),\qquad M_j=\int\alpha^j\,d\mu(\alpha),\qquad
 f(z)=\exp\left[-\int\frac{1+\alpha z}{1-\alpha z}\,d\mu(\alpha)\right].
\]
An arbitrary constant factor of modulus one may be restored.
The direct coefficient bounds below are proved for this entire positive
measure class, not merely for stationary candidates.

For the connection with global extremizers,
Section~\ref{F:sec:self-contained-stationary} proves the standard finite
atomic stationary reduction developed in the cited structural
work and supplied source \cite{F:agler,F:lei,F:wik,F:source}.
A deficient candidate has $N<n$ distinct atoms of positive masses,
total mass $t$, and $d=n-N$.  Its stationary nonnegative trigonometric
polynomial has a spectral factor $Q$ of degree $n$ and satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:standing-stationarity}
 (n-D)h=\Phi h,\qquad h=|Q|^2,\qquad
 \Phi(\theta)=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\frac{\lambda_j}{2}
                \csc^2\frac{\theta-\theta_j}{2}.
\end{equation}
Here $D$ multiplies Laurent coefficient $k$ by $|k|$.
The physical pole is $\zeta_j=e^{i\theta_j}$, while the moment
convention is $\alpha_j=\overline{\zeta_j}$.
These reflected circle conventions are not interchanged silently.

Two elementary consequences explain the domains used in the finite
continuation.  At a pole, evaluating
\eqref{F:eq:standing-stationarity} after cancelling the double zero gives
\[
 \lambda_j=
 \left\|\frac{Q(z)}{(z-\zeta_j)Q'(\zeta_j)}\right\|_{H^2}^2
 \ge\frac1n.
\]
Indeed the displayed polynomial has degree at most $n-1$ and value
one at $\zeta_j$, so Cauchy--Schwarz for its $n$ coefficients gives
the inequality.  The identity at a boundary zero follows by expanding
$D|Q|^2$ in Fourier coefficients; if $Q=(z-\zeta)B$, then
$D|Q|^2(\zeta)=-2\|B\|_2^2$.  A multiple zero at a pole would make
the right side of \eqref{F:eq:standing-stationarity} vanish there but
leave the left side strictly positive, so the pole zeros are simple.

The other consequence is $t\ge n/N$.  To see it without a positivity
assumption on a moment relaxation, write $Q(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}q_jz^j$.
For $s_r(j)=1$ if $j>r$ and $s_r(j)=-1$ otherwise,
\[
 \frac n2-|i-j|=\frac12\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}s_r(i)s_r(j).
\]
This positive Gram representation proves $(n/2-D)|Q|^2\ge0$ on
the circle.  Thus \eqref{F:eq:standing-stationarity} gives
$\Phi\ge n/2$ off the poles, first where $h>0$ and then by
continuity.  The boundary phase of the Herglotz function has the
Cauchy pushforward law, proved again in the phase section below.
The positive inverse-branch derivatives are continuous, so the density
identity holds at every finite phase value. At phase zero, its $N$
inverse branches consequently satisfy
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{N}\frac1{\Phi(\beta_j)}=\frac2t.
\]
The bound $\Phi\ge n/2$ gives $2/t\le2N/n$, as required.
The strict coefficient tail for every $n\ge2$ and $t\ge n$ is
reproduced with its exact certificate in
Section~\ref{F:sec:inherited-n-tail}; thus competitive deficient
candidates have $t<n$. This is an inherited theorem, not an inference
from the finite rows here. Every finite result states its actual tested
closed mass interval explicitly.

\subsection{Proof, computation and inherited results}
The first-third, cyclic and residue theorems are analytical
all-degree statements.  The compact part of the cubic core uses a
complete finite list of rational interval inequalities, with its
unbounded mass tail treated analytically.  The phase specializations
use whole mass intervals, not values at a finite sample of unknown
angles.  The four-atom certificate checks a cover by closed mass
boxes and bounds the full angle continuum by interpolation with
explicit rounding allowances.

The reproduced Laurent witnesses and their original arithmetic
certificates are credited to the supplied rounds.  Downward reuse
does not convert a support-dependent low-mass result into a
support-free one.  Statements of progress in this paper are relative
to the supplied baseline; no first-in-literature assertion is made.
Our internal independent checks are not a proof-assistant
formalization or external refereeing.

\section{A self-contained stationary reduction}\label{col:F:02}
\label{F:sec:self-contained-stationary}

For completeness, this section proves the standard reduction used
throughout the paper.  The finite-atomic extremal framework is part of
the Agler--McCarthy programme \cite{F:agler}; the argument below is a
reproduction of the necessary variational structure, not a new
coefficient exclusion.  In particular, it does not assume that a
global extremizer already has full support.

\begin{proposition}[Existence and the complete finite stationary model]
\label{F:prop:complete-stationary-reduction}
Fix $n\ge1$.  The maximum of $|[z^n]f|$ over the zero-free
holomorphic functions with $|f|\le1$ in the disk is attained.
After a constant rotation and an input rotation, a maximizing
function satisfies $a_0=e^{-t}>0$ and $a_n>0$ and has the form
\[
 f(z)=\exp[-g(z)],\qquad
 g(z)=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\lambda_j
                      \frac{1+\alpha_jz}{1-\alpha_jz},
 \quad \lambda_j>0,\quad |\alpha_j|=1,
 \quad 1\le N\le n.
\]
The support points $\alpha_j$ are distinct.  With
\[
 R(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}a_jz^j+
                  \sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\overline{a_j}z^{2n-j},
 \qquad h(z)=z^{-n}R(z)\quad(|z|=1),
\]
one has $h\ge0$ and a polynomial factorization $h=|Q|^2$ with
$\deg Q=n$.  Its unit-circle zeros are precisely the physical
support points $\zeta_j=\overline{\alpha_j}$, and all are simple.
Writing $D(z^k)=|k|z^k$ for Laurent monomials, one has
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:reduction-boundary-identity}
 (n-D)h=\Phi h,\qquad
 \Phi(z)=-2\sum_{j=1}^{N}
                 \frac{\lambda_j\alpha_jz}{(1-\alpha_jz)^2}.
\end{equation}
On the circle away from the poles,
\[
 \Phi(e^{i\theta})=
 \sum_{j=1}^{N}\frac{\lambda_j}{2}
                 \csc^2\frac{\theta-\theta_j}{2},
 \qquad \zeta_j=e^{i\theta_j}.
\]
The identity extends continuously across each pole after multiplication
by $h$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The functions
$\exp[-(1+z^n)/(1-z^n)]$ show that the supremum is at least
$2/e$, and Cauchy's coefficient estimate bounds it by one.
Choose a maximizing sequence.  Montel's theorem gives a subsequence
converging uniformly on compact subsets to a holomorphic function
bounded by one.  Its $n$th coefficient has modulus at least $2/e$,
so the limit is neither zero nor constant.  Hurwitz's theorem makes
it zero-free, and the maximum principle gives strict modulus less
than one in the disk.  Thus the limit is an admissible maximizer.
A constant unit factor makes $a_0>0$; an input rotation then makes
$a_n>0$ without changing $a_0$.

The analytic logarithm $g=-\log f$, chosen with $g(0)=t>0$ real,
has positive real part.  The Herglotz representation supplies a
positive finite measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb T$ such that
\[
 g(z)=\int_{\mathbb T}\frac{1+\alpha z}{1-\alpha z}\,d\mu(\alpha),
 \qquad \mu(\mathbb T)=t.
\]
One may obtain this representation directly by taking weak limits
of the positive boundary densities of $\operatorname{Re}g(rz)$:
their means equal $t$, the Poisson formula determines the limiting
harmonic function, and its harmonic conjugate is fixed by
$\operatorname{Im}g(0)=0$.  No atomicity has yet been assumed.

For any $\alpha\in\mathbb T$ and $\delta\ge0$, adding
$\delta\delta_\alpha$ to the measure gives the admissible function
\[
 f_\delta(z)=f(z)
       \exp\!\left[-\delta\frac{1+\alpha z}{1-\alpha z}\right].
\]
Since the real part of its $n$th coefficient cannot exceed $a_n$,
its right derivative at zero is nonpositive.  Direct coefficient
differentiation gives
\[
 \left.\frac{d}{d\delta}\operatorname{Re}[z^n]f_\delta
       \right|_{\delta=0+}
 =-a_n-2\operatorname{Re}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}a_j\alpha^{n-j}
 =-h(\overline\alpha).
\]
Therefore $h\ge0$ on the entire circle.  It is not the zero
polynomial: its mean is $a_n>0$, and its outer Laurent coefficients
are $a_0$ and $\overline{a_0}$.

Scaling the whole measure by $1+\delta$ is admissible for both
signs of sufficiently small $\delta$.  The derivative of the same
real coefficient must therefore vanish.  Integrating the preceding
finite coefficient formula yields
\[
                         \int h(\overline\alpha)\,d\mu(\alpha)=0.
\]
Positivity and continuity imply that $\mu$ is supported on the
zeros of $h$.  A nonzero nonnegative trigonometric polynomial of
degree $n$ has at most $n$ distinct circle zeros: multiplying it by
$z^n$ gives a degree-$2n$ polynomial, and each circle zero has even
multiplicity.  The measure is consequently atomic with $1\le N\le n$
and positive masses $\lambda_j$ at distinct points $\alpha_j$.
Every physical support point $\zeta_j=\overline{\alpha_j}$ is a
zero of $R$ of order at least two.

Define $\Phi$ as in \eqref{F:eq:reduction-boundary-identity}.
Its double poles cancel against these zeros of $R$, so
$L=\Phi R$ is a polynomial of degree at most $2n-1$.
Moreover $\Phi=-zg'$ and hence $\Phi f=zf'$.
Since $R-f=O(z^{n+1})$ at zero, the coefficients of $L$ through
degree $n$ are
\[
                         [z^j]L=j a_j\qquad(0\le j\le n).
\]
The function $z^{-n}L=\Phi h$ is real on the circle away from
the finitely many poles, and by continuity on the whole circle.
Thus its Laurent coefficients are conjugate-symmetric.  Reflection
determines the remaining coefficients of $L$ as
$[z^{2n-j}]L=j\overline{a_j}$ for $0\le j<n$.
For a term of Laurent degree $j-n$, the multiplier is therefore
$n-|j-n|$.  This proves \eqref{F:eq:reduction-boundary-identity}
with the stated convention for $D$.

Here is also the polynomial spectral factorization directly.
The reflected polynomial satisfies
$R(z)=z^{2n}\overline{R(1/\overline z)}$, has nonzero constant
and leading coefficients, and has even multiplicities at all circle
zeros.  Its non-circle roots occur in reciprocal-conjugate pairs.
Choose the exterior root from each such pair, and half the copies
of every circle root, to form a degree-$n$ polynomial $Q_0$.
Then $R$ is a constant multiple of $Q_0Q_0^*$, where reflection is
taken relative to degree $n$.  On the circle this says
$h=c|Q_0|^2$.  Since $h\ge0$ and is not identically zero, the
constant $c$ is positive.  Absorb $\sqrt c$ into $Q_0$ to obtain
$h=|Q|^2$.  This choice of $Q$ has no zeros in the open disk.

To identify all its circle zeros, let $Q=(z-\zeta)B$ for any
$\zeta\in\mathbb T$.  The exact Fourier identity is
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:reduction-circle-zero-D}
                         D|Q|^2(\zeta)=-2\|B\|_2^2.
\end{equation}
Indeed rotate $\zeta$ to $1$ and write
$|B|^2=\sum_k b_kz^k$.  Then
$|Q|^2=(2-z-z^{-1})|B|^2$, and evaluation of its absolute-frequency
derivative gives
\[
 \sum_k\bigl(2|k|-|k+1|-|k-1|\bigr)b_k=-2b_0=-2\|B\|_2^2.
\]
Rotation preserves both $D$ and the Hardy norm.
Consequently the left side of \eqref{F:eq:reduction-boundary-identity}
at $\zeta$ is $2\|B\|_2^2>0$.
If $\zeta$ were not an actual support point, $\Phi$ would be finite
there and the right side would be zero, a contradiction.  If it
were a multiple zero of $Q$ at a support point, $h$ would vanish
to order at least four while $\Phi$ has only a double pole, again
making the right side zero.  Thus every circle zero is an actual
support point and every such zero is simple, as claimed.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Individual masses and the complete log-jet equations.}
At a physical pole $\zeta_j$, cancellation in the last identity gives
\[
 2\left\|\frac{Q(z)}{z-\zeta_j}\right\|_2^2
                   =2\lambda_j|Q'(\zeta_j)|^2.
\]
The cardinal polynomial
$Q(z)/((z-\zeta_j)Q'(\zeta_j))$ has degree at most $n-1$ and
value one at $\zeta_j$.  Cauchy--Schwarz on its $n$ coefficients
therefore gives the necessary bound $\lambda_j\ge1/n$ used in
the phase and finite certificates.

There are exactly $d=n-N$ remaining reciprocal-conjugate root pairs
of $R$.  Their interior members $s_\ell$ are nonzero and satisfy
$|s_\ell|<1$.  Put $\sigma_\ell=\overline{s_\ell}$; then
\[
 R(z)=e^{-t}\prod_{j=1}^{N}(1-\alpha_jz)^2
       \prod_{\ell=1}^{d}(1-\sigma_\ell z)
                         (1-\overline{\sigma_\ell}^{-1}z).
\]
The equality $R-f=O(z^{n+1})$ and their common nonzero constant
term imply $\log R-\log f=O(z^{n+1})$, for the local logarithms
with constant term $-t$.  Comparing all coefficients through $n$
therefore proves
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:reduction-full-log-jets}
 \boxed{\quad
 \sum_{j=1}^{N}(r\lambda_j-1)\alpha_j^r
   =\frac12\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}
            (\sigma_\ell^r+\overline{\sigma_\ell}^{-r}),
 \qquad 1\le r\le n.\quad}
\end{equation}
All these equations refer to the same positive measure and the same
auxiliary-root tuple.  They are necessary for a maximizing function;
the proof does not assert that their scalar consequences alone
characterize a global maximizer.

\section{A robust first-third moment certificate}\label{col:F:03}
\label{F:sec:first-third}

The half-band tests in the supplied tournament control all moments below
roughly $n/2$.  The following argument only charges moments through
$\lfloor n/3\rfloor$.  It treats the intervening band collectively, using
positivity of the original Herglotz measure.  In particular, deleting
the low moments is not assumed to preserve positivity.

Let $\mu$ be a finite positive measure on $\mathbb T$, let
$t=\mu(\mathbb T)>0$, and put
\[
 M_j=\int_{\mathbb T}\alpha^j\,d\mu(\alpha),\qquad
 f(z)=e^{-t}\exp\left(-2\sum_{j\ge1}M_jz^j\right).
\]
For an integer $n\ge2$ define
\[
 m=\lfloor n/3\rfloor+1,\qquad
 \epsilon=2\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}|M_j|.
\]
The measure may be continuous or atomic; stationarity is not required.

\begin{lemma}[A quadratic moment block with a small Gram error]
\label{F:lem:third-block}
If $2m\le k<3m$, then
\[
 \left|M_k-\sum_{j=m}^{k-m}M_jM_{k-j}\right|
 \le t\max\{1,|t-1|+\epsilon\}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Work in $L^2(\mu/t)$, with inner product linear in the first argument,
and write $X(\alpha)=\alpha$, $\rho_j=M_j/t$.
Let $\mathcal E$ be the span of the monomials
$X^m,\ldots,X^{k-m}$ and let $P$ be its orthogonal projection.
Set $p=P1$, $q=PX^k$.  The antiunitary map
$Uu=X^k\overline u$ preserves $\mathcal E$ and interchanges $1$ and
$X^k$.  It therefore commutes with the orthogonal projection in the
appropriate antilinear sense, and
\[
 \|p\|^2=\|q\|^2=:H\le1.
\]
Put $C=\langle q,p\rangle$.  Orthogonality of the projection and
Cauchy--Schwarz give
\[
 |\rho_k-C|\le1-H,\qquad |C|\le H.
\]

Consider the frame operator
\[
 Fv=\sum_{j=m}^{k-m}\langle v,X^j\rangle X^j.
\]
The corresponding Gram matrix has diagonal entries $1$ and
off-diagonal entries $\rho_{i-j}$.  Its row sums away from the
diagonal are at most
\[
 \eta=2\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}|\rho_j|=\epsilon/t,
\]
because $(k-m)-m\le m-1$.  Thus every Gram eigenvalue lies in
$[1-\eta,1+\eta]$.  The nonzero eigenvalues of this Gram matrix are
exactly those of $F$ restricted to $\mathcal E$, so
$\|F-I_{\mathcal E}\|\le\eta$.  This remains valid if the monomials
are linearly dependent: only the nonzero Gram eigenvalues occur on
$\mathcal E$.  No invertibility or assumption $\eta<1$ is needed.

With $S=\sum_{j=m}^{k-m}\rho_j\rho_{k-j}$, the frame definition gives
\[
 S=\langle FX^k,1\rangle=\langle Fq,p\rangle,
 \qquad |S-C|\le\eta H.
\]
Consequently
\begin{align*}
 |\rho_k-tS|
 &\le |\rho_k-C|+|1-t|\,|C|+t|C-S|\\
 &\le1-H+(|t-1|+\epsilon)H\\
 &\le\max\{1,|t-1|+\epsilon\}.
\end{align*}
Multiplication by $t$ proves the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Robust first-third coefficient bound]
\label{F:thm:first-third}
For $t\ge1/2$ and every $n\ge2$,
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:first-third-bound}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 |[z^n]f|\le
 2t\exp(-t+\epsilon)\max\{1,|t-1|+\epsilon\}.}
\end{equation}
In particular, each of the following closed parameter sets is strictly
subcompetitive:
\begin{align}
 t\ge3/2,\quad\epsilon\le1/12
   &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad |[z^n]f|<2/e,
   \label{F:eq:third-slab-low}\\
 t\ge2,\quad\epsilon\le1/10
   &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad |[z^n]f|<2/e.
   \label{F:eq:third-slab-high}
\end{align}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let
\[
 L(z)=-2\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}M_jz^j,\qquad
 V(z)=-2\sum_{j=m}^{n}M_jz^j.
\]
Through degree $n$, the exponential of $V$ is
$G=1+V+V^2/2$, since $3m>n$.
For $m\le k<2m$, its coefficient has modulus at most $2t$.
For $2m\le k\le n$, Lemma~\ref{F:lem:third-block} bounds that coefficient
by $2t\max\{1,|t-1|+\epsilon\}$.
The other positive-degree coefficients below $m$ vanish.
Also $G_0=1$ is bounded by the same expression because $t\ge1/2$.
The coefficient $\ell^1$ norm of $e^L$ is at most $e^{\epsilon}$,
by the Banach algebra exponential estimate.  Taking the coefficient
of $z^n$ in $e^{-t}e^LG$ proves \eqref{F:eq:first-third-bound}.

Here is an exact scalar proof of the two advertised regions.
For $t\ge2$ the right side of \eqref{F:eq:first-third-bound} increases
with $\epsilon$, so set $\epsilon=1/10$ and write $y=t-2\ge0$.
The desired strict inequality is equivalent to
\[
 (y+2)(y+11/10)<e^{y+9/10}.
\]
The degree-five exponential sum proves $e^{9/10}>49/20$.
It is therefore enough that
\[
 P(y)=\frac14-\frac{13}{20}y+\frac9{40}y^2+\frac{49}{120}y^3>0.
\]
Put $u=y-1/2\ge-1/2$.  Direct expansion and the inequality
$u^3\ge-u^2/2$ yield
\[
 P(y)\ge \frac{19}{30}u^2-\frac{19}{160}u+\frac{31}{960}
 \ge\frac{821}{30720}>0.
\]
This proves \eqref{F:eq:third-slab-high} on its entire unbounded ray.

For $t\ge3/2$ and $\epsilon\le1/12$, consider the two branches of
the maximum in \eqref{F:eq:first-third-bound} separately.
The branch equal to $1$ is bounded by $3e^{-17/12}<2/e$;
the degree-three exponential sum proves $e^{5/12}>3/2$.
For the other branch, $|t-1|=t-1$ and monotonicity in
$\epsilon$ permits the larger value $1/10$.
For $3/2\le t\le2$, the function
$t(t-9/10)e^{-t}$ is increasing: its derivative has the sign
of $-t^2+(29/10)t-9/10$, a concave quadratic positive at both
endpoints.  Its value is therefore at most its value at $2$,
already covered above.  All $t\ge2$ were covered by
\eqref{F:eq:third-slab-high}.  This proves
\eqref{F:eq:third-slab-low}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A necessary first-third moment floor]
\label{F:cor:first-third-floor}
Suppose a positive atomic measure with $N<n$ is a competitive
stationary candidate and satisfies the established mass inequality
$t\ge n/N$.  Put $d=n-N$.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:first-third-floor}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 2\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor n/3\rfloor}|M_j|
 >\min\left\{\frac{d^2}{2nN},\frac1{12}\right\}.}
\end{equation}
The stronger necessary bound is $\epsilon>1/12$ whenever
$t\ge3/2$, and $\epsilon>1/10$ whenever $t\ge2$.
Thus these stronger statements hold automatically when
$N\le2n/3$ and $N\le n/2$, respectively.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The two mass slabs have just been proved.  Otherwise $1<t<3/2$.
If $\epsilon$ were at most the right side of
\eqref{F:eq:first-third-floor}, then $\epsilon\le1/12$ and
$t-1+\epsilon<1$.  The maximum in
\eqref{F:eq:first-third-bound} is therefore $1$.
Competitiveness would imply
\[
 \epsilon\ge t-1-\log t>
 \frac{(t-1)^2}{2t}\ge\frac{(n/N-1)^2}{2n/N}
 =\frac{d^2}{2nN},
\]
which is a contradiction.  The strict middle inequality follows
by differentiating the difference: its derivative is
$(t-1)^2/(2t^2)>0$ for $t>1$.  The function
$(t-1)^2/(2t)$ is increasing on that range.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{An irregular family illustrating the enlarged band.}
For each $n\ge9$ take $m=\lfloor n/3\rfloor+1$ and
\[
 W(z)=z^m\frac{z+1/2}{1+z/2},\qquad
 H(z)=3\frac{1+W(z)}{1-W(z)},\qquad f=e^{-H}.
\]
The Herglotz measure is positive and has $N=m+1<n$ atoms.
The fiber $W(\zeta)=1$ has $m+1$ simple unit-circle points,
since its argument derivative is
$m+(3/4)/|\zeta+1/2|^2>0$ and its winding number is $m+1$.
Comparison of residues shows that its masses are
$3/(m+(3/4)/|\zeta+1/2|^2)$.
Its support polynomial is
$z^{m+1}+z^m/2-z/2-1$, so it is not a regular polygon.
Its moments satisfy
\[
 M_1=\cdots=M_{m-1}=0,\qquad M_m=3/2,
 \qquad M_{m+1}=9/4.
\]
Our first-third error is zero, while the earlier half-band error
$2\sum_{1\le j<\lceil n/2\rceil}|M_j|$ is at least $3$.
The new theorem applies, including after sufficiently small
independent perturbations of masses and angles, as long as
$t\ge2$ and the stated first-third bound remains satisfied.
This compares the particular first-half and first-third certificates;
it does not assert that the family passes every other old test,
nor that it solves the stationary equations.

\paragraph{Attribution and the remaining obligation.}
The exact vanishing of the first $\lfloor n/3\rfloor$ coefficients
is related to MacDonald's structural theorem and the subsequent
work of Instanes--Llinares--Vukoti\'c, \emph{On extremal problems related
to the Krzy\.{z} conjecture}, arXiv:2610.23817.
No novelty is claimed for that zero-error implication.
Here the explicit nonzero first-third error, its dimension-independent
frame estimate, and the strict rational mass slabs are proved directly.
The prior half-band comparison is Heisei, supplied focused Round~01.
The reproduction script \texttt{verify\_\allowbreak third\_\allowbreak band.py} performs 100
exact checks of the scalar polynomial certificate, rational exponential
comparisons, finite-jet convolution, and complex projection/frame identities,
including linearly dependent frames.  Their role is to audit the formulas;
the all-degree conclusion follows from the preceding proof.
There is no proof that every deficient stationary candidate must
enter these new regions.  Large first-third moment vectors therefore
remain in the unrestricted all-degree problem.

\section{Cubic harmonic sectors and a second-order cyclic error}\label{col:F:04}
\label{F:sec:r5-cubic}

The following bounds are direct coefficient bounds for positive Herglotz
measures.  They do not require the stationary equations, auxiliary roots,
or assumptions on support geometry.  They retain both the first and
second harmonics of a three-step cyclic core.  Thus a substantial moment
at frequency $n/3$ is permitted; it is not charged to the error.

Let $\mu$ be a finite positive measure on the unit circle, set
\[
 t=\mu(\mathbb T),\qquad M_j=\int_{\mathbb T}\alpha^j\,d\mu(\alpha),
 \qquad
 f(z)=\exp\!\left[-\int_{\mathbb T}
                 \frac{1+\alpha z}{1-\alpha z}\,d\mu(\alpha)\right].
\]
A constant factor of modulus one has no effect on the statements.
All coefficient norms below are at the origin.

\subsection{A cyclic core with a quadratic perturbation error}

\begin{lemma}[Cyclic-core coefficient transfer]
\label{F:lem:r5-cyclic}
Let $n=mk$ with positive integers $m,k$, and define
\[
 F(w)=\exp\!\left[-\int_{\mathbb T}
              \frac{1+\alpha^k w}{1-\alpha^k w}\,d\mu(\alpha)\right],
 \qquad
 \varepsilon=2\sum_{\substack{1\le j\le n\\ k\nmid j}}|M_j|.
\]
Then
\[
 \left|[z^n]f-[w^m]F\right|
 \le e^\varepsilon-1-\varepsilon.
 \tag{C1}\label{F:eq:r5-cyclic}
\]
In particular any bound $|[w^m]F|\le C_m(t)$ valid for positive
Herglotz measures of mass $t$ transfers as
$|[z^n]f|\le C_m(t)+e^\varepsilon-1-\varepsilon$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The pushforward of $\mu$ by $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^k$ is positive.
Consequently $|F(w)|\le1$ in the disk and all its Taylor
coefficients have modulus at most one.  Put
\[
 P(z)=-2\sum_{\substack{1\le j\le n\\k\nmid j}}M_jz^j.
\]
The two logarithmic Taylor jets give
$f(z)=F(z^k)e^{P(z)}+O(z^{n+1})$.  Since the core has only
degrees divisible by $k$, while every monomial of $P$ has degree
not divisible by $k$, the coefficient of $z^n$ in $F(z^k)P(z)$
is zero.  The sum of the absolute coefficients of $P$ is
$\varepsilon$.  Submultiplicativity of this coefficient norm
therefore bounds the sum of the absolute coefficients of
$e^P-1-P$ by $\sum_{q\ge2}\varepsilon^q/q!$.
Convolution with the core's coefficients of modulus at most one
proves \eqref{F:eq:r5-cyclic}.  This argument also covers $k=1$,
when $P=0$.
\end{proof}

The subtraction of the linear term is essential.  It follows
from divisibility of degrees, rather than from an estimate of
individual phases.  No assertion of stationarity is used.

\subsection{An explicit third-coefficient bound at fixed mass}

\begin{lemma}[Uniform cubic core]
\label{F:lem:r5-third}
For the positive Herglotz function $F$ above, with arbitrary
positive total mass $t$, one has
\[
 |[w^3]F|\le 2te^{-t}\quad(1\le t\le3/2),
 \qquad
 |[w^3]F|<\frac{67}{100}\quad(t\ge3/2).
 \tag{C2}\label{F:eq:r5-third}
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $\rho_j=M_{jk}/t$.  A rotation makes $\rho_1=a\in[0,1]$.
The first two steps of the elementary Schur transform of the
normalized positive-real function give parameters $b,c$ with
$|b|,|c|\le1$ and
\begin{align*}
 \rho_2&=a^2+(1-a^2)b,\\
 \rho_3&=a^3+(1-a^2)
           \{2ab-ab^2+(1-|b|^2)c\}.
\end{align*}
For completeness, if $H=-\log F$, then
$(H/t-1)/(H/t+1)=w\varphi(w)$ with $|\varphi|\le1$.
Write
$\varphi(w)=(a+w\psi(w))/(1+aw\psi(w))$,
where $\psi(0)=b$ and
$\psi'(0)=(1-|b|^2)c$ by Schwarz--Pick at zero.
Expanding through the third degree yields the displayed formulas.
If a Schur parameter is on the boundary, the same formulas follow
by a limit; in particular $a=1$ is allowed.

Set
\[
 s=t-1,\qquad A(t)=1-2t+\frac23t^2,\qquad y=|b|.
\]
The exact exponential coefficient is
\[
 [w^3]F=-2te^{-t}
  \left\{\rho_3-2t\rho_1\rho_2+\frac23t^2\rho_1^3\right\}.
\]
Thus, for $t\ge1$, the modulus of the braced expression is at
most
\[
 |A(t)|a^3+(1-a^2)\{1+2say-(1-a)y^2\}.
 \tag{C3}\label{F:eq:r5-schur-majorant}
\]
When $1\le t\le3/2$, maximizing the quadratic over all real $y$
gives the upper bound
\[
 1+a^2\{s^2-1+(s^2+|A(t)|)a\}.
\]
Here $0\le s\le1/2$, $A(t)<0$, and
$2s^2+|A(t)|=(1+2s+4s^2)/3\le1$.  The bound is at most one.
The endpoint $a=1$ follows directly from \eqref{F:eq:r5-schur-majorant}.
This proves the first assertion.

For the second assertion it is useful to retain the restriction
$0\le y\le1$.  Its maximizing value is
$\min\{1,sa/(1-a)\}$ when $a<1$.  Consequently the maximum over
$a\in[0,1]$ in \eqref{F:eq:r5-schur-majorant} is at most
\[
 \max\left\{1,\ \max_{0\le a\le1}
       \left[(2t-1)a+\{|A(t)|-2t+1\}a^3\right]\right\}.
 \tag{C4}\label{F:eq:r5-cubic-majorant}
\]
Indeed on $0\le a\le1/t$ the first branch is
$1+(s^2-1)a^2+(s^2+|A|)a^3$.  Its derivative, after division by
$a$, is increasing, so its maximum is at an endpoint.  At $a=0$
it is one, and at $a=1/t$ it agrees with the second branch in
\eqref{F:eq:r5-cubic-majorant}.

For $3/2\le t\le7/3$, $A(t)<0$ and
$2t-1-|A(t)|=2t^2/3$.  Maximizing the cubic over all $a\ge0$
therefore yields
\[
 |[w^3]F|\le
 \max\left\{2te^{-t},\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}(2t-1)^{3/2}e^{-t}\right\}
 \le\max\{3e^{-3/2},2\sqrt6e^{-2}\}<\frac{67}{100}.
 \tag{C5}
\]
The second scalar term has its unique maximum at $t=2$;
the first is decreasing for $t>1$.  The last comparisons follow
after squaring from the positive exponential Taylor sums, as
recorded in the exact verifier.

Here is a finite rational certificate for the compact interval
$7/3\le t\le9/2$.  For each integer $j=280,\ldots,539$, put
\[
 l=j/120,\quad u=(j+1)/120,\quad
 A_j=\max\{|A(l)|,|A(u)|\},\quad B_j=2u-1,\quad C_j=B_j-A_j.
\]
Since $A$ is increasing for $t\ge7/3$, its absolute value on
the interval is at most $A_j$.  The cubic in
\eqref{F:eq:r5-cubic-majorant} is increasing separately in the
nonnegative upper parameters $|A|$ and $2t-1$ on $0\le a\le1$.
Its maximum is therefore at most
$\sqrt{4B_j^3/(27C_j)}$, and $C_j>0$ on every listed interval.
As $2te^{-t}$ decreases,
the following two exact inequalities imply the desired bound
throughout each entire interval:
\[
 C_j>0,\qquad
 4l^2\max\left\{1,\frac{4B_j^3}{27C_j}\right\}
 <\left(\frac{67}{100}\right)^2
       \sum_{q=0}^{40}\frac{(2l)^q}{q!}.
 \tag{C6}\label{F:eq:r5-rational-slabs}
\]
All 260 instances of \eqref{F:eq:r5-rational-slabs} are verified
using rational arithmetic by the included reproduction script.
The intervals touch and include both endpoints.  This is an
interval certificate, not a set of sampled values of $F$.

Finally, for $t\ge9/2$, one has $A(t)>1$ and
$3A(t)-2(2t-1)=2t^2-10t+5>0$.  The cubic in
\eqref{F:eq:r5-cubic-majorant} is increasing on $[0,1]$, so its
maximum is $A(t)$.  The derivative of $2tA(t)e^{-t}$ is
\[
 e^{-t}\left(-\frac43t^3+8t^2-10t+2\right)<0
 \qquad(t\ge9/2).
\]
The polynomial in parentheses equals $-5/2$ at $9/2$ and
has negative derivative there and thereafter.  Thus this whole
infinite tail is bounded by $(99/2)e^{-9/2}<67/100$, again
certified by a positive Taylor lower bound for the exponential.
This proves \eqref{F:eq:r5-third}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Closed exclusion regions in every multiple of three}

\begin{theorem}[Robust cubic resonance exclusions]
\label{F:thm:r5-cubic-exclusion}
Let $n=3k$ and retain the positive Herglotz setup above.  Define
\[
 \varepsilon_{3,k}
   =2\sum_{\substack{1\le j\le3k\\k\nmid j}}|M_j|.
\]
Each of the following conditions implies $|[z^n]f|<2/e$:
\begin{align*}
 t\ge3/2,&\qquad \varepsilon_{3,k}\le1/3;
 \tag{C7}\label{F:eq:r5-high-cubic}\\
 1<t\le3/2,&\qquad \varepsilon_{3,k}\le\frac35(t-1).
 \tag{C8}\label{F:eq:r5-low-cubic}
\end{align*}
More explicitly, the upper bound in \eqref{F:eq:r5-high-cubic}
is $293/400$, and that in \eqref{F:eq:r5-low-cubic} is strictly
less than $2/e-13(t-1)^2/9000$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For the first region combine Lemmas \ref{F:lem:r5-cyclic}
and \ref{F:lem:r5-third}.  The exact exponential bounds
$e^{1/3}<67/48$ and $e<30/11$ give
\[
 |[z^n]f|
 <\frac{67}{100}+\frac1{16}
 =\frac{293}{400}<\frac{11}{15}<\frac2e.
\]
For the second, set $s=t-1\in(0,1/2]$.
Since $e^{-v}\ge1-v$ for $v\ge0$,
\[
 \frac2e-2te^{-t}
 =\frac2e\int_0^s v e^{-v}\,dv
 \ge\frac1e\left(s^2-\frac23s^3\right)
 \ge\frac{2s^2}{3e}>\frac{11s^2}{45}.
\]
For $\varepsilon\le3s/5\le3/10$, the integral Taylor
remainder and $e^{3/10}<27/20$ give
\[
 e^\varepsilon-1-\varepsilon
 \le\tfrac12 e^\varepsilon\varepsilon^2
 <\frac{243}{1000}s^2.
\]
The difference of the last two rational constants is
$11/45-243/1000=13/9000$.  Apply
\eqref{F:eq:r5-cyclic} and the first part of
\eqref{F:eq:r5-third}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A necessary residual moment floor]
\label{F:cor:r5-cubic-floor}
For any competitive deficient stationary candidate with
$n=3k$, $N=n-d<n$, and $t\ge n/N$, it is necessary that
\[
 \varepsilon_{3,k}>
 \begin{cases}
 \dfrac35(t-1)\ge\dfrac{3d}{5N},&t<3/2,\\[4pt]
 \dfrac13,&t\ge3/2.
 \end{cases}
\]
The mass range $t<3/2$ can occur only if $N>2n/3$.
\end{corollary}

This is a floor for the moments outside the complete three-step
harmonic lattice.  It must not be confused with the earlier
one-high-frequency floor, which also charges the moment at $n/3$.
The near-one floor here is linear in $d/N$; the error is quadratic
because of the cyclic cancellation.  The result is an additional
necessary condition and does not supply a complete cover.

\subsection{A concrete separation from the one-wave test}

Take any $k\ge2$, $n=3k$, and two rotated regular $k$-gons whose
images under $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^k$ are $1$ and $-1$.  Give
the two orbits total masses $19/20$ and $13/20$, respectively,
distributed equally within each orbit.  Then $t=8/5$, $N=2k$,
$M_k=3/10$, $M_{2k}=8/5$, $M_{3k}=3/10$, and all the
off-lattice moments through $n$ vanish.  Hence
\eqref{F:eq:r5-high-cubic} applies.  Every one-wave test keeping a
single index $j$ with $n/2\le j<n$ must still charge $M_k$ to
its error, producing an error at least $3/5$, above its stated
$1/14$ threshold at this mass.  This is a comparison of
specified sufficient tests, not a stationary example and not a
claim of separation from every earlier exclusion.

There is a nonzero angular neighborhood as well.  Keep the masses
and move each support point by chord distance at most
$\delta=1/(10n^2)$ from its reference.  Telescoping powers gives
$|M_j-M_j^{(0)}|\le tj\delta$, hence
\[
 \varepsilon_{3,k}\le t\delta n(n+1)
 =\frac4{25}\left(1+\frac1n\right)\le\frac{14}{75}<\frac13.
\]
The new certificate still applies throughout this closed tube,
even after rotational symmetry is lost.  Also
$2|M_k|\ge3/5-2tk\delta>1/2$ for $k\ge2$, so the stated
one-wave comparison persists.  The tube is described to show
that the exclusion has positive width; no full stationary
feasibility is asserted for its reference points.

\paragraph{Reproduction and scope.}
The exact script \texttt{verify\_\allowbreak cubic\_\allowbreak resonance.py} proves
the 260 rational mass-interval certificates and the rational
exponential comparisons, checks the symbolic third-coefficient
and Schur formulas, and tests the integer divisibility identity.
There are 632 exact checks in the accompanying log.  Infinite
validity follows from the analytical reductions and the stated
closed interval coverage, rather than from the number of checks.
Schur transforms, coefficient norm submultiplicativity, and the
cyclic pushforward are standard tools.  No historical priority
claim is made.  These results close the displayed regions in
all degrees divisible by three; they do not prove the unrestricted
Krzy\.{z} conjecture.

\section{A residue-sensitive transfer from finite coefficients to all degrees}\label{col:F:05}
\label{F:sec:residue-transfer}

The cubic coefficient bound in the preceding section has a transfer that
retains the arithmetic positions of the perturbing moments.  This is
useful because a large moment need not contribute to the target coefficient.
All measures in this section are positive, but need not be stationary or
atomic.  In particular, no sign-indefinite deletion of moments is used.

Let $n=sk$, where $s\ge1$ and $k\ge2$ are integers, and use the positive
measure, total mass $t$, and moments $M_j$ defined earlier.  Its pushforward
under $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^k$ is again positive and defines
\[
 F(w)=\exp\left(-t-2\sum_{r\ge1}M_{kr}w^r\right)
      =\sum_{r\ge0}c_rw^r,\qquad |F|\le1.
\]
Equivalently, $F(z^k)$ is the exponential of the cyclic average of the
original Herglotz function.  Define the finite, nonnegative polynomial
and its exponential coefficients by
\[
 B(z)=\sum_{\substack{1\le j\le n\\k\nmid j}}\beta_jz^j,
 \qquad \beta_j=2|M_j|,\qquad e^{B(z)}=\sum_{r\ge0}b_rz^r.
\]
Only coefficients through degree $n$ are needed.  They satisfy
\[
 b_0=1,\qquad r b_r=\sum_{j=1}^{r}j\beta_j b_{r-j},
 \qquad \beta_j=0\text{ at the omitted indices}.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Finite arithmetic majorant]\label{F:thm:residue-majorant}
For every such positive measure,
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:residue-majorant}
 \left|[z^n]f-c_s\right|
 \le\sum_{r=1}^{s}|c_{s-r}|b_{kr}
 \le E_{n,k}:=\sum_{r=1}^{s}b_{kr}.
\end{equation}
In particular, any proved bound $|c_s|\le C_s(t)$ implies
$|[z^n]f|\le C_s(t)+E_{n,k}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
As an equality of Taylor jets through degree $n$,
\[
 f(z)=F(z^k)e^{R(z)},\qquad
 R(z)=-2\sum_{\substack{1\le j\le n\\k\nmid j}}M_jz^j.
\]
The coefficientwise absolute values of $e^R$ are bounded by those
of $e^B$, by expanding each exponential in powers of its polynomial.
The constant term of $e^R$ is one, and the other terms that can pair
with $F(z^k)$ at degree $n$ have degrees $k,2k,\ldots,sk$.
This proves the first inequality.  Since $F$ is a bounded holomorphic
function of modulus at most one, Cauchy's coefficient estimate gives
$|c_j|\le1$.  This proves the second inequality.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Cancellation order and a closed-form envelope]
\label{F:cor:residue-order}
Set $\epsilon=B(1)$ and
$\rho_a=\sum_{j\equiv a\pmod k}\beta_j$ for $1\le a<k$.
Let $h$ be the least positive number of elements, with repetition,
from the set $\{a:\rho_a>0\}$ whose sum is zero modulo $k$.
Put $h=\infty$ if this set is empty.  For finite $h$,
\begin{align}
 E_{n,k}
 &\le \frac1k\sum_{\ell=0}^{k-1}
 \exp\left(\sum_{a=1}^{k-1}\rho_a e^{2\pi i\ell a/k}\right)-1
 \le \sum_{q=h}^{\infty}\frac{\epsilon^q}{q!}.
 \label{F:eq:residue-filter}
\end{align}
The middle expression is real and nonnegative.  In particular $h\ge2$,
so the universal error is at most $e^\epsilon-1-\epsilon$.
If only residue $a$ is present, then $h=k/\gcd(a,k)$.
For $\epsilon<h+1$, a wholly rational envelope is
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:residue-geometric}
 E_{n,k}\le
 \frac{\epsilon^h}{h!}\frac1{1-\epsilon/(h+1)}.
\end{equation}
If every nonzero coefficient of $B$ has index greater than $n/2$,
then $E_{n,k}=0$ and $[z^n]f=c_s$ exactly.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Averaging $e^{B(z)}$ over the $k$th roots of unity keeps exactly
its coefficients of degree divisible by $k$.  These coefficients
are nonnegative, so dropping degrees greater than $n$ only lowers
their sum.  In the expansion in powers of $B$, no power below $h$
has a monomial of degree divisible by $k$.  The total coefficient
sum of $B^q/q!$ is $\epsilon^q/q!$.  This proves
\eqref{F:eq:residue-filter}.  Consecutive terms of the final tail have
ratio at most $\epsilon/(h+1)$, proving
\eqref{F:eq:residue-geometric}.  For the final assertion, every
nonlinear power of $B$ has degree greater than $n$, whereas its
linear term has no degree divisible by $k$.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Two concrete infinite families.}
Combine this theorem with the cubic core bound $C_3(t)<67/100$ for
$t\ge3/2$ proved in this paper.  It gives the following statements
for every $n=3k$ with $k\ge2$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If all off-lattice moments with $j\le n/2$ vanish, then
      $|a_n|<67/100$ regardless of the sizes of the off-lattice
      moments above $n/2$.
\item If the active off-lattice residues have cancellation order
      $h\ge10$ and $2\sum_{k\nmid j,\,j\le n}|M_j|\le3$, then
      \[
      |a_n|<\frac{67}{100}
               +\frac{11\,3^{10}}{8\,10!}<\frac7{10}<\frac2e.
      \]
      For example, one may use a single residue whose order in
      $\mathbb Z/k\mathbb Z$ is at least ten.  Repetition is
      included when calculating that order.
\end{enumerate}
These statements do not assert that arbitrary moment arrays arise
from positive measures.  Positivity of the original measure is a
hypothesis throughout.  They compare sufficient coefficient tests;
they do not establish that a tuple passing all previous stationary
equations lies in either family.  The finite quantity $E_{n,k}$ is
usually stronger than its residue or total-size envelopes.

\paragraph{What this transfer does and does not close.}
The transfer removes complete parameter sectors at infinitely many
degrees from a finite core coefficient estimate.  It supplies no
reason for a general extremizer to have small $E_{n,k}$ for any
divisor $k$ of its target degree.  In particular, this alone is not
a reduction of all degrees to the cases $s\le3$.

\section{Retaining the total-mass floor in the phase derivative}\label{col:F:06}
\label{F:sec:new-phase-strip}

This section adds a quantified exclusion to the attachment's unresolved
four-atom branch at index $26$.  The two analytic estimates below hold
in arbitrary degree and require no symmetry of the support.  Their
joint numerical specialization is an exact rational continuum
certificate, rather than a sample of support angles.

Write the boundary phase of an atomic singular inner function as
\[
 f(e^{i\theta})=e^{i\phi(\theta)},\qquad
 \phi(\theta)=-\sum_{j=1}^N\lambda_j
       \cot\frac{\theta-\theta_j}{2},\qquad
 \Phi=\phi'=\sum_{j=1}^N\frac{\lambda_j}{2}
       \csc^2\frac{\theta-\theta_j}{2}.
\]
The poles $e^{i\theta_j}$ are distinct.  In the stationary model,
the cardinal-polynomial mass floor gives $\lambda_j\ge1/n$.
Only this mass floor, positivity and atomicity are needed in this
section.  Put $t=\sum_j\lambda_j$.

\begin{lemma}[A derivative bound with the baseline potential retained]
\label{F:lem:baseline-derivative}
At every point away from the poles, with $R=\Phi-t/2\ge0$,
\[
 \boxed{\quad |\Phi'|\le\sqrt{tR/2}+\sqrt{2n}\,R^{3/2}.\quad}
 \tag{PD}
\]
More generally $\sqrt{2n}$ can be replaced by
$\sqrt{2/\lambda_{\min}}$ if only
$\lambda_j\ge\lambda_{\min}>0$ is known.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Set $a_j=\lambda_j/2$ and
$x_j=|\cot((\theta-\theta_j)/2)|$.
Then $\Phi=\sum_j a_j(1+x_j^2)$ and
$R=\sum_j a_jx_j^2$.  Differentiation and the triangle inequality give
\[
 |\Phi'|\le\sum_j a_jx_j+\sum_j a_jx_j^3.
\]
The first sum is at most $\sqrt{(t/2)R}$ by Cauchy--Schwarz.
Writing $y_j=a_jx_j^2\ge0$, the second is
$\sum_j y_j^{3/2}/\sqrt{a_j}$, which is at most
$\sqrt{2n}(\sum_j y_j)^{3/2}$.
The last step uses the elementary superadditivity of $y^{3/2}$
on the nonnegative half-line.  The more general statement is identical.
\end{proof}

Fix $1<k$, and use the three level sets
\[
 J=\{\Phi<n\},\qquad M=\{n\le\Phi\le kn\},\qquad
 K=\{\Phi>kn\}.
\]
Boundaries have measure zero, except harmless isolated level tangencies.
Let $r=N/(\pi n)$, let $r_1$ be the number of positive-length
components of $J$ divided by $\pi n$, and set
\[
 u=\frac{|K|}{2\pi},\quad
 L=\frac1{2\pi}\int_J(1-\Phi/n),\quad
 G=\frac1{2\pi}\int_M(\Phi/n-1),\quad
 F=\frac1{2\pi n}\int_{K^c}\Phi.
\]
The function $\Phi$ is strictly convex in every pole-free gap.
This follows by differentiating each positive multiple of $\csc^2$
twice.  It diverges at the ends of a gap, so $0\le r_1\le r$.

For later use, the elementary oscillatory estimate from the attachment
is reproduced in the form
\begin{equation}
 |a_n|\le\frac{2r}{k-1}+
 \min\{1-u,\ 1-u-L+r_1,\ F+r_1-G\}.
 \label{F:eq:new-phase-base}
\end{equation}
Indeed, split $K$ at the gap minima into at most $2N$ intervals.
There $\phi'-n>(k-1)n$ is monotone.  After the change of phase
variable, the amplitude is monotone and bounded by $1/((k-1)n)$;
integration against a primitive of $e^{iy}$ of modulus at most $2$
costs at most $2/((k-1)n)$ per interval.  After division by $2\pi$
this is $2r/(k-1)$.  The trivial integral bound on $K^c$ gives
$1-u$.  On each component of $J$, integration against
$e^{-in\theta}$ instead costs $1/(\pi n)$ in endpoints and
replaces its length by its $\Phi/n$ integral.  This gives
$1-u-L+r_1$.  Finally $F=1-u-L+G$.  Truncation near poles
and dominated convergence justify the same bounds at the improper
endpoints.

\begin{proposition}[An explicit larger middle-band gain]
\label{F:prop:new-middle}
Suppose $t_-\le t\le t_+$ and $0<t_-<2n$.
Define
\[
 a=1-\frac{t_-}{2n},\qquad
 A=1+\frac{\sqrt{t_+/n}}{2na},\qquad
 v=\sqrt{k-\frac{t_-}{2n}},\qquad
 g_* =\frac{\sqrt2}{A}
       \left(v+\frac{a}{v}-2\sqrt a\right).
\]
Then $G\ge r_1g_*$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
On each monotone transition through $n\le\Phi\le kn$, put
$s=\Phi/n$ and $y=s-t_-/(2n)\ge a$.
Lemma~\ref{F:lem:baseline-derivative} gives
\[
 |\Phi'|\le n^2\sqrt2\,y^{3/2}
       \left(1+\frac{\sqrt{t_+/n}}{2ny}\right)
 \le n^2\sqrt2 A y^{3/2}.
\]
Every component of $J$ has two disjoint monotone transitions through
the entire middle band before its adjacent poles.  Integrating the
reciprocal derivative bound over these transitions proves
\[
 G\ge \frac{r_1}{\sqrt2 A}
       \int_1^k\frac{s-1}{(s-t_-/(2n))^{3/2}}\,ds=r_1g_*.
\]
The antiderivative follows by writing $s-1=y-a$.
\end{proof}

\section{Charging the compulsory mass in every high component}\label{col:F:07}

Assume $0<u<u_0<1/2$.  Merge high intervals across isolated
complementary level points.  Every resulting high component contains
at least one pole, by convexity.  Let there be $s$ such components,
$1\le s\le N$, with half-lengths $x_i$ and enclosed masses $t_i$.
Then $\sum_i x_i=\pi u$, $\sum_i t_i=t$, and crucially
$t_i\ge1/n$ for every $i$.

For a high interval $[a,b]$, put $x=(b-a)/2$.  Its endpoints have
$\Phi=kn$.  The cotangent difference formula, with
$v_j(q)=\sqrt{\lambda_j/2}\csc((q-\theta_j)/2)$, gives
\[
 \phi(a)-\phi(b)=-2\sin x\sum_jv_j(a)v_j(b).
\]
The product is negative for an enclosed pole and positive for an
exterior pole.  For an exterior pole its magnitude is at least
$\lambda_j/(2\cos^2(x/2))$, because the product of the two
endpoint sines is at most $\cos^2(x/2)$.
Cauchy--Schwarz bounds the sum of absolute products by $kn$.
Summing these phase drops over the high components therefore gives
\begin{equation}
 F\le\frac1\pi\left(k\sum_i\sin x_i
      -\frac{2t}{n}\sum_i\tan(x_i/2)
      +\frac2n\sum_i t_i\tan(x_i/2)\right).
 \label{F:eq:new-exterior}
\end{equation}

Let $x=\max_i x_i$, and single out one maximizing component.
Since each other component has mass at least $1/n$,
\[
 \sum_i t_i\tan(x_i/2)
 \le t\tan(x/2)
      -\frac1n\sum_{i\ne i_{\max}}
          \bigl(\tan(x/2)-\tan(x_i/2)\bigr).
\]
This retains information lost when all mass is assigned to the largest
component in the upper bound.  Consequently, with
$c=t_-/n-1/n^2\ge0$, (\ref{F:eq:new-exterior}) yields
\begin{equation}
 F\le\frac1\pi\left[
 k\sin x-\frac{2(s-1)}{n^2}\tan(x/2)
 +\sum_{i\ne i_{\max}}\bigl(k\sin x_i-2c\tan(x_i/2)\bigr)
 \right].
 \label{F:eq:compulsory-mass-flux}
\end{equation}

The function $h(y)=k\sin y-2c\tan(y/2)$ is concave on
$[0,\pi/2)$.  If
\begin{equation}
 k\cos\frac{\pi u_0}{s-1}
  -c\sec^2\frac{\pi u_0}{2(s-1)}>0 \qquad (2\le s\le N),
 \label{F:eq:phase-monotonic}
\end{equation}
then it is also increasing throughout the intervals needed below:
its derivative is decreasing, so checking the stated upper endpoint
suffices.  Jensen's inequality and enlargement of $u$ to $u_0$ now
give, for $s\ge2$,
\[
 F\le F_s(u_0):=\frac1\pi\max_{0\le x\le\pi u_0}
 \left[k\sin x-\frac{2(s-1)}{n^2}\tan(x/2)
 +(s-1)h\!\left(\frac{\pi u_0-x}{s-1}\right)\right].
\]
For $s=1$ use $F_1(u_0)=k\sin(\pi u_0)/\pi$.
There is no assertion that all $N$ high components exist: the
maximum over all $1\le s\le N$ is retained.

\begin{theorem}[Combined degree-uniform phase certificate]
\label{F:thm:new-phase-certificate}
Assume the preceding hypotheses, including
(\ref{F:eq:phase-monotonic}), $0\le g_*<1$, and $\ell\le L$.
Then
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 |a_n|\le\frac{2r}{k-1}+
 \max\left\{\min(1-u_0,1-u_0-\ell+r),\
       \max_{1\le s\le N}F_s(u_0)+(1-g_*)r\right\}.\quad}
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $u\ge u_0$, use the first two bounds in
(\ref{F:eq:new-phase-base}).  If $u<u_0$, use its third bound,
Proposition~\ref{F:prop:new-middle}, $r_1\le r$ and
(\ref{F:eq:compulsory-mass-flux}).  This includes all possibilities
for the number of high components.  The case $u=0$ cannot occur
for a nonempty atomic support; the case $u=1$ belongs to the first
alternative.
\end{proof}

\section{An exact new strip at index twenty-six}\label{col:F:08}

For completeness a usable $\ell$ is provided by the phase pushforward
law.  Put $H=-\log f$, so $H(0)=t$ and
$(H-t)/(H+t)$ is inner and vanishes at zero.  Its boundary values
push normalized circle measure to itself, as follows by applying the
mean-value formula to its positive and negative integer powers.
Thus the boundary phase $\phi$ has Cauchy density
$t/(\pi(t^2+y^2))$.  There are $N$ inverse branches, and at a
regular phase value their inverse speeds sum to $2t/(t^2+y^2)$.
The positive-part inequality therefore gives, for $0\le b\le1$,
\[
 L\ge\max\left\{0,\frac{2\arctan b-(Nt_+/n)b}{\pi}\right\}.
\]
This proof also fixes the normalization of the phase law.

\begin{theorem}[A strictly larger closed four-atom mass region]
\label{F:thm:n26-new-strip}
At $n=26$ and $N=4$, every positive atomic function with
$\lambda_j\ge1/26$ and
\[
 \frac{46}{5}\le t\le\frac{93}{10}
\]
satisfies $|a_{26}|<2943/4000<2/e$.
In particular no competitive stationary tuple lies in this closed
mass interval.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Partition the mass interval into the forty closed intervals
\[
 \left[\frac{46}{5}+\frac{j}{400},
       \frac{46}{5}+\frac{j+1}{400}\right],\qquad 0\le j<40.
\]
In Theorem~\ref{F:thm:new-phase-certificate} take $k=93/50$,
$b=63/100$ and the rational $u_0$ and tangency parameters recorded
in \texttt{phase\_\allowbreak strip\_\allowbreak parameters.json}.  These are fixed choices
for whole mass intervals, independent of the unknown angles.

For $s\ge2$, the numerator defining $F_s$ is concave in $x$.
At the recorded $x_0=p\pi u_0$, let its derivative be $D$.
Its maximum on $[0,\pi u_0]$ is at most its value at $x_0$ plus
$\pi u_0\max(0,-pD,(1-p)D)$.  The verifier encloses that value
and derivative by rational alternating sine and cosine sums and
positive cosine denominators.  It separately checks
(\ref{F:eq:phase-monotonic}) for each possible $s$.
Square roots in $g_*$ are enclosed by integer-square comparisons;
the lower bound uses that $v+a/v$ increases for $v\ge\sqrt a$.
Machin's identity supplies a rational interval for $\pi$, and an
exponential Taylor sum with a geometric tail gives an upper bound
for $e$.  The arctangent is reduced by
$\arctan b=\pi/4-\arctan((1-b)/(1+b))$.

\texttt{verify\_\allowbreak phase\_\allowbreak strip.py} checks all forty mass intervals
and all four component counts, with the resulting exact rational
upper bound strictly below $2943/4000$ in each case.  It also checks
$2943/4000<2/e$.  There is no floating-point acceptance and no
uncovered mass or angular boundary.
\end{proof}

The attachment's Taisho round 10 already excludes the lower band
through $46/5$ and the upper band starting at $39/4$, at $n=26,N=4$.
Joining the new theorem with those two certified intervals reduces
the unresolved mass window for that support stratum to
\[
 \boxed{\qquad \frac{93}{10}<t<\frac{39}{4}.\qquad}
\]
The earlier window had width $11/20$; the new one has width $9/20$.
Thus $1/10$ of mass width, or $2/11$ of that previously reported
window, is newly excluded.  This comparison concerns that exact
mass window and makes no claim about the volume of a full parameter
space, a number of surviving boxes, or global Krzy\.{z} closure.

The exact verification proves the displayed interval result.  The
preceding analytic inequalities are uniform in degree wherever their
explicit hypotheses hold.  Neither the new lower-band gain nor the
compulsory-component correction puts every surviving support geometry
into an excluded region; the full conjecture remains outside this
section's proved scope.

\section{An all-mass nine-atom exclusion beginning at degree seventy-three}\label{col:F:09}
\label{F:sec:new-nine-atom-ray}

The phase certificate of Section~\ref{F:sec:new-phase-strip} also improves
one of the attachment's all-mass support rays.  The improvement is from
$n\ge74$ to $n\ge73$ at $N=9$; relative to that previously certified ray,
the newly closed whole support stratum is exactly $(n,N)=(73,9)$.

\begin{lemma}[Monotonic extension of a base-degree phase certificate]
\label{F:lem:phase-ray-monotonic}
Fix $N\ge2$, $n_0\ge3$, and a closed mass-ratio interval
$[\tau_-,\tau_+]\subset[1,N]$, with $\tau_-<2N$.
Assume also $n_0^2\tau_-\ge N$, so the coefficient
$c_n=\tau_-/N-1/n^2$ is nonnegative for every $n\ge n_0$.
Use $t_-=n\tau_-/N$, $t_+=n\tau_+/N$ in
Theorem~\ref{F:thm:new-phase-certificate}.  Fix $k\in[3/2,5/2]$,
$u_0\in(0,1/2)$ and an $n$-independent lower bound $\ell$ for $L$.
Suppose that
\[
 k\cos\frac{\pi u_0}{s-1}
 -\frac{\tau_-}{N}\sec^2\frac{\pi u_0}{2(s-1)}>0,
 \qquad 2\le s\le N,
\]
and that the middle-band gain $g_0$ from
Proposition~\ref{F:prop:new-middle} at $n=n_0$ lies in $(0,1)$.
Then the resulting coefficient upper bound at any $n\ge n_0$
is at most the bound obtained at $n_0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In the middle-band formula,
$a=1-\tau_-/(2N)$ and $v=\sqrt{k-\tau_-/(2N)}$ are independent
of $n$, while $A=1+\sqrt{\tau_+/N}/(2na)$ decreases with $n$.
Thus $g_*\ge g_0$, and $G\ge r_1g_0$ is valid at every $n\ge n_0$.
The limiting derivative condition in the statement implies the
required enlargement condition because
$c_n=\tau_-/N-1/n^2\le\tau_-/N$.

For $s\ge2$, write the expression inside the maximum defining
$\pi F_s(n)$ as
\[
 f_{s,\infty}(x)-\frac{2}{n^2}D_s(x),\qquad
 D_s(x)=(s-1)\left[\tan\frac{x}{2}
  -\tan\frac{\pi u_0-x}{2(s-1)}\right].
\]
For $0\le x\le\pi u_0$ one has
$D_s(x)\le(s-1)\tan(\pi u_0/2)<N$.  No lower bound for
$D_s$ is needed.  Put $C=2/(k-1)+1-g_0\ge4/3$.
At each such $x$,
\[
 \frac{d}{dn}\left[
   \frac{f_{s,\infty}(x)-2D_s(x)/n^2}{\pi}
          +\frac{CN}{\pi n}\right]
 =\frac{4D_s(x)-CNn}{\pi n^3}<0
 \qquad(n\ge3).
\]
Taking the maximum over the same compact $x$ interval preserves
monotonicity.  This controls the full high-set term
$2r/(k-1)+F_s(n)+(1-g_0)r$.  For $s=1$, $F_1$ is independent
of $n$ and the conclusion is immediate.
The low-set alternative
$2r/(k-1)+\min(1-u_0,1-u_0-\ell+r)$ is nondecreasing in
$r=N/(\pi n)$, hence decreases with $n$.
Taking the maximum of the two alternatives completes the proof.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Nine atoms, all masses, all degrees at least seventy-three]
\label{F:thm:nine-atom-ray}
Let $n\ge73$.  An atomic singular inner function with exactly
nine distinct atoms, $\lambda_j\ge1/n$, and
$n/9\le t<n$ satisfies
\[
 |a_n|<\frac{2943}{4000}<\frac2e.
\]
Consequently the entire nine-support stationary competitive
stratum is excluded for every $n\ge73$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Put $\tau=9t/n$, so $1\le\tau<9$.  The interval is covered by
the following closed sets:
\[
 [1+j/1000,1+(j+1)/1000]\quad(0\le j<1000),
 \qquad [2,9].
\]
For each set, \texttt{sparse\_\allowbreak ray\_\allowbreak parameters.json} records fixed
rational $k,u_0,b$ and eight tangency parameters for the possible
component counts $s=2,\ldots,9$.  At $n_0=73$, the exact verifier
\texttt{verify\_\allowbreak sparse\_\allowbreak ray.py} checks the certificate in
Theorem~\ref{F:thm:new-phase-certificate} for every row, using the
same rational Taylor and square-root enclosures as the preceding
four-atom certificate.  The $s=1$ case is checked separately.
For the last interval take $b=0$, so $\ell=0$; both its finite
lower endpoint and the upper endpoint $9$ enter the derivative
gain.  Thus it is not an extrapolation from a single mass value.

The verifier also checks the limiting derivative inequalities
in Lemma~\ref{F:lem:phase-ray-monotonic}, and bounds the actual
base-degree middle-band gain above by a number below $1$.
All $1001$ rational coefficient upper bounds are strictly below
$2943/4000$.  Lemma~\ref{F:lem:phase-ray-monotonic} extends each
whole mass-ratio certificate to every $n\ge73$.  The closed
mass-ratio intervals cover all allowed masses and all their
shared boundaries.  This completes the proof.
\end{proof}

The present result imposes no angular or auxiliary-root symmetry.
It covers all admissible masses in the indicated support ray.
The stronger start $n=73$ follows from the total-mass term in
Lemma~\ref{F:lem:baseline-derivative} combined with the compulsory
mass in every high component.  The attachment already supplies
the ray starting at $74$; it is not counted a second time as a
newly discovered infinite collection.  The surviving lower degrees
at $N=9$, other support sizes, and dense support configurations
are not closed by this theorem.

\section{Closed low-mass prefixes for the remaining four-atom degrees}\label{col:F:10}
\label{F:sec:four-atom-prefixes}

The phase certificate in Theorem~\ref{F:thm:new-phase-certificate}
provides a short angularly uniform alternative to a mass--angle
subdivision on the following complete lower-mass prefixes.

\begin{theorem}[Eight four-atom low-mass prefixes]
\label{F:thm:four-atom-prefixes}
For $N=4$, $\lambda_j\ge1/n$, and each row of this table, every
total mass $n/4\le t\le T_n$ satisfies
$|a_n|<2943/4000<2/e$.
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|r}
 n&T_n&\text{closed mass cells}\\\hline
 18&23/5&20\\
 19&5&50\\
 20&11/2&100\\
 21&61/10&170\\
 22&33/5&220\\
 23&36/5&290\\
 24&79/10&380\\
 25&17/2&450
\end{array}
\]
There is no angular symmetry assumption.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For a row $n$, let $m_n=\lceil200(T_n-n/4)\rceil$ and split
its entire closed mass interval into the $m_n$ closed intervals
\[
 \left[\frac n4+\frac{j}{m_n}\left(T_n-\frac n4\right),
       \frac n4+\frac{j+1}{m_n}\left(T_n-\frac n4\right)\right],
 \qquad 0\le j<m_n.
\]
Their endpoints are rational and their widths are at most $1/200$.
The file \texttt{four\_\allowbreak atom\_\allowbreak prefix\_\allowbreak parameters.json} specifies
rational choices of $k,u_0,b$ and the three tangency parameters
for component counts $2,3,4$ on each interval.  These choices are
independent of the unknown atom positions and masses within that
interval.

The exact rational verifier \texttt{verify\_\allowbreak four\_\allowbreak atom\_\allowbreak prefixes.py}
checks Theorem~\ref{F:thm:new-phase-certificate} in every case.
It verifies the complete ordered list of degrees and mass intervals,
the concavity enlargement inequalities, upper and lower bounds for
the actual middle-band gain, the Cauchy-deficit lower bound, and all
four possible component counts.  All transcendental comparisons
use the same rational Taylor and integer-square enclosures as in
Theorem~\ref{F:thm:n26-new-strip}.  Its $1680$ mass-cell checks,
covering $6720$ component cases, all give a strict rational bound
below $2943/4000$.  Closed cells include every shared endpoint,
so no boundary is omitted.
\end{proof}

These certificates cover a full prefix, not merely selected total
masses or point samples of angles.  They can be used to start a
remaining four-atom computation at $T_n$ instead of $n/4$; in
particular the degree-25 interval needing a separate argument is
reduced from $[25/4,39/4]$ to $[17/2,39/4]$ when the supplied
support-free upper slab is used.  Whether a subsequent finite
computation closes that remaining interval must be decided from its
completed certificate.  This theorem alone makes no claim of
complete four-atom closure at any of its eight indices, and no
claim of closing the all-degree conjecture.

\section{Keeping more of the existing uniform support-density bound}\label{col:F:11}
\label{F:sec:density-arithmetic-refinement}

The attachment's Meiji round 10 proves a general phase inequality and
prints the convenient consequence $N/n>209/2000=0.1045$.  The same
inequality, with exactly the same choice $k=43/25$, gives a slightly
larger rational constant if its arithmetic margin is retained.  This
section credits the analytic inequality to that supplied round and
claims only the explicit tighter consequence.

\begin{proposition}[A uniform arithmetic refinement]
\label{F:prop:density-arithmetic}
Every stationary competitive atomic tuple in the shared model satisfies
\[
 \boxed{\qquad \frac{N}{n}>\frac{52279}{500000}=0.104558.\qquad}
\]
More precisely, with
\[
 k=\frac{43}{25},\qquad
 g=\sqrt2\left(\sqrt{k}+\frac1{\sqrt{k}}-2\right),\qquad
 D=\frac{2}{k-1}+\frac{1-g}{k+1},
\]
one has the exact necessary condition
\[
 \frac Nn\ge
 C_0:=\frac{\pi}{D}\left(\frac2e-\frac{k}{k+1}\right)
 >\frac{52279}{500000}.
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The elementary mass floor $\lambda_j\ge1/n$ implies
$|\Phi'|\le\sqrt{2n}\,\Phi^{3/2}$, by differentiating each
atom potential and summing its $3/2$ power.  The two transitions
adjacent to every low component therefore give $G\ge r_1g$,
where $r=N/(\pi n)$ and $r_1\le r$ have the meanings in
Section~\ref{F:sec:new-phase-strip}.  This is also the
$t_-=t_+=0$ limiting gain of the calculation there; the direct
positive-potential derivative estimate avoids any limiting issue.

For the high-set half-lengths $x_i$, the unsigned endpoint flux
estimate gives
\[
 F\le\frac{k}{\pi}\sum_i\sin x_i\le ku.
\]
This remains valid for all possible high-set lengths; if the high
set is the full circle use the trivial $1-u=0$ alternative.
Equation~\eqref{F:eq:new-phase-base} now implies
\[
 |a_n|\le\frac{2r}{k-1}
       +\min\{1-u,ku+(1-g)r\}
 \le\frac{k}{k+1}+Dr.
\]
The last step bounds the minimum by the convex combination with
weights $k/(k+1)$ and $1/(k+1)$, which cancels $u$ exactly.
Since a competitive tuple has $|a_n|\ge2/e$, the exact lower bound
$N/n\ge C_0$ follows.

The accompanying \texttt{verify\_\allowbreak density\_\allowbreak refinement.py} uses
Machin's identity for $\pi$, a positive exponential sum with its
geometric remainder for an upper bound on $e$, and integer-square
enclosures for the square roots.  It checks the strict rational
inequality
\[
 \frac{k}{k+1}
  +\left(\frac{2}{k-1}+\frac{1-g_{\rm lower}}{k+1}\right)
      \frac{52279}{500000\,\pi_{\rm lower}}
 <\frac{2}{e_{\rm upper}}.
\]
Thus the displayed rational density bound is strict and uniform
over all support sizes, all degrees, all total masses and all
support angles satisfying the stationary mass floor.  No finite
support-size table is extrapolated.
\end{proof}

The increase over the attachment's printed constant is
$29/500000=0.000058$.  It is an arithmetic strengthening of an
already proved formula, not a new proof method or a global
covering theorem.  The stronger total-mass derivative and
component-mass corrections used above for particular sparse
support strata vanish in the proportional-$N/n$, bounded-total-mass
large-degree regime.  A larger uniform constant would therefore need
an additional argument covering that regime; it does not follow just
by extrapolating the finite sparse-support certificates above.

\section{An exact endpoint constraint coupling a high component to its mass}\label{col:F:12}
\label{F:sec:endpoint-mass-coupling}

The following algebraic constraint strengthens the unsigned endpoint
Cauchy estimate by retaining the mass inside each component.  It is
independent of the large finite computations and requires neither
stationarity nor a lower bound on the individual masses.

\begin{lemma}[Mass-coupled endpoint flux]
\label{F:lem:endpoint-mass-coupling}
Let $\lambda_j>0$ and let $\phi,\Phi$ be the atomic boundary phase
and its derivative used above.  Suppose an arc $[a,b]$ has
half-length $x=(b-a)/2\in(0,\pi/2)$, contains an atom, and has
\[
 \Phi(a)=\Phi(b)=kn,
 \qquad k>0,\quad n>0.
\]
Neither endpoint is an atom.  Let $t_i$ be the total mass of the
atoms strictly inside this arc, $t$ the total mass, and set
\[
 c=t/n,\qquad c_i=t_i/n,\qquad
 w=\frac{\phi(a)-\phi(b)}{2n},\qquad T=\tan(x/2).
\]
If $w\ge0$, then
\begin{align}
 0\le w&\le k\sin x,\label{F:eq:ep-w-range}\\
 c_i&\ge c-\frac{k\sin x-w}{2T}.\label{F:eq:ep-linear}
\end{align}
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\quad
 c_i\ge
 \frac{(w+cT)^2}{k+w(\cot x+2T)+cT^2}.
 \quad}\label{F:eq:ep-coupled}
\end{equation}
The weaker one-sided consequence
$c_i\ge w^2/(k+w\cot x)$ also holds.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose consistent lifts of the atom angles and put
\[
 v_j(q)=\sqrt{\lambda_j/2}
          \csc((q-\theta_j)/2),\qquad
 s_j=v_j(a)v_j(b).
\]
Products $s_j$ are negative for an enclosed atom and positive for an
exterior atom.  Write
$I=-\sum_{\rm inside}s_j$, $E=\sum_{\rm outside}s_j$ and $X=I-E$.
The cotangent difference identity gives
$\phi(a)-\phi(b)=2\sin x\,X$, so $w=\sin x\,X/n$.
Cauchy--Schwarz and the endpoint levels imply $I+E\le kn$,
proving \eqref{F:eq:ep-w-range}.

For an exterior atom the product of its endpoint sines is positive
and at most $\cos^2(x/2)$.  Consequently
\[
 E\ge\frac{t-t_i}{2\cos^2(x/2)}
      =\frac{t-t_i}{1+\cos x}.
\]
Together with $X=I-E\le kn-2E$, this proves
\eqref{F:eq:ep-linear}.

There is also an exact endpoint identity.  The elementary formula
\[
 \sin^2 A+\sin^2(A+x)-2\cos x\sin A\sin(A+x)=\sin^2x
\]
gives, after multiplication and division by the endpoint sines,
\[
 v_j(a)^2+v_j(b)^2-2\cos x\,s_j
     =\frac{2\sin^2x}{\lambda_j}s_j^2.
\]
Summing and using the endpoint levels yields
\begin{equation}
 kn+\cos x\,X
   =\sin^2x\sum_j\frac{s_j^2}{\lambda_j}.
 \label{F:eq:ep-exact}
\end{equation}
If $t_i<t$, apply weighted Cauchy--Schwarz separately inside and
outside:
\[
 \sum_j\frac{s_j^2}{\lambda_j}
 \ge\frac{(X+E)^2}{t_i}+\frac{E^2}{t-t_i}.
\]
For $X\ge0$ the right-hand side increases with $E\ge0$, so the
lower bound $E\ge(t-t_i)/(1+\cos x)$ may be substituted.
In normalized variables \eqref{F:eq:ep-exact} therefore implies
\[
 k+w\cot x\ge
 \frac{[w+(c-c_i)T]^2}{c_i}+(c-c_i)T^2.
\]
Multiplication by $c_i$ and collection of its terms gives
\[
 c_i\,[k+w(\cot x+2T)+cT^2]\ge(w+cT)^2.
\]
The bracket is positive, proving \eqref{F:eq:ep-coupled}.
If $t_i=t$, there are no exterior atoms.  Then $E=0$ and the
same final inequality follows directly from the inside
Cauchy--Schwarz bound in \eqref{F:eq:ep-exact}; expansion shows the
terms involving $T$ cancel as required.  Dropping the exterior
term and using $I=X+E\ge X$ gives the stated weaker consequence.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A closed conditional exclusion]
\label{F:cor:ep-exact-example}
No arc as in Lemma~\ref{F:lem:endpoint-mass-coupling} can satisfy all
of the following conditions:
\[
 k=2,\qquad
 \frac{59}{100}\le\cos x\le\frac{61}{100},\qquad
 \frac13\le\frac tn\le\frac25,\qquad
 \frac{t_i}{n}\le\frac14,\qquad
 \phi(a)-\phi(b)\ge2n\sin x.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Put $C=\cos x$ and $y=w/(2\sin x)$.  The last inequality
and \eqref{F:eq:ep-w-range} give $1/2\le y\le1$.
The right side of \eqref{F:eq:ep-coupled} increases with $c$.
Indeed its derivative has the positive factor
$2k+2w\cot x+3wT+cT^2$ after the common positive factors
are removed.  It also increases with $w$ under the present
bounds: the derivative has positive factor
$2k+w(\cot x+2T)-c\cos x/(1+\cos x)$.
Thus it may be evaluated at $c=1/3$ and $y=1/2$ to obtain
\[
 c_i\ge
 \frac{(1-C)(1+C+1/3)^2}
      {(4-C)(1+C)+(1-C)/3}.
\]
The denominator increases on $[59/100,61/100]$, because its
derivative is $3-2C-1/3>0$.  Using the independent safe endpoints
in its numerator gives the rational lower bound
\[
 c_i\ge
 \frac{(39/100)(577/300)^2}{55879/10000}
 =\frac{4328077}{16763700}>\frac14,
\]
a contradiction.  The companion exact script checks these endpoint
computations and the polynomial collection step in the lemma.
\end{proof}

This is a condition on a component's endpoint level, length, mass and
phase drop.  The corollary excludes an entire closed region in those
derived variables, independently of the degree and the number of
atoms.  It does not prove that every surviving coefficient candidate
has such a component.  No additional complete support-size ray or
coefficient theorem is claimed from this lemma.  The exploratory
optimization used while finding it is not used in its proof or in
the exact conditional exclusion above.

\section{Downward reuse of support-free Laurent witnesses}\label{col:F:13}
\label{F:sec:r5-downward}

Several upper-mass certificates in the supplied tournament were
presented in proofs of the three-atom stratum.  Their upper-mass
part in fact used no bound on the number of atoms.  Moreover, a
Laurent completion prescribed through degree $q$ also bounds every
coefficient of smaller positive degree.  Keeping these two facts
separate from the support-dependent lower-mass proofs makes the
existing witnesses useful in the four-atom continuation.

\begin{lemma}[Downward coefficient transfer]
\label{F:lem:r5-downward}
Let $q\ge1$, $t>0$, and write
\[
 F_t(w)=\exp[-t(1+w)/(1-w)]=\sum_{j\ge0}b_j(t)w^j.
\]
Suppose a Laurent polynomial $W_t$ has coefficient $b_j(t)$
at each frequency $1\le j\le q$.  Then every zero-free analytic
disk function $f$ with $|f|\le1$ and $|f(0)|=e^{-t}$ satisfies
\[
 \boxed{\quad |[z^n]f|\le\|W_t\|_{L^1(\mathbb T)}
       \quad(1\le n\le q).\quad}
 \tag{H1}\label{F:eq:r5-downward}
\]
The same inequality holds simultaneously throughout any mass
interval on which admissible completions and their norm bounds
are supplied.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Multiply $f$ by a unit constant to make $f(0)=e^{-t}$, and
choose its analytic logarithm $H=-\log f$ with $H(0)=t$.
Then $\Re H\ge0$ and
\[
 B(z)=\frac{H(z)-t}{H(z)+t},\qquad B(0)=0,\quad |B(z)|\le1,
 \qquad f=F_t\circ B.
\]
For any fixed $|w|<1$, the function
$(1+wB(z))/(1-wB(z))$ has nonnegative real part and constant
coefficient one.  Its degree-$n$ coefficient therefore has
modulus at most two.  To see this directly, integrate its
positive real part on a circle of radius $r<1$ against
$e^{-in\theta}$; the mean of the real part is one, giving
the coefficient bound $2r^{-n}$, and let $r\uparrow1$.
Since $B(0)=0$, that coefficient equals twice
\[
 Q_n(w)=\sum_{j=1}^n [z^n]B(z)^j\,w^j.
\]
Hence $|Q_n(w)|\le1$ on the closed disk by continuity.
Fourier orthogonality and $q\ge n$ now give
\[
 [z^n]F_t(B(z))
 =\int_{\mathbb T}W_t(w)Q_n(w^{-1})\,dm(w).
\]
Only the prescribed frequencies $1,\ldots,n$ contribute.
Frequencies $n+1,\ldots,q$ are immaterial for this lower
index, just like the other free frequencies.  Taking absolute
values proves \eqref{F:eq:r5-downward}.  Here $dm$ is normalized
arclength.  This argument applies separately at every $t$ in
the supplied interval.
\end{proof}

This lemma transfers a particular verified upper certificate.
It makes no assertion that the exact fixed-mass extremal values
are monotone in the coefficient index.
