\subsection{Independent replay and continuous validity}

The three original witness bundles were copied byte for byte
and independently rerun.  The copies are
\texttt{taisho\_\allowbreak r09}, \texttt{meiji\_\allowbreak r09}, and
\texttt{taisho\_\allowbreak r10} in the reproduction material.  Together
they certify 5,536 rational mass knots in eleven source
degrees, all with zero rejected knots.  Some replayed source
degrees are unnecessary for the table; retaining them preserves
the original verifier and its witness indexing unchanged.

The relevant maximal endpoint bounds and the uniform mass
interpolation pads are as follows.  The numbers in the third
column already include the angular continuum correction and
the exact Fourier arithmetic allowances.
\[
\begin{array}{r|c|c|c}
 q&T&\text{endpoint upper bound}&\text{mass pad}\\\hline
15&567/100&732390386/10^9&1/1152\\
17&189329/30000&733994096/10^9&1/20000\\
18&174/25&733860118/10^9&1/2312\\
19&4579/600&732645945/10^9&1/2312\\
20&25/3&732852107/10^9&1/2312\\
21&903/100&731854739/10^9&1/2312\\
26&39/4&733662900/10^9&1/3200
\end{array}
\]
Each sum is strictly below $2/e$, checked with the rational
upper bound $e<1359141/500000$.

For clarity, the continuous certificate used by these files
is recalled here.  The exact required coefficients are
$b_j(t)=e^{-t}C_j(t)$, where
\[
 C_0=1,\quad C_1=-2t,\qquad
 (j+1)C_{j+1}=2(j-t)C_j-(j-1)C_{j-1}.
\]
At each mass knot the witness supplies rational free modes
$-35,\ldots,0$ and $q+1,\ldots,q+35$, of denominator $10^{10}$.
Between successive knots retain the exact required coefficients
and interpolate only the free ones linearly.  Thus the
completion remains admissible throughout each closed interval.

If $v(t)=(b_0(t),\ldots,b_q(t))$ and $A$ is the lower-triangular
matrix of truncated multiplication by $(1+w)/(1-w)$, then
$v''=A^2v$ and $\|A\|\le2q+1$.  The lower diagonals of
$A^2$ are $1,4,8,\ldots,4q$.  The exact endpoint audit gives
$\|A^2v\|_2<1.251$.  Nearest-knot distances are at most
$1/48$, $1/200$ or $1/68$, and $1/80$ in the respective
bundles.  The bounds
\[
 1.251e^{33/48}<4,\qquad
 1.251e^{45/68}<4,\qquad
 1.251e^{57/80}<4
\]
therefore give $\|\partial_t^2W_t\|_1<4$ on every open
knot interval.  Only the prescribed coefficients have a
nonzero second derivative.  Linear interpolation in the
normed space $L^1(\mathbb T)$ incurs error at most
$4h^2/8$ when the interval width is at most $h$; this follows
by integrating the nonnegative Dirichlet Green kernel for
the second derivative.  The resolutions $h\le1/24,1/100,
1/34,1/40$ give exactly the stated pads.

At a knot the angular mesh has $M=8192$ points.  Integrated
linear interpolation, followed by Parseval, yields
\[
 \|W_t\|_1\le \frac1M\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}|W_t(e^{2\pi ij/M})|
       +\frac{\pi^2}{2M^2}
           \left(\sum_r r^4|[w^r]W_t|^2\right)^{1/2}.
\]
Every quantity on the right is bounded outward.  The fixed-point
scale is $S=2^{55}$.  The positive exponential sum through
degree 112 and the geometric bound on its first omitted term
give error less than $1/S$ for $0\le t\le29$; the encoded
required coefficients have error below $2/S$.  A separate
scale $2^{40}$ computes the angular derivative norm, with an
additional unit in its upper bound to absorb all input errors.

The angular Fourier transform uses 13 radix-two stages.
Machin's identity and alternating rational Taylor sums bound
the initial sine and cosine.  Repeated fixed-point multiplication
then puts every twiddle within $3\cdot10^{-12}$ of its exact
unit root.  The code verifies that the input coefficient
$\ell^1$ norm is below 7, or below 8 in the degree-26--28
bundle.  Every exact butterfly intermediate is consequently
below 8, respectively 9, in modulus.  The stage error is
bounded by
\[
 D\longmapsto 2.001D+24\cdot10^{-12}+2/S
 \quad\hbox{or}\quad
 D\longmapsto 2.001D+27\cdot10^{-12}+2/S.
\]
The supplied rational ledgers place the final error below
$10^{-6}$.  This allowance is included in the endpoint table.
Coordinates fit signed 64-bit integers, and products and
squared norms use signed 128-bit integers.  A floating square
root is only an initial guess: the checker corrects it using
exact integer square comparisons before accepting a bound.
Thus the retained endpoint bounds, angular interpolation,
and mass interpolation certify full closed rectangles.

The new step here is the explicit downward reuse and the
resulting collection of lower upper-slab cutoffs.  The original
Laurent witnesses, their optimizations, and their exact Fourier
certificates belong to the supplied rounds and are credited
without a separate novelty claim.  The high-mass statements
alone do not exclude the remaining low-mass four-atom branch.

\section{The inherited all-degree high-mass cutoff, with its full proof}\label{col:F:14}
\label{F:sec:inherited-n-tail}

The mass restriction $t<n$ used in the stationary residual is justified
by the following support-free theorem from the supplied Revision~4.
It is reproduced here with its analytic proof and exact checking data
to make the present continuation self-contained.  It is an inherited
result, not a new exclusion discovered in this continuation.

\begin{theorem}[Inherited cutoff at the coefficient index]
\label{F:thm:inherited-n-tail}\label{F:thm:uniform-n-tail}
Let $f$ be holomorphic and zero-free in the unit disk, with $|f|\le1$
and $|f(0)|=e^{-t}$.  For every integer $n\ge2$,
\[
 t\ge n\quad\Longrightarrow\quad |[z^n]f|<2/e.
\]
For $n\ge3$ the proof gives the stronger uniform estimate
\[
 |[z^n]f|^2<\frac{1353}{2500}<\frac4{e^2}.
\]
No stationarity, finite-support or angular hypothesis is imposed.
\end{theorem}

\subsection{Coefficient energy and an exact probability tail}

After a constant rotation write $f=e^{-tH}$, with $H(0)=1$ and
$\Re H>0$.  Set $B=(H-1)/(H+1)$, so $B(0)=0$ and $|B|<1$, and
\[
 F_t(w)=\exp\!\left[-t\frac{1+w}{1-w}\right]
       =\sum_{j\ge0}b_j(t)w^j,
 \qquad b_0(t)=e^{-t}.
\]
For a fixed target index let $q_j=[z^n]B(z)^j$ and
$Q_n(w)=\sum_{j=1}^nq_jw^j$.  The function
$(1+wB)/(1-wB)$ has positive real part and constant coefficient one
for each $|w|=1$.  Its $n$th coefficient is $2Q_n(w)$ and has
modulus at most two: on each smaller circle its nonconstant
Fourier coefficient is twice that of its nonnegative real part,
whose average is one, and then the radius tends to one.
Thus $|Q_n(w)|\le1$, and Parseval gives $\sum_j|q_j|^2\le1$.
Composition preserves the coefficient through degree $n$, so
Cauchy--Schwarz proves
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:inherited-tail-energy}
 |[z^n]f|^2
   =\left|\sum_{j=1}^n b_j(t)q_j\right|^2
   \le\sum_{j=1}^n b_j(t)^2.
\end{equation}

Put $S_n(t)=\sum_{j=0}^n b_j(t)^2$ and define
\[
 L_n(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n(-1)^j\binom nj\frac{x^j}{j!}.
\]
Differentiating $F_t$ gives
$b_k'=-b_k-2\sum_{j<k}b_j$, whence
\[
 S_n'=-2\left(\sum_{k=0}^n b_k\right)^2,
 \qquad \sum_{k=0}^n b_k(t)=e^{-t}L_n(2t).
\]
The latter identity follows by multiplying $F_t$ by $(1-w)^{-1}$
and using the Laguerre generating function.  Each $b_k$ is an
exponential times a polynomial and tends to zero at infinity.
Integrating the derivative therefore yields
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:inherited-tail-probability}
 S_n(t)=\int_{2t}^{\infty}e^{-x}L_n(x)^2\,dx.
\end{equation}
At $t=0$ one has $S_n(0)=1$.  Thus $e^{-x}L_n(x)^2dx$ is a
probability distribution on $[0,\infty)$; let $X_n$ denote a
variable with this distribution.  The function $S_n$ is
nonincreasing, and
\[
 |[z^n]f|^2\le S_n(t)-e^{-2t}.
\]

All moments $M_j(n)=\mathbb E X_n^j$ can be generated exactly.
Rodrigues' identity
$e^{-x}L_r(x)=\frac1{r!}(d/dx)^r(e^{-x}x^r)$ and integration
by parts give $\int_0^\infty e^{-x}L_rL_s\,dx=\delta_{rs}$.
The boundary terms vanish, and for $r=s$ the integral reduces
to $(r!)^{-1}\int_0^\infty e^{-x}x^r\,dx=1$.
Consequently the recurrence
\[
 xL_r=(2r+1)L_r-(r+1)L_{r+1}-rL_{r-1}
\]
computes $M_j(n)$ as the coefficient of $L_n$ after $j$
multiplications starting from $L_n$.  For an explicit symbolic
construction set $v_0^{(0)}=1$ and all other $v_h^{(0)}=0$, and use
\[
 v_h^{(j+1)}=(2n+2h+1)v_h^{(j)}
      -(n+h)v_{h-1}^{(j)}-(n+h+1)v_{h+1}^{(j)},
 \qquad M_j(n)=v_0^{(j)}.
\]
Each moment is a polynomial in $n$ of degree at most $j$.
At integer $n\ge0$, a formal path that would cross the Laguerre
index zero has a zero downward-transition factor, so this
polynomial construction remains valid at the small indices too.

\subsection{One fixed polynomial covers every degree at least 512}

Take the following rational numbers:
\[
 (a_1,\ldots,a_6)=
 \left(\frac{73}{5000},\frac{13}{100},\frac{177}{500},
       \frac{3369}{5000},\frac{5353}{5000},\frac{7607}{5000}\right),
 \qquad c_j=4-a_{7-j}.
\]
They satisfy $a_1<\cdots<a_6<2<c_1<\cdots<c_6$.
Let $p$ be the rational polynomial of degree at most $24$ defined by
the $25$ Hermite conditions
\[
 p(a_i)=p'(a_i)=0,\quad p(2)=1,\quad
 p(c_i)=1,\quad p'(c_i)=0\qquad(1\le i\le6).
\]
Existence and uniqueness follow from ordinary Hermite interpolation;
equivalently, the homogeneous conditions give $25$ zeros counting
multiplicity for a polynomial of degree at most $24$.

These conditions alone prove the global majorant inequalities
\[
 p(x)\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R),\qquad p(x)\ge1\quad(x\ge2).
\]
Indeed $p'$ has its twelve prescribed roots at the $a_i,c_i$,
five further roots between consecutive $a_i$, and six further
roots between consecutive points of $2,c_1,\ldots,c_6$ by Rolle's
theorem.  These are $23$ distinct roots, the maximum possible.
The polynomial is nonconstant, so all those roots are simple and
there are no others.  On $(a_6,2)$ the derivative is positive
because $p$ rises from zero to one without a critical point.
Its alternating signs make every $a_i$ a minimum of value zero
and every $c_i$ a minimum of value one.  The polynomial rises away
from the outermost minima on the exterior rays.  This proves both
inequalities on their full domains, without sampled positivity.

Write $p(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{24}p_jx^j$ and form the rational polynomial
\[
 D(n)=\frac{27}{50}n^{24}
       -\sum_{j=0}^{24}p_jM_j(n)n^{24-j}.
\]
The exact checker reconstructs $p$ from the displayed contacts,
reconstructs all moment polynomials by the displayed recurrence,
and verifies that all $25$ coefficients of $D(512+s)$ are
strictly positive.  All contacts and all coefficients are stored
as exact fractions in its included output.  Therefore $D(n)>0$
for every real $n\ge512$, and for every integer $n\ge512$,
\[
 S_n(n)=\Pr\{X_n\ge2n\}
 \le\mathbb E p(X_n/n)<\frac{27}{50}.
\]
This positive-coefficient argument supplies the infinite degree
range; the proof does not extrapolate from a finite list of degrees.

\subsection{The 509 rational base cases and the degree-two case}

For an integer $n\ge3$, write $b_k(n)=e^{-n}c_k$.
The differential equation $(1-w)^2F_n'(w)=-2nF_n(w)$ gives
\[
 c_0=1,\qquad c_1=-2n,\qquad
 (k+1)c_{k+1}=2(k-n)c_k-(k-1)c_{k-1}.
\]
With $B_0=7389/1000$, the included exact checker verifies all
$509$ inequalities
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^n c_k^2<\frac{1353}{2500}B_0^n,
 \qquad 3\le n\le511.
\]
The largest tested normalized ratio is attained at $n=7$ and is
exactly
\[
 \frac{52711168520000000000000000000}
      {97405770215605396912332422949}<\frac{1353}{2500}.
\]
All comparisons use fractions.  Positive exponential Taylor terms
and a geometric bound for the omitted tail give
\[
 B_0<\sum_{j=0}^{12}\frac{2^j}{j!}<e^2
 <\sum_{j=0}^{8}\frac{2^j}{j!}
      +\frac54\frac{2^9}{9!}<\frac{739}{100},
 \qquad \frac{1353}{2500}\frac{739}{100}<4.
\]
Thus the finite base has $S_n(n)<1353/2500$.  The infinite
degree range has the stronger bound $27/50<1353/2500$.
By monotonicity in \eqref{F:eq:inherited-tail-probability}, every
real $t\ge n$ and every integer $n\ge3$ consequently satisfy
\[
 |[z^n]f|^2\le S_n(t)-e^{-2t}\le S_n(n)
       <1353/2500<4/e^2.
\]

For $n=2$ write $B(z)=az+bz^2+\cdots$.
Schwarz--Pick applied to $B(z)/z$ gives $|b|\le1-|a|^2$.
Direct expansion yields
\[
 [z^2]f=2te^{-t}\bigl((t-1)a^2-b\bigr),
 \qquad |[z^2]f|\le2t(t-1)e^{-t}\quad(t\ge2).
\]
If $x=t-1\ge1$, then
\[
 e^x-x(x+1)>1-\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{x^3}{6}
   =\frac{(x-2)^2(x+1)+2}{6}>0.
\]
Hence $2t(t-1)e^{-t}<2/e$, proving the remaining case and
Theorem~\ref{F:thm:inherited-n-tail}.

\paragraph{Included replay and use in the residual.}
The byte-identical inherited checker
\texttt{spectral\_\allowbreak uniform\_\allowbreak n\_\allowbreak tail.py} uses only exact polynomial
helpers from \texttt{spectral\_\allowbreak tail\_\allowbreak certificate.py}; both require
only Python's standard library.  The rational interpolation nodes
are embedded in the checker, so no separate external data or
optimization is needed.  The fresh continuation replay completed
with exit code zero, reconstructed the degree-$24$ majorant and
all $25$ positive shifted coefficients, and passed all $509$
finite-base comparisons.  Its exact output and source hashes are
included in \texttt{inherited\_\allowbreak tail/replay\_\allowbreak uniform\_\allowbreak n\_\allowbreak tail.json}
and \texttt{inherited\_\allowbreak tail/replay\_\allowbreak receipt.json}.
Consequently a competitive candidate at any $n\ge2$ must have
$t<n$.  Combining this with the separate stationary lower bound
gives $n/N\le t<n$, exactly the mass interval used in the
four-support joining argument.

\section{Exact lower-mass certificates for four atoms}\label{col:F:15}
\label{F:sec:finite-four-lower}

This section proves the continuum validity of the finite checks used
in the four-atom continuation.  The method is the integer angular and
mass-interpolation method of the supplied Keio focused Round~10.
The continuation uses its original exponential enclosure at indices
$11,12$ and a longer, uniformly valid enclosure in the generalized
implementation.  A theorem is asserted only for the completed rows
of the table below.  A parameter selection, an interrupted run, or
an assertion failure is not a completed certificate.

Write
\[
 f(z)=\prod_{j=1}^4
 \exp\left[-\lambda_j\frac{1+\alpha_jz}{1-\alpha_jz}\right],
 \qquad |\alpha_j|=1,\quad \lambda_j>0,
 \qquad t=\sum_{j=1}^4\lambda_j.
\]
All support angles are covered, without separation or symmetry
assumptions.  Repeated angles are harmless for the coefficient
bound, although a four-support stationary candidate has distinct
angles.  The only mass hypotheses in a row $(n,A,T,L)$ are
\[
 \lambda_j\ge1/n\quad(1\le j\le4),\qquad A\le t\le T,
 \qquad n/4\le A<T\le n.
\]
Here $L$ is the number of grid points in each of three independent
angular variables.  When $A>n/4$, the row certifies only the
displayed closed band; it makes no assertion about the masses below
$A$.

\begin{theorem}[Completed lower-band rows]
\label{F:thm:finite-four-lower}
For each completed row $(n,A,T,L)$ in the following table,
every function satisfying that row's hypotheses obeys
\[
 \boxed{\quad |[z^n]f|<\frac{2943}{4000}<\frac2e.\quad}
\]
Thus no competitive stationary four-support tuple occurs in any
of the listed closed mass bands.
\end{theorem}

\subsection{Exact one-atom coefficients and exponential enclosures}

Put
\[
 C_0(x)=1,\qquad
 C_k(x)=\sum_{r=1}^k
       \frac{(-2)^r}{r!}\binom{k-1}{r-1}x^r
       \quad(k\ge1),\qquad b_k(x)=e^{-x}C_k(x).
\]
Expanding $\exp[-2xz/(1-z)]$ proves that $b_k(x)$ is the
$k$th Taylor coefficient of one atomic factor at phase $1$.
All $C_k$ have rational coefficients.
Let $E_p(x)=\sum_{r=0}^p x^r/r!$.
For $0\le x\le25/4$, the original code uses
\[
 E_{24}(x)\le e^x\le E_{24}(x)+\frac{2x^{25}}{25!}.
\]
Indeed every subsequent ratio in the omitted positive tail is at
most $(25/4)/26<1/2$.
For the generalized checks, $0\le x\le26$ and
\[
 E_{112}(x)\le e^x\le
 E_{112}(x)+\frac{x^{113}}{113!}\frac1{1-x/114}.
\]
The last assertion follows by bounding the subsequent ratios by
$x/114<1$.  Inverting these positive endpoints encloses $e^{-x}$.
If $e_c\pm e_r$ denotes the midpoint and radius of that interval,
the integer approximation $v_k(x)$ at scale $G=10^8$ is accepted
only after the exact rational test
\[
 \left|C_k(x)e_c-\frac{v_k(x)}G\right|
                 +|C_k(x)|e_r<\frac1G.
 \tag{F1}\label{F:eq:finite-atom-rounding}
\]
Thus every single-atom coefficient has complex, and here real,
error strictly below $1/G$.

After one common input rotation we may set $\alpha_4=1$.
The target coefficient is an angular polynomial with nonnegative
frequency triples $(a,b,c)$ and fourth index $d=n-a-b-c$:
\[
 P_{\boldsymbol\lambda}(z_1,z_2,z_3)
 =\sum_{a+b+c+d=n}
 b_a(\lambda_1)b_b(\lambda_2)b_c(\lambda_3)b_d(\lambda_4)
                       z_1^az_2^bz_3^c.
\]
The common rotation changes its coefficient only by a unit factor.
For a mass vertex let $v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4$ be the four integers for
one tuple.  Round their product back to scale $G$:
\[
 w_{a b c}=\operatorname{round}
           \left(\frac{v_1v_2v_3v_4}{G^3}\right).
\]
Its error from the true product is bounded by
\[
 \frac{\prod_{j=1}^4(|v_j|+1)-\prod_{j=1}^4|v_j|}{G^4}
          +\frac1{2G}.
 \tag{F2}\label{F:eq:finite-product-pad}
\]
This is the expansion of the product with four errors of magnitude
at most $1/G$, followed by the nearest-integer rounding allowance.
The sum of these pads over all tuples bounds the polynomial error
uniformly in the three angles.

\subsection{Integer angular evaluation and overflow control}

Use the $L$th roots of unity in each angular variable.
Every needed root, including every power appearing in a monomial,
is computed directly at scale $R=10^8$ by reducing its index modulo
$L$.  There is consequently no error accumulation proportional to
the frequency index.  Machin's identity
\[
 \pi=16\arctan(1/5)-4\arctan(1/239)
\]
and alternating rational sums enclose $\pi$ between
$\pi_0=31415926535897932/10^{16}$ and
$\pi_0+10^{-16}$.
For $0\le x<2\pi$, the degree-$51$ Taylor sum for $e^{ix}$ has
error at most
\[
 \frac{(44/7)^{52}}{52!}<10^{-20}.
\]
The integral Taylor remainder along the real segment gives this
bound directly.  The additional error from replacing $\pi$ by
$\pi_0$ is below $2\cdot10^{-16}$.  Rounding both coordinates to
scale $R$ changes the complex number by at most
$\sqrt2/(2R)$.  Their sum is strictly below $1/R$.
Each rounded real or imaginary coordinate has absolute value at
most $R$: before rounding the possible overshoot beyond $1$ is
less than $2\cdot10^{-16}+10^{-20}<1/(2R)$.

The polynomial with coefficients $w_{abc}/G$ is evaluated by three
integer tensor contractions, one variable at a time.  After each
contraction the real and imaginary coordinates are rounded back
to scale $G$ by integer division of their numerators by $R$.
Let
\[
 D=n+1,\qquad M=\sum_{a+b+c+d=n}|w_{abc}|.
\]
Replacing three exact phases by their approximations changes one
phase product by at most $(1+1/R)^3-1<4/R$.  Summing over the
coefficients gives error at most $4M/(GR)$.
Each complex rounding at one contraction has magnitude less than
$1/G$.  At a fixed final angular triple, the first-stage errors
pass through at most $D^2$ subsequent terms, the second-stage
errors through at most $D$, and the last error occurs once.
Since $(1+1/R)^2<2$ and $D\ge2$, their total is at most
\[
 \frac{D^2(1+1/R)^2+D(1+1/R)+1}{G}
 <\frac{4D^2}{G}.
\]
Thus the explicit contraction pad is
\[
 \frac{4M}{GR}+\frac{4D^2}{G}.
 \tag{F3}\label{F:eq:finite-contraction-pad}
\]

Overflow is checked before any tensor contraction.  For fixed
previously evaluated angles, the sum of absolute real and
imaginary integer values across the remaining frequency indices
is at most $2M+D^2$ after the first stage and
$4M+2D^2+D$ after the second.  To see this, the sum of absolute
coordinates of each phase is at most $2R$, and rounding both
coordinates adds at most one per output.  These bounds also
control the sums of absolute products inside every integer
contraction and the subsequent real/imaginary additions.
The sufficient check used by the implementation is
\[
             20R(M+8D^3)<2^{63}.
 \tag{F4}\label{F:eq:finite-overflow}
\]
It dominates all these intermediate sums and the rounding offsets.
Products forming $w_{abc}$ and rational pads are computed as
unbounded integers before entering the tensor arrays.
Before squaring the final real and imaginary integer outputs,
the verifier checks that each absolute value is below $2^{30}$.
Their sum of squares therefore fits in signed $64$-bit arithmetic.
Its integer square root, increased by one, gives an outward bound
for the maximum sampled modulus.  Floating-point arithmetic is
not used in an accepted angular comparison.

\subsection{The angular continuum between the sampled points}

Fix the other two variables and regard $P$ as a polynomial of
degree at most $n$ in one unit variable $e^{i\theta}$.
Multiplying by $e^{-in\theta/2}$ centers its frequencies in
$[-n/2,n/2]$ without changing its modulus.  Bernstein's inequality
applied twice bounds the second angular derivative by
$(n/2)^2\|P\|_\infty$.  This also holds for odd $n$: the centered
polynomial is a trigonometric polynomial in $\theta/2$.
At a point where its modulus is maximal, multiply by a unit
scalar to make its value positive real.  The real part then has
zero first derivative.  A grid point within distance $\pi/L$
therefore captures at least
\[
 I=1-\frac{n^2}{8}\left(\frac{22/7}{L}\right)^2
\]
times the maximum.  All listed grids have $L>2n$, so $I>0$.
Applying this argument successively in all three variables gives
\[
 \max_{\mathbb T^3}|P|
 \le I^{-3}\max_{\text{angular grid}}|P|.
 \tag{F5}\label{F:eq:finite-angular-continuum}
\]
Here the sampled maximum includes the product pad
\eqref{F:eq:finite-product-pad} and the contraction pad
\eqref{F:eq:finite-contraction-pad}.  Equivalently, their sum and
the outward integer sampled bound are all multiplied by $I^{-3}$.
This gives a certified angular supremum at each mass vertex.

\paragraph{Optional conjugation reduction of the angular grid.}
All coefficients of $P_{\boldsymbol\lambda}$ are real.  Therefore
$|P(z_1,z_2,z_3)|=|P(\overline z_1,\overline z_2,\overline z_3)|$.
It is enough to evaluate the first grid index
$0\le j_1\le\lfloor L/2\rfloor$, retaining all $L$ values in each
of the other two coordinates.  Any omitted grid triple is mapped
into this half-grid by simultaneous conjugation.  This is an
identity for the exact grid values, so the computed root
approximations need not themselves obey exact conjugate symmetry.
The existing error pads at the retained representative bound its
exact value and hence that of its omitted partner.  The continuous
multiplier $I^{-3}$ and all rounding and overflow bounds are
unchanged.

\subsection{Mass interpolation and complete closed-box coverage}

For a mass interval $[a,b]$ write $y=(a+b)/2$, $h=(b-a)/2$.
If a polynomial is $C(x)=\sum_k c_kx^k$, define the rational
shift bound
\[
 \mathcal S(C;y,h)=
 \sum_{r\ge0}\left|\sum_{k\ge r}c_k\binom{k}{r}y^{k-r}\right|h^r.
\]
It bounds $|C(x)|$ throughout $[a,b]$.  Since
\[
 b_k''(x)=e^{-x}\{C_k''(x)-2C_k'(x)+C_k(x)\},
\]
valid interval bounds are
\begin{align*}
 V_k&=U(a)\mathcal S(C_k;y,h),\\
 E_k&=\tfrac12 h^2 U(a)
           \mathcal S(C_k''-2C_k'+C_k;y,h),
\end{align*}
where $U(a)=1/E_p(a)\ge e^{-a}$ with $p=24$, $40$, or $112$ as
specified above.  The implementation rounds each bound upward
to an integer multiple of $1/G$.
Here $V_k$ bounds both the actual coefficient and its linear
interpolant between the two endpoints.  The quantity $E_k$
bounds their difference: the elementary linear-interpolation
remainder is at most $(b-a)^2\sup|b_k''|/8=h^2\sup|b_k''|/2$.

For a four-dimensional mass box use these bounds separately in
each coordinate.  Telescoping the four-factor product before
and after interpolation gives uniform coefficient error
\[
 \mathcal E=
 \sum_{\kappa_1+\cdots+\kappa_4=n}
 \sum_{i=1}^4 E_{i,\kappa_i}
                   \prod_{j\ne i}V_{j,\kappa_j}.
 \tag{F6}\label{F:eq:finite-mass-error}
\]
The interpolated angular polynomial is a convex combination of
the sixteen vertex polynomials.  Thus its angular modulus is
at most the largest certified vertex bound.  Adding
$\mathcal E$ encloses every mass point and every angle in the
whole box.  Permuting masses does not change the supremum over
all angles, so sorting a vertex before its angular evaluation
is legitimate even when that sorted vertex is not a vertex
of the original coordinate box.

The initial box is $[1/n,T]^4$.  It contains every admissible
mass tuple in the row because $t\le T$ implies
$\lambda_j\le T$.  Without loss of generality the masses are
sorted.  A closed box with endpoints $a_j,b_j$ is discarded
only if one of
\[
 \sum_j a_j>T,\qquad \sum_j b_j<A,\qquad
 a_j>b_{j+1}\text{ for some }j\in\{1,2,3\}
\]
holds.  Each condition proves that no admissible sorted mass
tuple lies in that box.  Endpoint equality is retained.
A remaining box is certified only if its largest vertex
bound plus \eqref{F:eq:finite-mass-error} is strictly below
$2943/4000$.  Otherwise its widest mass interval is bisected,
and both closed children are retained.  They share their
midpoint and exactly cover their parent.  A minimum-width
assertion is a failure guard, not a rule for discarding a box.

For each completed row the recorded run terminates with an
empty list of unresolved children and a final \texttt{PASS}.
Induction through the binary subdivision shows that the certified
and discarded leaves cover the initial box.  The discard proofs
and vertex/interpolation bounds consequently cover every
admissible mass and angle, including all boundaries.
Finally,
\[
 \frac{2943}{4000}
 \left(\sum_{j=0}^{20}\frac1{j!}+\frac2{21!}\right)<2,
 \qquad
 e<\sum_{j=0}^{20}\frac1{j!}+\frac2{21!},
\]
are exact rational comparisons, so the accepted target is
strictly below $2/e$.  This proves
Theorem~\ref{F:thm:finite-four-lower} for precisely the completed
rows.

\paragraph{Joining other certificates.}
A row starting at $A=n/4$ can be joined to a support-free
upper-mass certificate beginning at the same closed endpoint
$T$ to exclude the entire four-support stationary branch at
that index.  A row with $A>n/4$ also needs an independent
certificate below $A$ before that conclusion is valid.
The displayed rows themselves assert only their stated mass
bands.  They imply neither a complete coefficient theorem
with arbitrary support size nor an all-degree conclusion
until the separate support-size and degree joins have been
explicitly verified.

\subsection{A contracted sorted domain and a shorter exponential enclosure}
\label{F:sec:r5-contracted}

The optional verifier \texttt{four\_\allowbreak atoms\_\allowbreak contracted.py} preserves
the coefficient, angular, and interpolation proof above.  It
changes the initial containing box, contracts each mass box using
necessary linear constraints, and uses a shorter exponential
enclosure on the restricted range $T\le39/4$.  A completed run of
this verifier has the same mathematical meaning as a completed
uncontracted run.  Partial progress is never used as an exclusion.

Write $a=1/n$ and suppose the masses are ordered.  The domain
$\lambda_i\ge a$, $A\le\sum_i\lambda_i\le T$ is contained in
the initial box
\[
 \lambda_i\le \frac{T-(i-1)a}{5-i}\quad(1\le i\le4),
 \qquad
 \lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3\ge a,\qquad
 \lambda_4\ge\max\{a,A/4\}.
 \tag{F7}\label{F:eq:r5-sorted-root}
\]
Indeed the last $5-i$ masses are all at least $\lambda_i$,
while the first $i-1$ are at least $a$.  Also the largest
mass is at least one quarter of the total mass.

For a current box $\prod_i[l_i,u_i]$, the contractor repeatedly
uses the replacements
\begin{align*}
 l_i&\leftarrow\max\left\{l_i,
               A-\sum_{j\ne i}u_j,\ l_{i-1}\right\},\\
 u_i&\leftarrow\min\left\{u_i,
               T-\sum_{j\ne i}l_j,\ u_{i+1}\right\},
 \tag{F8}\label{F:eq:r5-mass-contraction}
\end{align*}
omitting the adjacent-bound term when it has no index in
$\{1,2,3,4\}$.  Each replacement is individually necessary
for an admissible point in the current box.  Updated bounds
may therefore be used immediately in later replacements:
by induction every admissible point is retained after each
step.  A box is discarded only if some new lower endpoint
strictly exceeds its upper endpoint.  Equality is retained.
The implementation performs at most four complete passes,
or stops earlier if no bound changed.  Reaching a fixed point
is unnecessary for correctness; an incomplete contraction
only leaves a larger containing box.

After contraction, the same certified interpolation test is
applied.  If it fails, the widest remaining coordinate is
bisected into two closed children.  The children cover the
contracted box, which contains every admissible point of
the parent.  Thus the original induction proving closed-domain
coverage still applies.  The parts removed by contraction
are justified by necessary constraints rather than by a
coefficient estimate.  Zero-width coordinates do not create
an omission; their interpolation error is zero, and the
minimum-width failure guard still cannot silently discard
an unresolved box.

On $0\le x\le39/4$ the contracted verifier uses
\[
 E_{40}(x)\le e^x\le E_{40}(x)+R_{40}(x),\qquad
 R_{40}(x)=\frac{x^{41}}{41!}\frac1{1-x/42}.
 \tag{F9}\label{F:eq:r5-exp40}
\]
All omitted positive-series ratios after the first term are
at most $x/42<1$, proving the enclosure.  The ratio
$R_{40}(x)/E_{40}(x)$ is increasing for $0<x\le39/4$:
its logarithmic derivative is
\[
 \frac{41}{x}+\frac1{42-x}
       -\frac{E_{39}(x)}{E_{40}(x)}>\frac{41}{x}-1>0.
\]
At $x=39/4$ an exact rational comparison gives
\[
 \frac{R_{40}(39/4)}{E_{40}(39/4)}<10^{-12}.
\]
This proves a uniform accuracy bound, not just validity of
the exponential interval.  Since $|e^{-x}C_j(x)|\le1$ for
every single-atom coefficient, writing $L=E_{40}(x)$ and
$U=L+R_{40}(x)$ gives
\[
 |C_j(x)|\left(\frac1L-\frac1U\right)
 \le U\left(\frac1L-\frac1U\right)
 =\frac{R_{40}(x)}L<10^{-12}.
\]
Here $|C_j(x)|\le e^x\le U$ was used.  Nearest rounding of
the midpoint coefficient to scale $G=10^8$ consequently has
error below $1/(2G)+10^{-12}/2<1/G$.  The exact per-vertex
test \eqref{F:eq:finite-atom-rounding} remains in the code.
The bound $1/E_{40}(x)\ge e^{-x}$ also remains valid for the
mass-interpolation bounds.  No angular error budget or integer
overflow assertion is reduced by this optimization.

\paragraph{Optional first-angle conjugation reduction.}
For even $L$, the half-grid implementation
retains only first grid indices $0,1,\ldots,L/2$, while keeping all $L$
indices for each of the other two angles.  Every coefficient of the
fixed-mass trigonometric polynomial is real.  Consequently simultaneous
negation of all three angles conjugates its value without changing its
modulus.  An omitted triple with first index $\ell>L/2$ therefore has the
same exact modulus as the retained triple
$(L-\ell,-m\bmod L,-k\bmod L)$.  The largest exact modulus on the full grid
is unchanged.  Rounding errors need not respect this symmetry: the existing
integer error envelope is applied to every retained triple and bounds its
exact value; exact conjugation is invoked only afterward.  The continuous
angular interpolation factor and all integer overflow bounds are therefore
unchanged.  Only the number of first-stage rows is reduced.

\subsection{A bounded-error binary64 tensor implementation}
\label{F:sec:finite-blas}

The optional implementation \texttt{four\_\allowbreak atoms\_\allowbreak contracted\_\allowbreak blas.py}
replaces the three integer tensor contractions by real binary64 matrix
products.  It retains the exact rational coefficients, rounded integer
root data, sorted-domain contractor, forty-term exponential enclosure,
mass interpolation bounds and final integer norm bound.  This is a
mixed-arithmetic implementation and is not described as integer-only.
Its acceptance theorem is unchanged because the additional matrix
arithmetic error fits strictly inside the existing per-contraction
complex rounding allowance of $1/G$.

Let $d=n+1\le27$, let $M$ be the integer coefficient $\ell^1$ sum,
and put $U=M+8d^3$.  The existing exact guard is
\[
 20RU<2^{63},\qquad R=10^8.
\]
The integer phase coordinates have absolute value at most $R$.
The matrix coefficients are converted to binary64 only after this
guard, so their absolute values are at most $M<2^{33}$ and they
are represented exactly.  The phase coordinates are also represented
exactly.  Every rounded intermediate is an integer of magnitude below
$16U+1<2^{37}$; hence each is represented exactly when passed to the
next matrix product.

Use binary64 unit roundoff $u=2^{-53}$ and
\[
 \gamma_{64}=\frac{64u}{1-64u},\qquad
 \eta=16U\gamma_{64}.
\]
For the real dot products of length at most $27$, followed when
needed by the addition or subtraction of two such dot products and
division by $R$, the standard absolute forward-error bound is less
than $\gamma_{64}$ times the corresponding scaled sum of absolute
products.  The generous index $64$ exceeds $2d+6$.
This estimate permits arbitrary reassociation of an ordinary real
dot product: in any addition tree, each product encounters at most
$d-1$ additions; fused multiplication and addition requires no larger
error allowance.  No reduced-precision multiplication is used.
The implementation uses NumPy binary64 matrix products and checks
the binary64 machine precision.  As with the inherited padded
floating certificates, ordinary correctly rounded IEEE binary64
arithmetic is an explicit computational assumption.

Here is a direct bound on the sums entering this estimate.  After
the first stage, for a fixed first angle, the sum of absolute real
and imaginary integer coordinates over the two remaining frequency
indices is at most
\[
 2M+2d^2.
\]
After the second stage, for fixed first and second angles, the
corresponding sum over the remaining frequency index is at most
\[
 4M+4d^2+2d.
\]
Indeed each phase multiplication increases the coordinate
$\ell^1$ sum by at most a factor of two.  Each rounded output
contributes less than two to the real-plus-imaginary error, as
verified just below.  Induction yields the two displayed bounds.
Every scaled absolute product sum at every stage is therefore
strictly below $16U$, including the sum of the two real dot products
used for a complex coordinate.  These bounds also prove the claimed
$2^{37}$ bound for intermediate rounded integers.  All products and
sums remain far below binary64 overflow, and the nonzero operands
are integers before division by $R$, so underflow cannot occur.

The exact guard implies the uniform rational inequality
\[
 \eta<\frac{64}{2^{53}-64}\frac{16\,2^{63}}{20\cdot10^8}
 <\frac1{1000}.
\]
At each stage the code divides the binary64 matrix result by $R$
and applies nearest-integer rounding.  Each resulting real coordinate
therefore differs from the exact contraction, divided by $R$, by at
most $1/2+\eta$.  The complex error is strictly below
\[
 \sqrt2(1/2+\eta)<1.
\]
After restoring scale $G$, this is precisely the $1/G$ allowance
used in the proof of the original tensor-contraction pad.  The same
reasoning applies stage by stage, which supplies the induction used
for the intermediate sums.  The code also checks both rational
inequalities $\eta<1/1000$ and $2(1/2+\eta)^2<1$ at every mass vertex.
The allowance $4d^2/G$ for propagation of these stage errors and the
phase-data pad $4M/(GR)$ consequently remain valid without change.

Before conversion of the final rounded integer-valued binary64
arrays to signed integers, the verifier checks finiteness and the
coordinate bound $2^{30}$.  This conversion is exact.  The final
squared norm, its upward integer square root, all coefficient pads,
the angular interpolation division, the mass interpolation remainder
and the comparison with $2943/4000$ are then evaluated exactly as in
the preceding verifier.  A full exit-zero \texttt{PASS}, with the
matching source and parameters, is still required for any finite-band
claim.  Timing measurements or agreement at a few vertices provide
no such continuum claim.

\subsection{A Hardy-space mass remainder and exact integer polynomial arithmetic}
\label{F:sec:finite-hardy-mass}

The optional implementation \texttt{four\_\allowbreak atoms\_\allowbreak contracted\_\allowbreak fast.py}
combines two independent improvements.  The first is a stronger
mathematical mass-interpolation bound.  The second evaluates the
same polynomial enclosures with unbounded integer arithmetic instead
of repeated fraction arithmetic.  All angular bounds, the binary64
tensor error allowance, the domain contractor and the completion
requirements remain as proved above.

\begin{lemma}[A whole-coefficient Hardy mass remainder]
\label{F:lem:finite-hardy-mass}
For a product of $N\ge1$ positive atomic factors, let
$X=\prod_{i=1}^N[a_i,b_i]$ be a nonnegative mass box, let
$h_i=(b_i-a_i)/2$, and let the integers $E_{i,k}$ satisfy
\[
 \frac{E_{i,k}}G\ge\frac{h_i^2}{2}
      \sup_{x\in[a_i,b_i]}|b_k''(x)|,\qquad0\le k\le n.
\]
For every choice of the $N$ support angles, the error between
$A_n(\boldsymbol\lambda)=[z^n]f(z)$ and its multilinear
interpolant on the vertices of $X$ is at most
\[
 \mathcal E_H=\frac1G\sum_{i=1}^N
                   \left(\sum_{k=0}^n E_{i,k}^2\right)^{1/2}.
\]
The square roots may be rounded upward to integers before dividing
by $G$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fix $i$ and write the product of the other $N-1$ atomic factors as
$G_i(z)=\sum_{r\ge0}c_rz^r$.  Those masses are nonnegative, so
$|G_i(z)|\le1$ in the disk, and Parseval gives
$\sum_{r=0}^n|c_r|^2\le1$.  Differentiating the target coefficient
twice in the $i$th mass gives the finite convolution
\[
 \partial_i^2 A_n
    =\sum_{k=0}^n b_k''(\lambda_i)\alpha_i^k c_{n-k}.
\]
Cauchy--Schwarz therefore yields
\[
 |\partial_i^2 A_n|
 \le\left(\sum_{k=0}^n|b_k''(\lambda_i)|^2\right)^{1/2}.
\]
Only this finite coefficient prefix is used; no assertion that
the full second mass derivative belongs to $H^2$ is needed.

Let $L_i$ be linear interpolation in the $i$th mass coordinate,
acting on the entire target function $A_n$.  Its interpolation
remainder is bounded by $h_i^2\sup_X|\partial_i^2A_n|/2$.
Combining the last bound with the hypotheses gives
\[
 \|(I-L_i)A_n\|_{\infty,X}
     \le G^{-1}\left(\sum_{k=0}^nE_{i,k}^2\right)^{1/2}.
\]
Each $L_i$ is a positive weighted average of two endpoint values
and hence a contraction for the supremum norm.  The operator
identity
\[
 I-\prod_{i=1}^N L_i
 =\sum_{i=1}^N\left(\prod_{j<i}L_j\right)(I-L_i)
\]
proves the asserted sum of $N$ remainders.  The multilinear
interpolant is a convex combination of the $2^N$ vertex values,
so the same certified angular vertex bounds can be used.
\end{proof}

The present four-factor implementation computes each upward integer square root by
$r=\lfloor\sqrt S\rfloor$ and adds one if $r^2<S$, where
$S=\sum_kE_{i,k}^2$ is an unbounded integer.  Thus no floating
square root is used.  Both this new remainder and the original
four-factor remainder are valid on the whole box; their minimum
is a valid and never worse bound.  In the original remainder,
one may also cap every integer $V_{i,k}$ by $G$, since the
one-atom Schur function has $|b_k(x)|\le1$ for $x\ge0$.
The same bound holds for its linear interpolant, so this cap
preserves the original telescoping proof.

\paragraph{Exact integer evaluation of the polynomial enclosures.}
Let $F=n!$, and write a coefficient polynomial as
$C(x)=F^{-1}\sum_{r=0}^{m}A_rx^r$, where $m\le n$ and all
$A_r$ are integers.  This representation exists for every $C_k$
because each coefficient denominator divides $n!$.  It also
represents $C-2C'+C''$, with integer coefficients
\[
 A_r-2(r+1)A_{r+1}+(r+2)(r+1)A_{r+2},
\]
where out-of-range coefficients are zero.

For the mass interval let $y=(a+b)/2=Y/q$ and
$h=(b-a)/2=H/q$, choosing $q$ to be a common positive
denominator.  Then
\[
 Fq^m C(y+hu)=\sum_{r=0}^{m}A_rq^{m-r}(Y+Hu)^r.
\]
This polynomial is evaluated by an integer affine Horner
recurrence: start from the constant polynomial $A_m$ and,
for $r=m-1,\ldots,0$, multiply the current polynomial by
$Y+Hu$ and add $A_rq^{m-r}$.  All operations are exact
unbounded integer additions and multiplications.  If the final
integer coefficients are $v_i$, then
\[
 \mathcal S(C;y,h)=\frac{\sum_i|v_i|}{Fq^m}.
\]
This is exactly the earlier shifted-polynomial bound, not a
different approximation.  The same recurrence for $C-2C'+C''$
gives its identical enclosure.

Write $1/E_{40}(a)=p_e/q_e$ as an exact fraction.  If $s$ and
$s_2$ are the two integer coefficient-norm numerators just
described, the output bounds are
\[
 V=\min\left\{G,\left\lceil\frac{Gp_es}{q_eFq^m}\right\rceil\right\},
 \qquad
 E=\left\lceil\frac{Gp_eH^2s_2}{2q_eFq^{m+2}}\right\rceil.
\]
The exponential bound is evaluated once per interval.  This
hoisting changes no value.  Point evaluation of $C(y)$ uses
the same integer recurrence with $H=0$; the resulting exact
fraction is passed to the unchanged midpoint exponential
enclosure and exact single-atom rounding test.

The new arithmetic therefore returns precisely the previous
$E$ integers, the previous $V$ integers capped by the proved
unit coefficient bound, and precisely the previous rounded
single-atom coefficient vectors.  Its improvement in the
accepted mass cover comes from Lemma~\ref{F:lem:finite-hardy-mass},
while the integer arithmetic changes the time needed to
evaluate those rigorous bounds.  Only a complete matching
finite run establishes a particular closed mass-band theorem.

\section{The four-support completion ledger}\label{col:F:16}
\label{F:sec:four-support-ledger}

This ledger distinguishes three logically different operations:
an inherited theorem, a newly completed computation, and the joining
of closed parameter intervals.  A source file prepared for a run is not
a theorem.  In the new finite rows, completion requires a matching
source hash and exact command, a terminal \texttt{PASS}, and a recorded
zero process exit code.  An interrupted attempt is retained as
provenance but contributes no certified interval.  All conclusions in
this section concern the deficient stationary stratum $N=4$; they do
not exclude candidates with five or more atoms.

Let $\mathcal C$ be the set of degrees in $\{11,\ldots,26\}$ for which
the completed finite rows, together with the upper and phase intervals
listed below, cover $[n/4,n]$.  This definition involves completed
certificates rather than proposed runs.  The current evaluated ledger
is as follows.

The newly completed whole four-support degrees are $11,\allowbreak 12,\allowbreak 13,\allowbreak 14,\allowbreak 15,\allowbreak 16,\allowbreak 17,\allowbreak 18,\allowbreak 19,\allowbreak 20,\allowbreak 21,\allowbreak 22,\allowbreak 23,\allowbreak 24,\allowbreak 25,\allowbreak 26$. All formerly remaining four-support degrees have now been joined; the larger-support residual remains open.


\begin{theorem}[Four-support join]
\label{F:thm:four-support-join}
Assume the stationary reduction and the inherited results identified
in this section.  No competitive deficient stationary candidate with
exactly four distinct support atoms exists at any degree
\[
 n\in\{5,6,7,8,9,10\}\ \cup\ \mathcal C\ \cup\ \{27,28,29,\ldots\}.
\]
In particular, $\mathcal C=\{11,\ldots,26\}$ would close the entire
deficient four-support stratum for every degree.  This assertion alone
would not close the unrestricted Krzy\.{z} residual.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
There is no deficient $N=4$ stratum when $n\le4$.  For $n=5,6,7$,
the new direct four-support base certificates proved below cover
$[n/4,n]$, and Theorem~\ref{F:thm:uniform-n-tail} covers $t\ge n$.
Thus no small-degree equality classification is an input to this
four-support join.  The support count here is
the number of distinct atoms of the positive Herglotz measure, whose
representation is unique after fixing the imaginary constant.

At $n=8$ only the direct at-most-four-atom component of the earlier
manuscript is used; its provenance and mechanism are specified below.
At $n=9$, the inherited Keio focused Round~9 covers the two closed
mass intervals $[9/4,9/2]$ and $[9/2,9]$.  At $n=10$, the inherited
Keio focused Round~10 covers $[5/2,11/2]$ and $[11/2,10]$.
The first interval at each degree uses the four-atom interpolation
certificate; the second uses a support-free Fourier coefficient
certificate.  These are identified inherited results, not new runs
of the present continuation.

For $11\le n\le25$, a competitive four-support candidate has
$\lambda_j\ge1/n$ and $n/4\le t<n$.  Every completed finite row
bounds its entire displayed band strictly below $2/e$.  A row
starting at $n/4$ covers the lower range directly.  At the eight
degrees below, Theorem~\ref{F:thm:four-atom-prefixes} instead supplies
a separate closed analytic prefix:
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrr}
n&18&19&20&21&22&23&24&25\\\hline
A_n&23/5&5&11/2&61/10&33/5&36/5&79/10&17/2
\end{array}
\]
At such a degree, a completed finite band $[A_n,T]$ joins the
prefix $[n/4,A_n]$.  The prefix does not turn an incomplete
finite run into a completed certificate; both pieces are required.
The upper witnesses cover the following closed ranges, either by
the original upper-mass certificate or by the downward transfer
proved in the upper-mass section:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{target degree }n&\text{upper interval}&\text{witness degree}\\\hline
11,12,13,14,15 &[567/100,n]&15\\
16,17 &[189329/30000,n]&17\\
18 &[174/25,18]&18\\
19 &[4579/600,19]&19\\
20 &[25/3,20]&20\\
21 &[903/100,21]&21\\
22,23,24,25 &[39/4,n]&26
\end{array}
\]
The lower rows at $n=11,12,13,14$ were run to
$25/4,6,7,27/4$, respectively; their overlap with the transferred
upper interval is harmless.  Thus the degree-$15$ witness also
supplies the upper ranges at $n=11,12$, without needing their
separate canonical upper witnesses in the minimal replay.
No upper certificate in this table assumes three-atom support.

At $n=26$, four separately justified closed intervals are needed:
\[
 [13/2,46/5],\quad [46/5,93/10],\quad
 [93/10,39/4],\quad[39/4,26].
\]
They are, respectively, the inherited Taisho Round~10 phase
certificate, the new exact phase strip, a completed finite band
if present in the ledger, and the reproduced degree-$26$ Laurent
witness.  The third interval is not inferred from the first two
and is not counted until its finite run completes.  Once it is
completed, every shared endpoint belongs to both adjacent closed
certificates, so no boundary mass is omitted.

At $n=27,28$, the inherited Taisho Round~10 low phase intervals end
at $499/50$ and $54/5$, respectively.  The reproduced Laurent
certificates begin at exactly these endpoints and extend through
$n$.  At every $n\ge29$, the inherited Meiji Round~10 four-support
phase theorem covers all masses $t\ge n/4$ and all support angles.
Its $201$ closed mass-ratio certificates at degree $29$ include
the ray beginning at ratio $2$; its analytic monotonicity in $n$
extends the bound to all larger degrees.  This is an infinite
degree argument, not extrapolation from finitely many degrees.
The closed joins just described prove the assertion.
\end{proof}

For each $n\in\{5,6,7\}$, every four-factor function with

$|a_n|<2/e$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
On the closed mass band $n/4\le t\le n$, the following completed

\subsection{The inherited eighth-degree four-atom component}

For clarity, the degree-eight input used here has a smaller scope
than the earlier manuscript's overall claim.  It states
\[
 N\le4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad |[z^8]f|<2/e
\]
for every positive atomic measure with at most four atoms.  No
stationarity is needed for this particular statement.  Zero masses
may be appended to reach four factors, and repeated phases are
allowed by the coefficient estimate.

On $0\le t\le13/4$ its one-atom coefficients are the same
$b_k(x)=e^{-x}C_k(x)$ as in the finite-certificate section, with
$0\le k\le8$.  There are $\binom{11}{3}=165$ four-factor terms.
The original root box is $[0,13/4]^4$, the angular grid is $48^3$,
and the continuous angular multiplier is
\[
 \left[1-8\left(\frac{22/7}{48}\right)^2\right]^{-3}.
\]
The mass interpolation proof and closed sorted-box coverage are
exactly the argument given for the later four-atom rows.  This
inherited implementation uses padded IEEE binary64 tensor
arithmetic for its angular values, followed by outward integer
norm evaluation and exact rational acceptance.  It must not be
described as an integer-only angular computation.

More explicitly, the scaled polynomial coefficients are integers
of magnitude below $2^{52}$, hence represented exactly in binary64.
Roots are rounded first to rational coordinates of denominator
$10^{10}$; their complex error after binary64 conversion is below
$2\cdot10^{-10}$.  Each tensor contraction has at most nine terms.
The arithmetic audit bounds the three phase approximations and
all three contraction errors by $10^{-8}$ times the coefficient
$\ell^1$ norm.  That pad is added explicitly, together with the
one-atom and product rounding pads.  The final absolute real and
imaginary coordinates are rounded upward to integers, their
squared sum is evaluated within checked integer bounds, and an
integer square root is rounded upward.  The remaining angular
division, interpolation remainder, and target comparison use
exact fractions.  Thus the displayed diagnostic maximum is not
used as a proof threshold.

The pinned prior completed replay has $15\,998$ visited boxes,
$6\,335$ accepted boxes and $7\,832$ vertex grids.  Its log ends
in \texttt{PASS}, and its separate prior process record has exit
code zero.  The accepted threshold is $2943/4000<2/e$.  These
records are inherited; copying and inspecting them in the present
continuation is not represented as a new run.

For the complementary mass range a support-free moment transfer
is available.  Let $H(0)=1$, $\Re H>0$ and $B=(H-1)/(H+1)$.
Define the real polynomials
\[
 m_j(t)=\frac{t}{j+1}L_j^{(1)}(2t),\qquad0\le j\le7.
\]
The Laguerre generating function gives, through degree eight,
\[
 e^{-t(1+w)/(1-w)}
 =e^{-t}\left(1-2\sum_{j=0}^7m_j(t)w^{j+1}\right)+O(w^9).
\]
If a finite complex measure $\nu$ on the unit circle has moments
$\int\alpha^j\,d\nu=m_j(t)$ for $0\le j\le7$, composition with
$B$ therefore gives
\[
 |[z^8]e^{-tH(z)}|\le2e^{-t}\|\nu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}.
\]
Indeed $B/(1-\alpha B)$ has every positive-degree coefficient
bounded by one, since $(1+\alpha B)/(1-\alpha B)$ has positive
real part and constant coefficient one.  This proves the transfer
without any restriction on the support of $H$.

For rational unit numbers $\alpha,\beta$, the real column
$(\Re(\beta\alpha^j))_{j=0}^7$ is the moment vector of
$(\beta\delta_\alpha+\overline\beta\delta_{\overline\alpha})/2$,
which has total variation at most one.  Eight independent such
columns form a rational matrix $V$.  The polynomial coordinates
$c(t)=V^{-1}(m_0(t),\ldots,m_7(t))^T$ consequently give a measure
with variation at most $\sum_i|c_i(t)|$.  On each of $207$
consecutive closed intervals covering $[13/4,81/5]$, the supplied
exact certificate expands these coordinates and $E_{18}(t-1)$ in
the degree-$18$ Bernstein basis and checks
\[
 (E_{18})_r>\sum_i|c_{i,r}|\quad(0\le r\le18).
\]
Positivity and partition of unity of that basis imply
$\|\nu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}<E_{18}(t-1)<e^{t-1}$ throughout each
interval.  The matrix bases and endpoints are embedded in the
pinned verifier, with a checked data hash.

For $t\ge16$, the density
$\sum_{j=0}^7m_j(t)\alpha^{-j}$ gives the same moments and has
variation at most $(\sum_jm_j(t)^2)^{1/2}$.  Exact polynomial
root counting verifies
\[
 E_{18}(t-1)^2-\sum_{j=0}^7m_j(t)^2>0\qquad(t\ge16).
\]
The overlap $[16,81/5]$ joins this infinite tail to the finite
interval certificate.  Together they cover every $t\ge13/4$.
Combining this with the four-atom lower range proves precisely
the inherited eighth-degree component used in the ledger.

\subsection{Identity and completion safeguards}

The reproduction files contain byte-identical copies of the
inherited eighth-degree low and high verifiers, their prior logs
and low-run status record, as well as the specific focused
Round~9 and Round~10 sources used in the joins.  Their hashes are
recorded in \texttt{inherited\_\allowbreak source\_\allowbreak manifest.json}.
The separate \texttt{certified\_\allowbreak prefix\_\allowbreak manifest.json} pins the
exact phase-prefix checker, its rational parameter file and its
completed $1680$-cell verification report.  The script
\texttt{build\_\allowbreak completion\_\allowbreak ledger.py} checks these identities,
inspects the new finite-run manifest, and joins the
closed intervals using exact rational endpoints.  It cannot
replace the proofs above; its purpose is to prevent an incomplete
or differently parameterized run from being counted accidentally.

The full four-support conclusion is therefore available only if
every degree in $11,\ldots,26$ actually appears in the completed
joined set.  Irrespective of that set, the unrestricted task still
requires exclusions for every remaining larger support count and
for all compatible moments, masses and auxiliary roots.

\section{The retained all-degree four-support completion}\label{col:F:17}
The completed lower-band indices retained from the preceding version are $11,\allowbreak 12,\allowbreak 13,\allowbreak 14,\allowbreak 15,\allowbreak 16,\allowbreak 17,\allowbreak 18,\allowbreak 19,\allowbreak 20,\allowbreak 21,\allowbreak 22,\allowbreak 23,\allowbreak 24,\allowbreak 25,\allowbreak 26$. Each is admitted only after a final PASS, a zero process exit, and matching verifier-source identity. A row beginning above $n/4$ is joined to the separately proved phase prefix; at index 26 it begins at $93/10$ and uses the inherited lower band and the new phase strip.

\begin{theorem}[Four support atoms in every deficient degree]
\label{F:thm:all-four-support}
Combining the completed rows with the inherited base cases and the
attached $n\ge27$ ray, no competitive stationary Krzy\.{z} extremizer
has exactly four atoms in any degree $n>4$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The new direct base certificates in Section~\ref{F:sec:small-four-bases}
exclude a four-atom extremizer at degrees five through seven.
The separately pinned four-atom eighth-degree certificate supplies
$n=8$.  The supplied focused rounds give $n=9,10$.
The completed table, together with the eight analytic phase prefixes,
supplies the lower mass portions for every $11\le n\le25$.
Their support-free upper certificates overlap those portions.
At degree $26$ the earlier low band, the new
phase strip through $93/10$, the completed middle band through
$39/4$ and the inherited high band cover every admissible mass.
Finally the attached Taisho and Meiji certificates give every
$n\ge27$.  These ranges cover every integer $n>4$.
\end{proof}
This is a complete support-size stratum, not a complete coefficient
index with arbitrary support size or the all-degree original conjecture.

\section{Notation for the revised exclusions}\label{col:F:18}
\label{F:sec:r6-notation}
The new arguments use three different root systems. Their roles are
kept separate throughout the revision.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{cp{105mm}}
\toprule
Objects&Meaning\\\midrule
$\zeta_j,\alpha_j$&Physical poles and their conjugate moment directions,
$\alpha_j=\overline{\zeta_j}$, on the unit circle.\\
$w_\ell,\sigma_\ell$&Interior auxiliary roots of the stationary reciprocal
polynomial and, where specified, their conjugate moment representatives.
There are $n-N$ of them with multiplicity.\\
$\beta_j$&Zeros of the Cayley map $B=(H-t)/(H+t)$, a Blaschke product
of degree $N$. One zero is at the origin; these are not the auxiliary
spectral roots.\\
$J,\varphi$&The calibrated map $J(z)=ze^{H(z)/n}$ and its inverse on
the sublevel $|J|<1$, introduced in Section~\ref{F:sec:r6calibrated}.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Every section explicitly declares any local polynomial notation. In
particular the coefficient polynomial called $B$ in the calibrated
Volterra construction is not the Cayley map used in the coefficient
transfer sections.

\section{Ground-state compression and a uniform mass hierarchy}\label{col:F:19}\label{F:sec:r6groundstate}
The analytic compression in this section is credited to the supplied Taisho R11. Its proof is reproduced so that the new mass exclusions do not depend on an external manuscript.
\subsection{Stationary input and a nonlocal comparison}
The Krzy\.{z} conjecture asks whether $|[z^n]f|\le2/e$
for each holomorphic zero-free disk function bounded by one.
Use the stationary reduction proved earlier in this paper.
A stationary maximizer has $f=e^{-H}$ after normalization,
\[
 H(z)=\sum_{j=1}^N\lambda_j\frac{\zeta_j+z}{\zeta_j-z},
 \qquad \lambda_j>0,\quad |\zeta_j|=1,\quad t=H(0).
\]
Distinct $\zeta_j$ are its $N$ support points, $1\le N\le n$.
There is a nonnegative trigonometric polynomial $h=|Q|^2$
with precisely double zeros at these points and no other
circle zeros, satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{F:r6gs:e}
 (D+\Phi)h=nh,\qquad
 D e^{ik\theta}=|k|e^{ik\theta},\qquad
 \Phi(z)=\sum_j\frac{2\lambda_j}{|z-\zeta_j|^2}\quad(z\in\mathbb T).
\end{equation}
The identity holds off the points and extends after multiplication
by $h$. Only this stationary input is used below, not the
competitive lower bound on the coefficient.

Let $dm$ denote normalized arclength. The quadratic form
of $D$ on smooth functions is
\[
 \langle p,Dp\rangle
  =\iint_{\mathbb T^2}\frac{|p(z)-p(w)|^2}{|z-w|^2}\,dm(z)dm(w).
\]
Indeed the equality is diagonal on the Fourier basis by
rotation; the integral of
$|(z^k-w^k)/(z-w)|^2$ is $|k|$ on that basis.
Polarization gives the bilinear version.

\begin{proposition}[Ground-state comparison with pole domain]\label{F:r6gs:ground}
For any smooth real trial $p$ with $p/h$ smooth across the
support, one has
\[
 \langle p,Dp\rangle+\int \Phi p^2\,dm-n\|p\|_2^2
 =\iint h(z)h(w)
 \frac{(p(z)/h(z)-p(w)/h(w))^2}{|z-w|^2}\,dm(z)dm(w)\ge0.
\]
Equality holds exactly when $p$ is a constant multiple of $h$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Writing $p=hq$, subtract from the double integral for
$\langle p,Dp\rangle$ the polarized integral for
$\langle D h,hq^2\rangle$. The algebra at each pair is
$(h_zq_z-h_wq_w)^2-
(h_z-h_w)(h_zq_z^2-h_wq_w^2)=h_zh_w(q_z-q_w)^2$.
The subtracted term equals $\int(n-\Phi)p^2$ by
\eqref{F:r6gs:e}. At the poles $p=O(|z-\zeta_j|^2)$ and all
integrals are finite. The smooth functions remove the
diagonal singularity; a zero set of finitely many support
points does not affect the equality argument. The kernel
is strictly positive off the diagonal and the support.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Exact one-variable compression}
The function $B=(H-t)/(H+t)$ is a finite Blaschke product
of degree $N$ and $B(0)=0$. Indeed it is rational inner,
its poles in the displayed representation of $H$ are
removable for $B$ with value $1$, and these give $N$
distinct preimages of $1$; its numerator and denominator
degrees are at most $N$. Each preimage of $1$ is simple,
also directly from the simple poles of $H$.
Put $\rho(z)=|B'(z)|$ on the circle; it is strictly positive.
The derivative of the increasing boundary argument of
$B$ is $\rho$. Equivalently on each support gap the phase
$-\operatorname{Im}H$ traverses $\mathbb R$ once, and
\[
 \Phi(z)=\rho(z)\frac{2t}{|1-B(z)|^2}
        =\rho(z)\frac{t}{U(B(z))},
 \qquad U(w)=1-\Re w\quad(w\in\mathbb T).
\]
This is the boundary chain rule applied to
$H=t(1+B)/(1-B)$. Unweighted $dm$ is preserved under
pushforward by $B$, since each nonzero Fourier moment
is zero by mean value, $B(0)=0$ and conjugation.
Meanwhile $\rho\,dm$ pushes forward to $N\,dm$
by winding with multiplicity $N$.

For a real trigonometric polynomial $v(w)$ divisible
by $U(w)$ in the real trigonometric algebra, $p=v\circ B$
is smooth and $p/h$ extends smoothly at the support:
both vanish to order at least two and $h$ has an exact
double zero. The harmonic extension of $v\circ B$
is the harmonic extension of $v$ composed with $B$.
Applying the circle normal derivative and using
$zB'(z)=\rho(z)B(z)$ gives the pointwise covariance
$D(v\circ B)=\rho (Dv)\circ B$.
It follows from Proposition~\ref{F:r6gs:ground} that
\begin{equation}\label{F:r6gs:compression}
 \langle v,Dv\rangle+t\int \frac{v^2}{U}\,dm
       \ge x\int v^2\,dm,\qquad x=n/N.
\end{equation}
The two exact pushforwards are crucial: the energy and
potential integrate with factor $N$, but the norm does not.

\subsection{Explicit mass bounds and equality cases}
\begin{theorem}\label{F:r6gs:main}
For every stationary candidate with $x=n/N\ge1$,
\[
 t\ge \frac{5x+\sqrt{5x^2-4x+8}}4-1.
\]
For $x>1$ this is strictly stronger than
$(3x-1)/2$. Equality in the displayed radical bound
forces $B(z)=\eta z^N$ and $x\in\{1,2\}$.
At $x=1$ it gives the canonical $t=1$ endpoint.
At $x=2$ it gives $t=(3+\sqrt5)/2$ and can occur at
subcompetitive stationary candidates.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use \eqref{F:r6gs:compression} on $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}
\{U,U^2\}$. The resulting positive semidefinite matrix is
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}
 t+(1-3x)/2 & (3t-5x+2)/2\\
 (3t-5x+2)/2 & (20t-35x+18)/8
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The first entry gives $t\ge t_0=(3x-1)/2$. Sixteen
times its determinant is
$4t^2-10tx+8t+5x^2-9x+2$.
At $t=t_0$ this is $-(x-1)^2$.
For $x>1$ the only admissible range is therefore above
or at the larger root, which is the stated bound and
is greater than $t_0$. At $x=1$ the larger root is 1,
which the first entry gives.

In an equality case the compression has a nonzero real
null vector $v$, and $v\circ B$ is proportional to $h$.
Scale its sign so $v>0$ off $1$. Put
$A_t v=Dv+(t/U)v$, which is a trigonometric polynomial.
The pointwise stationarity and covariance imply
$\rho(z)(A_tv)(B(z))=n v(B(z))$. Since $v(w)>0$
for $w\ne1$, all $\rho$ values in the fiber at $w$ are
equal. Preservation of $dm$ gives the pointwise Clark
identity $\sum_{B(z)=w}1/\rho(z)=1$ by the boundary
change of variable and continuity. Hence $\rho\equiv N$,
so $B(z)=\eta z^N$ by its constant boundary argument
derivative. Now $A_t v=xv$. Since $v/U$ has smaller
degree than $v$, the highest Fourier coefficient forces
$x=\deg v\in\{1,2\}$. The corresponding masses follow
from the bound. With $B=\eta z^N$ one has
$H=t(1+\eta z^N)/(1-\eta z^N)$, so $x=1,t=1$
is the standard extremal.
The harmonic stationary example at $n=2N$ realizes the second equality:
at $N=1$ its normalized $h$ is proportional to
$(1-\cos\theta)(t-1-\cos\theta)$ with
$t=(3+\sqrt5)/2$, and composition by $z^N$ gives all $N$.
\end{proof}

More generally, for $i,j\ge1$ put
\[
 M_{ij}=2^{-(i+j)}\binom{2(i+j)}{i+j},\qquad
 V_{ij}=2^{-(i+j-1)}\binom{2(i+j-1)}{i+j-1},
\]
\[
 E_{ij}=2^{1-i-j}\sum_{k=1}^{\min(i,j)}
              k\binom{2i}{i+k}\binom{2j}{j+k}.
\]
At any finite truncation, $E+tV-xM$ is positive
semidefinite by \eqref{F:r6gs:compression} on the trials $U^i$.
These entries follow by binomial expansion of $U^i$;
the $k$th coefficient is
$2^{-i}(-1)^k\binom{2i}{i+k}$.
All new finite trial tests are rational when $t,x$ are rational.

\begin{corollary}[Uniform large ratio bound]
For every $m\ge1$,
\[
 t\ge \frac{4m-1}{2m}(x-\kappa_m),\qquad
 \kappa_m=\frac{m\binom{2m}{m}^2}{2\binom{4m}{2m}}.
\]
In particular $t>2x-(5/2)x^{1/3}$ for every $x\ge1$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use the $U^m$ trial to obtain
$x\le\kappa_m+2mt/(4m-1)$.
The formula for $\kappa_m$ follows by telescoping
\[
 (m+k)^2\binom{2m}{m+k}^2-
 (m+k+1)^2\binom{2m}{m+k+1}^2
 =4mk\binom{2m}{m+k}^2 .
\]
Alternatively $\kappa_m$ is the mean absolute value
of $X-m$, where $X$ counts marked objects in a uniform
draw of $2m$ out of $4m$ with $2m$ marked.
Indeed the relevant probabilities are the squared
binomial coefficients divided by $\binom{4m}{2m}$.
The mean is $m$ and variance is $m^2/(4m-1)$:
compute the first two factorial moments by counting
marked singleton and ordered distinct pair inclusions.
So $\kappa_m\le m/\sqrt{4m-1}\le\sqrt{m/3}$.
Take $m=\lceil x^{2/3}\rceil\le2x^{2/3}$.
The two losses from $2x$ are at most
$x^{1/3}/2$ and $2\sqrt{2/3}\,x^{1/3}$, whose sum
is strictly below $(5/2)x^{1/3}$.
\end{proof}


\section{The inherited radial barrier and a new auxiliary-potential cut}\label{col:F:20}
\label{F:sec:r6radial}
The degree-uniform radial estimate of the supplied Taisho R02 is reproduced
here to make the defect-one mass floor in the residual ledger self-contained.
Its combination with the calibrated degree-nine inequality gives an
additional necessary potential bound.  Neither argument uses a symmetry
assumption on physical or auxiliary roots.

Let $w\ne0$ be an interior auxiliary root of the stationary reciprocal
polynomial $R$.  By flipping reciprocal factors and adjusting the constant,
choose a degree-$n$ Fej\'er--Riesz factor $Q$ with $Q(w)=0$ and
$h=|Q|^2$.  The stationary equation remains
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6radialstat}
 (n-D)h=\Phi h,\qquad
 \Phi(z)=2\sum_j\frac{\lambda_j}{|z-\zeta_j|^2},\qquad
 D(z^k)=|k|z^k.
\end{equation}
Here $\zeta_j$ are the physical circle poles.  No auxiliary root equals zero,
because $R(0)=a_0=e^{-t}>0$.  Thus the argument covers every interior
auxiliary root, including each occurrence of a repeated root.

\begin{lemma}[A necessary commutator Rayleigh equation]
\label{F:lem:r6radialcomm}
Rotate a selected root to $r=e^{-u}$ with $u>0$, and write
$P(z)=Q(z)/(z-r)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}b_jz^j$.  Then, with
$M_{ij}(u)=\sinh(u|i-j|)$ for $0\le i,j<n$,
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6radialrayleigh}
 b^*M(u)b=-\coth(u)\|b\|_2^2.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put $C(z)=(z+z^{-1})/2$, $q=(r+r^{-1})/2$, and let
$S(z)=\sum_{k=-(n-1)}^{n-1}s_kz^k$ be the Laurent extension of $|P|^2$.
Then $h=2r(q-C)S$.  Extend each squared denominator in
\eqref{F:eq:r6radialstat} as $(z-\zeta_j)(z^{-1}-\overline\zeta_j)$.
The resulting rational identity is valid away from the circle poles,
and $\Phi$ is holomorphic at $r$.  Since $h(r)=0$,
\[
 0=(n-D)((q-C)S)(r)=[D,C]S(r).
\]
Indeed
$(n-D)((q-C)S)=(q-C)(n-D)S+[D,C]S$.
Writing $S_\pm=\sum_{\pm k>0}s_kz^k$, the Fourier shifts give
\[
 [D,C]S=\tfrac12(z-z^{-1})(S_+-S_-)+s_0C.
\]
Take its real part at $r$, using $s_{-k}=\overline{s_k}$:
\[
 \sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(r^{-k}-r^k)\Re s_k=-\coth(u)s_0.
\]
Autocorrelation gives $s_0=\|b\|_2^2$ and identifies the left side
with $b^*M(u)b$.  The proof does not divide by an auxiliary factor
at its zero, so multiplicity causes no exception.
\end{proof}

Define $c_*\in(0,\pi)$ by
\[
 \tan(c_*/2)\tanh(c_*/2)=1.
\]
The product is continuous and strictly increasing from zero to infinity,
so this definition is unique.  It is equivalently the first positive
zero of $1+\cos c\cosh c$.

\begin{lemma}[Continuum positivity]
\label{F:lem:r6radialcontinuum}
On $L^2(0,1)$ let $K_c$ have kernel $\sinh(c|x-y|)$.  Then
$I+cK_c\succeq0$ for $0<c\le c_*$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
This is a norm-continuous family of compact self-adjoint perturbations
of $I$.  A loss of positivity starting at $c=0$ would require a nonzero
kernel vector at some first parameter.  Reflection about $1/2$ commutes
with the operator, so such a vector $f$ can be chosen even or odd.
If $g=K_cf=-f/c$, differentiation in the weak sense gives
$g''=c^2g+2cf$, the extra term coming from the derivative jump at $x=y$.
Thus $f''=-c^2f$, and $f$ is a classical sine or cosine.

In the odd case put
$J=\int_0^1\sinh(c(y-1/2))f(y)\,dy$.
The endpoint identities are
$g(0)=\cosh(c/2)J$ and $g'(0)=-c\sinh(c/2)J$.
For $f(x)=A\sin(c(x-1/2))$ they require
\[
 \cos(c/2)-\tanh(c/2)\sin(c/2)=0,
\]
which is impossible when $0<c<c_*$.
In the even case the corresponding endpoint factors are
$\sinh(c/2)$ and $-c\cosh(c/2)$.  Substituting
$f(x)=A\cos(c(x-1/2))$ requires
$\sin(c/2)+\coth(c/2)\cos(c/2)=0$, impossible for $0<c<\pi$.
Thus there is no first contact before $c_*$; norm continuity includes
the endpoint $c_*$ with positive semidefiniteness.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Every auxiliary root is separated on the $1/n$ radial scale]
\label{F:thm:r6radial}
Every interior auxiliary root $w$ of a stationary tuple obeys
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6radialbarrier}
 \boxed{n\log(1/|w|)>c_*>15/8.}
\end{equation}
Consequently $|w|^n<1/6$ and $1-|w|>15/(8n+15)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Suppose $c=nu\le c_*$.  Lift the vector in
Lemma~\ref{F:lem:r6radialcomm} to the step function equal to
$\sqrt n\,b_i$ on cell $[i/n,(i+1)/n)$.  Its squared norm is
$\|b\|_2^2$.  Exact cell integration gives
\[
 \langle f,K_cf\rangle
 =\frac1n\bigl(A(u)b^*M(u)b+B(u)\|b\|_2^2\bigr),
 \quad A(u)=\frac{2(\cosh u-1)}{u^2},\quad
 B(u)=\frac{2(\sinh u-u)}{u^2}.
\]
For distinct cells the average multiplies the midpoint value by
$(2\sinh(u/2)/u)^2=A(u)$; on one cell it is
$2\int_0^1(1-v)\sinh(uv)\,dv=B(u)$.
Continuum positivity therefore gives
\[
 b^*M(u)b\ge-\frac{1/u+B(u)}{A(u)}\|b\|_2^2
 >-\coth(u)\|b\|_2^2.
\]
The last strict comparison reduces to $u>2\tanh(u/2)$,
which follows from $\tanh x<x$ for $x>0$.  This contradicts
\eqref{F:eq:r6radialrayleigh}.

For the explicit rational constant put $x=15/16$.  The checker uses
alternating Taylor bounds of 10 cosine terms and 9 sine terms,
9 positive cosh terms, and 9 sinh terms with the geometric remainder
ratio $x^2/(18\cdot19)$.  They give exactly
$\cos x\cosh x>\sin x\sinh x$, hence $c_*>15/8$.
The positive exponential Taylor sum through degree four gives
$e^{15/8}>6$.  Finally
$1-e^{-u}>u/(1+u)>15/(8n+15)$.
All scalar comparisons are checked with rational arithmetic in
\path{revision2/spectral/radial/check.py}; the continuum argument supplies the
unbounded-degree scope.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The defect-one mass floor]
\label{F:cor:r6radialmass}
For every stationary tuple of defect $d=n-N=1$,
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6radialmass}
 \boxed{t>1+\frac7{3n}.}
\end{equation}
At $n=9,N=8$ this is precisely $t>34/27$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Put $\alpha_j=\overline\zeta_j$ and $\sigma=\overline w$.
The common-support top-moment identity proved in the stationary
reduction gives
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(n\lambda_j-1)\alpha_j^n
       =\tfrac12(\sigma^n+\overline\sigma^{-n}).
\]
The cardinal mass floor makes every coefficient $n\lambda_j-1$
nonnegative.  If $|\sigma|=e^{-u}$, the modulus of the right side
is $\cosh(nu)$, and consequently
\[
 nt-(n-1)\ge\cosh(nu)>\cosh(15/8)>10/3.
\]
The final strict inequality follows from the positive cosh Taylor
sum through degree eight, checked exactly in the same verifier.
Rearranging proves \eqref{F:eq:r6radialmass}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A new potential exclusion at every degree-nine auxiliary root]
\label{F:cor:r6radialpotential}
At degree $n=9$, every interior auxiliary root $w$ of a stationary
tuple satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6radialpotential}
 \boxed{\Re H(w)>11/8.}
\end{equation}
In particular any configuration containing an auxiliary root with
$\Re H(w)\le11/8$ is excluded, independently of the other roots.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Corollary~\ref{F:cor:r6ninecalibrated} gives
$9\log(1/|w|)-\Re H(w)<1/2$, whereas
\eqref{F:eq:r6radialbarrier} gives $9\log(1/|w|)>15/8$.
Subtracting yields \eqref{F:eq:r6radialpotential}.  The calibrated
inequality holds even when the adjusted depth is nonpositive,
so no additional sign assumption is needed.
\end{proof}

The radial theorem and the defect-one mass floor are inherited results
whose proofs are now internal to this paper.  The potential inequality
is a new consequence of their combination with the stronger calibrated
test.  These are individual-root and mass exclusions, not a proof that
every remaining stationary tuple violates one of them.

\section{Exact stronger lower mass cutoffs at degree nine}\label{col:F:21}
\label{F:sec:r6ninemass}
The finite matrices of Section~\ref{F:sec:r6groundstate} give exact rational
improvements without evaluating the infinite-dimensional spectral curve.
For $r=5$, write $A_x(t)=E+tV-xM$ on the basis $U,U^2,\ldots,U^5$.
Every stationary tuple must have $A_x(t)\succeq0$ at $x=n/N$.

\begin{theorem}[Three strictly improved degree-nine mass floors]
\label{F:thm:r6ninemass}
At degree $n=9$, every stationary tuple in the indicated support stratum
satisfies
\[
 \begin{array}{c|c|c}
 N&\text{previous general floor}&\text{new strict floor}\\\hline
 5&9/5&t>228091/100000\\
 6&3/2&t>178547/100000\\
 7&9/7&t>14413/10000.
 \end{array}
\]
The inherited defect-one inequality $t>34/27$ remains the stronger
available lower bound at $N=8$; no improvement of it is claimed here.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For each of the following rows, let $v=10^{-9}(q_1,\ldots,q_5)$ and let
$T$ be the asserted rational floor.  Use the trial
$\sum_{i=1}^5v_i U^i$:
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrr}
N&q_1&q_2&q_3&q_4&q_5\\\hline
5&675759415&1000000000&-152772708&43322929&-5895595\\
6&-908996083&-1000000000&364092983&-118979752&17096440\\
7&1000000000&728479929&-396769961&152183823&-24258803
\end{array}
\]
The exact verifier evaluates $v^{\mathsf T}A_{9/N}(T)v$ as a negative
rational number and $v^{\mathsf T}Vv$ as a positive rational number.
Consequently
\[
 v^{\mathsf T}A_{9/N}(t)v
 =v^{\mathsf T}A_{9/N}(T)v+(t-T)v^{\mathsf T}Vv<0
 \quad(t\le T),
\]
contrary to the ground-state comparison.  Thus the whole closed lower
mass region is excluded, including the stated endpoint.
The companion \texttt{verify\_\allowbreak mass\_\allowbreak witnesses.py} independently reconstructs
all 75 entries $E_{ij},M_{ij},V_{ij}$ from Fourier coefficients of $U^i$
and verifies all three signs using rational arithmetic.
The integer vectors printed here are the proof witnesses; their
numerical discovery method is not used for acceptance.
\end{proof}

These exclusions are uniform over all support angles and all admissible
auxiliary-root data in the specified support strata.  They remove mass
subintervals and do not, by themselves, eliminate any entire one of the
four remaining strata $N=5,6,7,8$.

\section{A support-free ninth-coefficient mass cutoff}\label{col:F:22}
\label{F:sec:r6-nine-mass}

The sparse evaluation idea of Taisho's focused Round~13 can be
applied to the entire ninth composition row, rather than only its
first five entries.  The following certificate is new to this
revision.  Its assumptions do not include stationarity, a support
bound, or an initial coefficient gap.

\begin{theorem}[All ninth-degree masses above $13/4$]
\label{F:thm:r6-nine-high}
Let $f$ be holomorphic and zero-free in the disk, with $|f|\le1$.
If $t=-\log|f(0)|\ge13/4$, then
\[
 |[z^9]f|\le \frac{941469}{1280000}
       =0.73552265625 < \frac2e.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
After multiplication by a unit constant write $f=e^{-H}$,
$H(0)=t$ and $\Re H\ge0$.  Set $B=(H-t)/(H+t)$, so $B(0)=0$,
$|B|\le1$, and $f=F_t\circ B$, where
\[
 F_t(w)=\exp\!\left(-t\frac{1+w}{1-w}\right)
       =\sum_{k\ge0}b_k(t)w^k.
\]
For $p_k=[z^9]B^k$ put $p(w)=\sum_{k=1}^9p_kw^k$.
The positive-real-part function $(1+wB)/(1-wB)$ has constant
term one and ninth coefficient $2p(w)$.  Taking the ninth Fourier
coefficient of its positive real part proves $|p(w)|\le1$ for
$|w|<1$.  Continuity and Schwarz's lemma imply that
$q(w)=p(w)/w$ is a Schur polynomial of degree at most eight.
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6-nine-row}
 [z^9]f=\sum_{j=0}^{8}b_{j+1}(t)[w^j]q.
\end{equation}

Put $C_k(t)=e^t b_k(t)$.  The recurrence
\[
 C_0=1,\quad C_1=-2t,\quad
 (k+1)C_{k+1}=2(k-t)C_k-(k-1)C_{k-1}
\]
computes these rational polynomials.  To bound the modulus of
\eqref{F:eq:r6-nine-row}, first rotate $q$ by a constant so the
row value is nonnegative real, and then replace it by
$(q(w)+\overline{q(\bar w)})/2$.  This preserves that row value,
preserves the Schur bound, and makes its coefficients
$a_0,\ldots,a_8$ real.  They obey $|a_j|\le1$.

For any unit complex numbers $\zeta,\omega$,
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^8\Re(\omega\zeta^j)a_j
       =\Re(\omega q(\zeta))\le1.
\]
Thus any list of nonnegative rational weights $v_l$ gives
the exact evaluation bound
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6-nine-dual}
 \sum_{j=0}^8 C_{j+1}(t)a_j
 \le\sum_l v_l+
 \sum_{j=0}^8\left|C_{j+1}(t)
              -\sum_l v_l\Re(\omega_l\zeta_l^j)\right|.
\end{equation}
All unit points in the accompanying certificate use the rational
parametrization
\[
 u(p)=\frac{S^2-p^2+2ipS}{S^2+p^2},\qquad S=10^8,
\]
together with the exceptional point $-1$.  In particular their
unit modulus is an exact identity, not a trigonometric rounding
assumption.  At most nine weighted evaluations occur at a knot.

The embedded data \path{revision2/nine_mass/witness.json} give the
following complete grid.  The exact checker evaluates
\eqref{F:eq:r6-nine-dual} and divides by
$E_{40}(t)=\sum_{r=0}^{40}t^r/r!<e^t$.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{cccc}
\toprule
Mass interval & Knot spacing & Knots & Row bound at every knot\\
\midrule
$[13/4,9/2]$ & $1/400$ & 501 & $147/200$\\
$[9/2,9]$ & $1/100$ & 451 & $29/40$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The common endpoint $9/2$ satisfies both bounds, so there are
951 distinct exact knots.  A numerical optimizer proposed the
data; acceptance uses rational arithmetic alone.

For each fixed Schur polynomial $q$, differentiation of $F_t$
gives
\[
 b_k''=b_k+4\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(k-j)b_j,\qquad
 \sum_{k=1}^9|b_k''|\le
       \sum_{k=1}^9(1+2k(k+1))=669.
\]
Here $|b_j|\le1$ follows from the Schur bound on $F_t$.
Linear interpolation of each fixed real row functional has error
at most $669h^2/8$ on an interval of length $h$.
The knot estimates therefore imply the continuum bounds
\[
 \frac{147}{200}+\frac{669}{8\cdot400^2}
       =\frac{941469}{1280000},\qquad
 \frac{29}{40}+\frac{669}{8\cdot100^2}
       <\frac{941469}{1280000}.
\]

Finally, for $S_9(t)=\sum_{k=0}^9|b_k(t)|^2$, the identity
$b_k'=-b_k-2\sum_{j<k}b_j$ yields
\[
 S_9'(t)=-2\left|\sum_{k=0}^9 b_k(t)\right|^2\le0.
\]
The same rational recurrence and exponential lower bound give
$S_9(9)<(18/25)^2$.  Cauchy--Schwarz in
\eqref{F:eq:r6-nine-row}, using $\sum|a_j|^2\le1$, bounds the
row by $18/25$ for every $t\ge9$.  This completes the infinite
tail.  The strict comparison with $2/e$ is checked with
\[
 e<E_{40}(1)+\frac{1}{41!}\frac1{1-1/42}.
\]
\end{proof}

This replaces the previous support-free ninth-degree cutoff
$t\ge9/2$ by $t\ge13/4$.  The new cutoff is a proved sufficient
condition; no claim that it is optimal is made.

\section{A sharp sixth-index gap theorem from exact five-row certificates}\label{col:F:23}
\label{F:sec:r6-sixth-gap}
This section supplies a self-contained proof of the coefficient theorem in Taisho R13; its exact rational witness and verifier are embedded in the reproducibility payload.
Let $f$ be holomorphic and zero-free in the unit disk with
$|f|\le1$ and write $a_j=[z^j]f$. The Krzy\.{z} conjecture
asks whether $|a_n|\le2/e$ for every such function and index.
The following result imposes only an initial gap, not stationarity.
\begin{theorem}\label{F:thm:r6-sixth-gap}
For every $n\ge1$, if $a_1=\cdots=a_{\lfloor n/6\rfloor}=0$,
then $|a_n|\le2/e$. Equality holds exactly for
\[
 f(z)=\xi\exp\!\left(-\frac{1+\eta z^n}{1-\eta z^n}\right),
 \qquad |\xi|=|\eta|=1.
\]
\end{theorem}

After a constant rotation, write $f=e^{-H}$, $H(0)=t>0$,
apart from the trivial constant boundary case. The branch
of the logarithm exists on the disk and $\Re H\ge0$.
Set $B=(H-t)/(H+t)$ so $|B|\le1$ and $B(0)=0$.
Then
\[
 f=F_t\circ B,\qquad F_t(w)=\exp[-t(1+w)/(1-w)]
                  =\sum_{k\ge0} b_k(t)w^k.
\]
The next transfer reduces the problem to a finite Schur-polynomial row.
For fixed $n$, let $p_k=[z^n]B(z)^k$ and
$p(w)=\sum_{k=1}^n p_kw^k$. Then $|p(w)|\le1$ on the
circle: the function $(1+wB(z))/(1-wB(z))$ has positive
real part and constant term 1, so its $n$th coefficient
$2p(w)$ has modulus at most 2. To see the last bound,
take the $n$th Fourier coefficient of the positive real
part on smaller circles and then let the radius increase
to one. Thus $p$ is Schur.

Since $F_t'(0)=-2te^{-t}\ne0$, the initial gap in $f$
is also the initial gap in $B$, unless both are constant.
