It implies $B^6=O(z^{n+1})$, so $p_k=0$ for $k\ge6$.
Consequently $q(w)=p(w)/w$ is a Schur polynomial of
degree at most four, and
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6-five-row}
 a_n=\sum_{k=1}^5 b_k(t)\,[w^{k-1}]q .
\end{equation}
Coefficients beyond the actual degree are understood to
be zero. We next prove a sharp uniform bound for the
right side over all Schur polynomials of degree four.
The coefficients $C_k=e^t b_k$ are real polynomials:
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6-five-rec}
 C_0=1,\quad C_1=-2t,\quad
 (k+1)C_{k+1}=2(k-t)C_k-(k-1)C_{k-1},
\end{equation}
by differentiating $F_t$.

\subsection{Low mass: a positive evaluation measure}
For $0<t\le11/10$, let $d_j=C_{j+1}/C_1$, $0\le j\le4$,
with $d_{-j}=d_j$. The Toeplitz matrix
$(d_{i-j})_{i,j=0}^4$ is positive definite. Its successive
leading minors, calculated from \eqref{F:eq:r6-five-rec}, are
\begin{align*}
 1,\quad&-t(t-2),\quad
 \frac{4t^2(t-3)(2t-3)}9,\\
 &\frac{t^3(t-6)(t^2-6t+6)(t^2+6t-18)}{81},\\
 &-\frac{t^4(t^4-8t^3+120t-180)
              (t^4-24t^3+240t^2-720t+540)}{6075}.
\end{align*}
The first four signs follow immediately for the stated
range. The first quartic factor in the last line is
bounded above by $(11/10)^4+120(11/10)-180<0$.
The second quartic has negative derivative there
(use $4(11/10)^3+480(11/10)-720<0$ as an upper bound),
and its value at $11/10$ is strictly positive.
The verifier independently replays the determinant
identities by their polynomial degree bounds.

The positive Toeplitz matrix gives a probability
measure $\mu$ on the circle satisfying
$\int w^j\,d\mu=d_j$, $0\le j\le4$.
For an elementary proof, realize its Gram vectors
$e_0,\ldots,e_4$ in a Hilbert space. The shift
$e_j\mapsto e_{j+1}$ for $j<4$ is an isometry on its
span and extends to a unitary. The spectral measure
at $e_0$ gives the prescribed moments. Its support
contains at least five points, since these Gram
vectors are independent. From \eqref{F:eq:r6-five-row},
\[
 |a_n|=|b_1(t)|\left|\int q(w)\,d\mu(w)\right|
          \le2te^{-t}\le 2/e.
\]
Equality requires $t=1$ and equality in the integral
norm. At each point of the measure's support the
polynomial $q$ must have the same unit value, so
$q$ is constant (it has degree at most four).
Hence $|p_1|=|[z^n]B|=1$ and $B(z)=\eta z^n$
by the $H^2$ norm bound for a Schur function.
This proves the stated equality characterization in
the only mass range where equality will be possible.

\subsection{Compact mass certificate}
For $11/10\le t\le5$ use 391 rational knots
$t_i=i/100$, $110\le i\le500$.
Because the row coefficients $b_k(t)$ are real,
to maximize the absolute row value it suffices to
make its real part nonnegative by a phase and then
symmetrize $q(w)$ with $\overline{q(\bar w)}$.
The resulting polynomial has real coefficient vector
$a=(a_0,\ldots,a_4)$, remains Schur, and preserves
that real row value. Each coefficient satisfies $|a_j|\le1$.

For any rational unit-circle points $\zeta,\omega$,
the linear form with coefficients
$u_j=\Re(\omega\zeta^j)$ has
$\sum u_j a_j=\Re[\omega q(\zeta)]\le1$.
At each knot the embedded \path{revision2/spectral/five_row/witness.json}
gives at most five such forms and nonnegative rational
weights $\lambda_l$. For $c=(C_1,\ldots,C_5)$ this yields
\[
 c\cdot a\le\sum_l\lambda_l
          +\sum_{j=0}^4\left|c_j-\sum_l\lambda_l u_{lj}\right|.
\]
The unit points are encoded by rational Cayley
parameters (and the exceptional point $-1$), and all
the quantities in this inequality are rational.
For each knot, division by the positive lower Taylor
bound $\sum_{j=0}^{24}t_i^j/j!$ for $e^{t_i}$ certifies
the row value below $733/1000$.
The checker tests all 391 inequalities exactly.
A numerical search proposed the sparse evaluation
weights, but there is no numerical assumption in
the certificate acceptance.

To control every point between knots, note that
$b_k''=b_k+4\sum_{j<k}(k-j)b_j$ by differentiating $F_t$
twice. Since $|F_t|\le1$, each $|b_j|\le1$ and
$\sum_{k=1}^5|b_k''|\le145$.
The interpolation error for a fixed row functional
on each closed mass interval has magnitude at most
$145/(8\cdot100^2)$: use the one-variable
Dirichlet Green kernel for linear interpolation and
$|a_j|\le1$.
Thus throughout the entire compact interval the
row norm is at most
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6-five-middle}
 M_*=\frac{733}{1000}+\frac{145}{80000}<\frac2e.
\end{equation}
This covers all real masses between the knots,
not only sampled ones.

\subsection{The unbounded mass ray}
From $b'_k=-b_k-2\sum_{j<k}b_j$,
\[
 \frac{d}{dt}\sum_{k=0}^5|b_k(t)|^2
     =-2\left|\sum_{k=0}^5 b_k(t)\right|^2\le0 .
\]
At $t=5$ the recurrence and rational lower exponential
bound give $\sum_{k=0}^5|b_k(5)|^2<(18/25)^2$.
Since the coefficient vector of $q$ has $\ell^2$ norm
at most one, Cauchy--Schwarz bounds the row by $18/25$
for every $t\ge5$. This is strictly below $2/e$.
Together with the low and compact mass proofs,
Theorem~\ref{F:thm:r6-sixth-gap} follows.


\section{A dimension-free coefficient transfer and a sharper degree-nine cut}\label{col:F:24}
\label{F:sec:r6-low-energy}

Let $f$ be zero-free and holomorphic in the disk, with $|f|\leq1$.
After an irrelevant constant phase assume $f(0)=e^{-t}$, $t>0$.
Set $H=-\log f$ and
\[
 B=\frac{H-t}{H+t},\qquad
 F_t(w)=\exp\!\left[-t\frac{1+w}{1-w}\right]
       =\sum_{k\geq0}b_k(t)w^k.
\]
Then $B$ is Schur, $B(0)=0$, and $f=F_t(B)$. For stationary
positive atomic data $B$ is a finite Blaschke product of degree
$N$; its zeros will be called \emph{Cayley zeros}.

Use the independently verified five-row bound from Taisho R13:
for a Schur map $G$ with $\operatorname{ord}_0G\geq m$ and $6m>n$,
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6-row-M}
 |[z^n]F_t(G)|\leq M(t):=
 \begin{cases}
 2te^{-t},&0<t\leq11/10,\\
 M_*:=11757/16000,&t>11/10.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
The constant $M_*=733/1000+145/80000$ includes interpolation
between all rational mass knots. The same constant is valid at
$t=11/10$. The manuscript's five-row section proves and certifies
\eqref{F:eq:r6-row-M}, including the unbounded mass ray.

\begin{theorem}[Low-energy transfer, with effective row length]
\label{F:thm:r6-energy-transfer}
Let $m=1+\lfloor n/6\rfloor$, $K=\lfloor n/m\rfloor\leq5$, and
\[
 E=\left(\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}|[z^j]B|^2\right)^{1/2},\qquad
 C_K=(1+\sqrt2)\left(K+1+
       \sqrt{K(K+1)(2K+1)/6}\right).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6-effective-energy}
 |[z^n]f|\leq M(t)+C_KE\leq M(t)+35E.
\end{equation}
In particular strict subcompetitiveness follows if either
\[
 1<t\leq11/10,\quad E\leq(t-1)^2/150,
 \qquad\hbox{or}\qquad
 t\geq11/10,\quad E\leq1/40000.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $P=\sum_{j<m}[z^j]B\,z^j$ and $T=z^{-m}(B-P)$.
On the circle $|T|\leq1+|P|$. Put $a=\log^+|T|$, so
$0\leq a\leq|P|$, and let $g$ be its analytic Herglotz transform,
with imaginary constant chosen to be zero. Set $O=e^{-g}$ and
$G=z^mOT$. Then $G$ is Schur, vanishes to order at least $m$,
and $|O|\leq1$. Fourier coefficients give
$\|g\|_2\leq\sqrt2\|P\|_2$. Since $\Re g\geq0$,
$|1-e^{-g}|\leq|g|$. The identity
$B-G=B(1-O)+OP$ proves
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6-clipping-distance}
 \|B-G\|_2\leq(1+\sqrt2)E.
\end{equation}
Here $T$ is bounded analytic, $g$ belongs to $H^2$, and $O$ is
bounded analytic. The norm estimates use their $H^2$ boundary
limits. The outer construction gives $|OT|\leq1$ almost
everywhere; since $OT$ is bounded analytic, the same bound holds
throughout the disk, and $G$ is Schur.

Telescoping powers of two Schur maps yields
$\|B^k-G^k\|_2\leq k\|B-G\|_2$. Since
$\sum_k|b_k(t)|^2\leq1$, the difference from $1\leq k\leq K$
is at most $\sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^K k^2}\|B-G\|_2$.
For the remaining tail write
$J(w)=\sum_{k\geq K+1}b_k(t)w^{k-K-1}$.
Composition by a Schur map fixing zero contracts $H^2$:
compose the harmonic majorant of $|J|^2$ and use its value at zero.
Thus $\|J(B)\|_2\leq1$ and the target coefficient of
$B^{K+1}J(B)$ is bounded by $\|P_{\leq n}B^{K+1}\|_2$.
Because $(K+1)m>n$, the corresponding prefix of $G^{K+1}$
vanishes, and this norm is at most $(K+1)\|B-G\|_2$.
Together with \eqref{F:eq:r6-clipping-distance} and
\eqref{F:eq:r6-row-M}, this proves the estimate.

For $1<t\leq11/10$ the canonical deficit is
\[
 2/e-2te^{-t}=\frac2e\int_0^{t-1}s e^{-s}\,ds
 \geq e^{-11/10}(t-1)^2>\frac14(t-1)^2.
\]
Now $35/150<1/4$. On the other ray,
$M_*+35/40000<20000/27183<2/e$, using $e<27183/10000$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Stationary residual and degree-nine specialization]
\label{F:cor:r6-n9-first-moment}
For a deficient stationary candidate put $x=n/N>1$. The
mass floor $t\geq(3x-1)/2$ implies that
\[
 E\leq H(x):=\min\{1/40000,(x-1)^2/70\}
\]
is impossible for a competitive candidate.
At degree $n=9$, a sharper necessary condition, valid for every
deficient support size $N\leq8$, is
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6-n9-first-moment}
 |M_1|>\frac{t}{27000}.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, write the Cayley zeros as $0,\beta_2,\ldots,\beta_N$
with multiplicities. Then
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6-n9-cayley-product}
 \prod_{j=2}^N|\beta_j|>\frac1{27000}.
\end{equation}
An additional zero at zero makes the product zero and is excluded.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The general claim follows from $t-1\geq(3/2)(x-1)$ and
$1/70<(3/2)^2/150$. For $n=9$, $m=2$, $K=4$, and
$E=|B'(0)|=|M_1|/t$. Every $N\leq8$ has
$t\geq19/16>11/10$. Moreover
\[
 C_4=(5+\sqrt{30})(1+\sqrt2)<127/5,
 \qquad
 M_*+\frac{127}{135000}<\frac{20000}{27183}<\frac2e.
\]
Hence $E\leq1/27000$ gives strict subcompetitiveness.
The product formula follows by differentiating a finite Blaschke
product at its zero at zero; its other factors have modulus
$|\beta_j|$ at zero. This concerns Cayley zeros, not auxiliary
spectral roots.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Provenance and scope.}
The outer clipping and the uniform constant $35$ are from Keio R14.
The effective-length constant $C_K$ and its degree-nine threshold
$1/27000$ refine that supplied argument. In particular the entire
$M_1=0$ slice is closed at degree nine even if the second and third
Herglotz moments are large. The general sixth-index gap theorem
also applies to arbitrary zero-free Schur functions when their
initial Taylor coefficients vanish; no stationarity is required
for that theorem. None of these statements proves that an
arbitrary remaining stationary configuration has low initial energy.

\subsection{All-mass exclusions from an aggregate Cayley depth}
Put $q=\lfloor n/6\rfloor$ and
\[
 S=\sum_{j=1}^N\frac{1-|\beta_j|}{1+|\beta_j|},
\]
where these are again the Cayley zeros, including their multiplicities.
Keio R19's aggregate criterion becomes an immediate consequence of
the preceding verified transfer: a deficient stationary candidate
is subcompetitive at every admissible mass if $S>q$ and
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6-cayley-depth}
 \frac43\frac{(S-q)^{3/2}}{\sqrt S}\geq\log(1/H(n/N)).
\end{equation}
Indeed Parseval on radius $r=e^{-u}$ gives
$E\leq r^{-q}\sup_{|z|=r}|B(z)|$. A zero of radius $a$
has factor modulus at most $(r+a)/(1+ra)$ there. With
$c=(1-a)/(1+a)$, the negative logarithm of this maximum is
$2\operatorname{arctanh}(c\tanh(u/2))\geq c(u-u^3/12)$.
The last inequality follows from $\operatorname{arctanh}v\geq v$
and $\tanh y\geq y-y^3/3$, the latter having derivative
$y^2-\tanh^2 y\geq0$ after rearrangement.
Multiplying the factors and choosing
$u=2\sqrt{(S-q)/S}$ proves
$E\leq\exp[-4(S-q)^{3/2}/(3\sqrt S)]$.
A sufficient condition depending only on $n$ and $S$ is
\[
 \frac Sn\geq\frac16+
 \left(\frac{3\log(40000n^2)}{4n}\right)^{2/3}.
\]
It uses $q\leq n/6$, $S\leq N\leq n$, and
$H(n/N)\geq1/(40000n^2)$. The criterion excludes explicit
infinite families, but it supplies no unconditional lower bound
on the aggregate depth of an unknown competitor.

\section{A four-row certificate strengthens the ninth-coefficient first-moment cut}\label{col:F:25}
\label{F:sec:r6-four-row-nine}

The effective composition length at degree nine after removing the first
Cayley coefficient is four, not five. A separate exact row certificate
therefore sharpens the general low-energy consequence substantially.

\begin{theorem}[Four-row mass ray]
\label{F:thm:r6-four-row}
Let $q(w)=\sum_{j=0}^3q_jw^j$ be a Schur polynomial, and let
$b_k(t)=[w^k]F_t(w)$. Then for every $t\geq5/4$,
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6-four-row-bound}
 \left|\sum_{k=1}^4 b_k(t)q_{k-1}\right|
 \leq\frac{14347}{20000}=0.71735.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The coefficient recurrence is the one in the five-row theorem:
$C_k(t)=e^t b_k(t)$, $C_0=1$, $C_1=-2t$, and
$(k+1)C_{k+1}=2(k-t)C_k-(k-1)C_{k-1}$.
After rotating the functional value and symmetrizing the polynomial,
it suffices to bound its value on real coefficient vectors
$a=(q_0,q_1,q_2,q_3)$. Such a vector has $|a_j|\leq1$ and
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^3\Re(\omega\zeta^j)a_j\leq1
 \qquad(|\zeta|=|\omega|=1).
\]
For each of the 376 rational knots $t_i=i/100$, $125\leq i\leq500$,
the embedded witness gives at most four such evaluation forms with
nonnegative rational weights. Their total weight plus the coefficient
$\ell^1$ residual bounds the row functional. All circle points are
encoded by rational Cayley parameters; the exceptional point $-1$
is represented explicitly. The exact verifier checks all unit norms,
all nonnegative weights, the complete consecutive knot list, and
\[
 \frac{\text{total weight}+\text{coefficient residual}}
      {\sum_{j=0}^{40}t_i^j/j!}<\frac{7163}{10000}
\]
at every knot. There is no floating-point acceptance in these checks.

For a fixed Schur row, $b_k''=b_k+4\sum_{j<k}(k-j)b_j$ and
$|b_j|\leq1$ imply
\[
 \sum_{k=1}^4|b_k''|\leq\sum_{k=1}^4(1+2k(k+1))=84.
\]
The error of linear interpolation on a mass interval of length
$1/100$ is therefore at most $84/80000$. It follows that the
row norm throughout the closed continuum $[5/4,5]$ is at most
\[
 \frac{7163}{10000}+\frac{84}{80000}
       =\frac{14347}{20000}.
\]
For the remaining ray, the exact identity
\[
 \frac{d}{dt}\sum_{k=0}^4|b_k(t)|^2
       =-2\left|\sum_{k=0}^4b_k(t)\right|^2\leq0
\]
and the rational endpoint check
$\sum_{k=0}^4|b_k(5)|^2<(7/10)^2$ give a row norm below
$7/10$ for every $t\geq5$, by Cauchy--Schwarz.
This is smaller than the stated compact bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Improved degree-nine first-moment and Cayley-product bounds]
\label{F:cor:r6-four-row-first-moment}
Every competitive deficient stationary candidate at degree nine satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6-four-row-first-moment}
 \boxed{|M_1|>t/1400},\qquad
 \boxed{\prod_{j=2}^N|\beta_j|>1/1400},
\end{equation}
where $0,\beta_2,\ldots,\beta_N$ are its Cayley zeros with multiplicities.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
If $N\leq7$, the ground-state mass floor gives
$t\geq(3\cdot9/N-1)/2\geq10/7>5/4$.
For $N=8$, Corollary~\ref{F:cor:r6radialmass} gives
$t>34/27>5/4$. Thus the four-row theorem applies in every deficient
stationary stratum at degree nine.

The outer clipping construction in Theorem~\ref{F:thm:r6-energy-transfer}
has $m=2$ and $K=4$ here. Use \eqref{F:eq:r6-four-row-bound} for its
order-two Schur map $G$ instead of the five-row bound. Then
\[
 |a_9|\leq\frac{14347}{20000}+C_4 E,
 \qquad E=|B'(0)|=|M_1|/t,\quad C_4<127/5.
\]
If $E\leq1/1400$, the exact rational comparison gives
\[
 |a_9|<\frac{14347}{20000}+\frac{127}{7000}
       =\frac{102969}{140000}
       <\frac{20000}{27183}<\frac2e.
\]
The last inequality follows from the previously verified exponential
bound $e<27183/10000$. This contradicts competitiveness.
Differentiating the finite Blaschke product at zero gives the
equivalent Cayley-product statement.
\end{proof}

The earlier $1/27000$ consequence remains valid but is superseded at
degree nine by \eqref{F:eq:r6-four-row-first-moment}. The new threshold
is $135/7$ times as large, so the excluded closed first-moment tube
is strictly broader. This is a certified geometric slice of the
remaining strata; it is not a complete degree-nine proof.

\section{Three stationary moments exclude a broad projected cluster tube}\label{col:F:26}
\label{F:sec:r6-three-stride}

The auxiliary spectral roots in this section are distinct objects from
the zeros of the Cayley Blaschke map used in the coefficient transfer.
Write the full stationary moments in the form
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6-cluster-moments}
 kM_k=\sum_{i=1}^N\alpha_i^k+
       \sum_{j=1}^{d}\cosh(k\ell_j)\xi_j^k,
 \qquad M_k=\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i\alpha_i^k,
 \quad 1\leq k\leq n,
\end{equation}
where $d=n-N$, $|\alpha_i|=|\xi_j|=1$, $\lambda_i>0$,
and $\ell_j>0$. The $n$ projected directions, counted with
multiplicities, are the $N$ physical directions $\alpha_i$ and
the $d$ auxiliary directions $\xi_j$. Put $t=\sum_i\lambda_i$.
No upper bound on $t$ or on the depths $\ell_j$ is assumed.

\begin{theorem}[Three-stride projected-cluster exclusion]
\label{F:thm:r6-three-stride}
Let $L\geq1$ be an integer with $3L\leq n$. There cannot be a
stationary configuration satisfying \eqref{F:eq:r6-cluster-moments}
for which a common angle $\psi$ obeys
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6-folded-tube}
 |\arg(e^{-i\psi}\alpha_i^L)|\leq\frac1{12},\qquad
 |\arg(e^{-i\psi}\xi_j^L)|\leq\frac1{12}
 \quad\hbox{for every }i,j.
\end{equation}
Here the arguments are chosen in $[-\pi,\pi]$. The conclusion
holds for every positive set of physical masses and every set of
positive, possibly very unequal, auxiliary depths.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Rotate all directions to make $\psi=0$. Write
$\alpha_i^L=e^{i\theta_i}$ and $\xi_j^L=e^{i\phi_j}$, with
$|\theta_i|,|\phi_j|\leq\delta=1/12$. Put
\[
 X=Lt>0,\qquad u_j=L\ell_j,\qquad
 R_k=N+\sum_{j=1}^{d}\cosh(ku_j),\quad k=1,2,3.
\]
Since $\cos(k\theta),\cos(k\phi)\geq c_k:=1-k^2/288>0$,
the real parts of the three stationary equations imply
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6-R-sandwich}
 c_k kX\leq R_k\leq kX/c_k\qquad(k=1,2,3).
\end{equation}
In particular $c_1,c_2\geq49/50$ and $c_3=31/32$.

First we show $X<4n$. Let $s_j=\cosh u_j$ and
$S_1=\sum_j s_j$. The elementary inequality
$\cosh(2u)=2\cosh^2u-1\geq\cosh^2u$ gives
$\sum_j s_j^2\leq R_2\leq2X/c_2$. Cauchy--Schwarz and
$d\leq n$ then give $S_1\leq\sqrt{2nX/c_2}$. The first
inequality in \eqref{F:eq:r6-R-sandwich} yields
\[
 c_1\leq\frac nX+\sqrt{\frac{2n}{Xc_2}}.
\]
If $X\geq4n$, its right side is at most
$1/4+5/7=27/28<49/50\leq c_1$, a contradiction.

Next, the exact identity
\begin{align*}
 &\cosh(3u)-3\cosh(2u)+3\cosh u-1\\
 &\hspace{20mm}=2(\cosh u-1)^2(2\cosh u+1)\geq0
\end{align*}
implies
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6-third-difference-lower}
 R_3-3R_2+3R_1\geq N+d=n.
\end{equation}
On the other hand, \eqref{F:eq:r6-R-sandwich} gives
\[
 |R_k-kX|\leq\frac{kX(1-c_k)}{c_k}
       \leq\frac{k^3\delta^2X}{2c_3}.
\]
The combination $3X-3(2X)+3X$ is zero. Therefore
\[
 |R_3-3R_2+3R_1|
 \leq\frac{(27+3\cdot8+3)\delta^2X}{2c_3}
 <\frac{108\delta^2}{c_3}\,n
 =\frac{24}{31}n<n,
\]
contradicting \eqref{F:eq:r6-third-difference-lower}.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Degree nine.}
Taking $n=9$ and $L=3$ closes, at every deficient support size,
the entire family in which all nine projected directions lie
within angular distance $1/36$ radians of one common rotated
regular three-grid. Arbitrary occupancy of its three arcs is
allowed, including repeated auxiliary projections; the physical
atoms themselves retain their required distinctness. In particular
this excludes such tubes in each of the previously residual
$N=5,6,7,8$ strata. It does not require the projected directions
to fill a grid bijectively, and does not close arbitrary geometry
within any one of these four strata.

\paragraph{Relation to the supplied rounds.}
Keio R28 used a first, an intermediate, and a top moment with
log-convex propagation of $\cosh$, obtaining, among other cases,
an eight-stride concentration exclusion. Theorem~\ref{F:thm:r6-three-stride}
uses the signed third finite difference instead. It requires only
three strides and admits folded angular halfwidth $1/12$.
Its proof is independent of any infinite-degree limiting argument,
finite numerical search, or coefficient competitiveness assumption.

\section{Projected full-grid tubes with unrestricted auxiliary depths}\label{col:F:27}
\label{F:sec:r6-projected-grid}

Retain the stationary moment notation of
\eqref{F:eq:r6-cluster-moments}. Suppose the $n$ projected directions
can be matched bijectively to a rotated regular $n$-grid. After
rotation, label the reference directions by $\zeta_i=e^{2\pi i i/n}$
and write the actual directions as
\[
 x_i=\zeta_i e^{is_i/n},\qquad 0\leq i<n.
\]
Let $S$ be the $N$ physical labels and $D$ the $d=n-N\geq1$
auxiliary labels. For distinct labels put
$m(i,h)=\min\{|i-h|,n-|i-h|\}$ and define
\[
 B_P=\max_{h\in D}\sum_{i\ne h}\frac{|s_i-s_h|}{m(i,h)},
 \qquad
 B_D=\max_{0\leq i<n}\sum_{\substack{h\in D\\h\ne i}}
                    \frac{|s_i-s_h|}{m(i,h)}.
\]

\begin{theorem}[All-depth projected-grid exclusion, Keio R24]
\label{F:thm:r6-projected-grid}
The stationary moment equations are impossible if
\[
 \max_i|s_i|\leq1/10,\qquad B_P\leq1/20,
 \qquad B_D\leq d/(20n).
\]
No mass upper bound or auxiliary depth upper bound is required.
In particular the exact projected regular $n$-grid is impossible
for every $n\geq2$ and $1\leq d<n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For $\ell>0$ set
\[
 a_\ell(k)=\frac{\cosh(k\ell)-1}{k}\ (k>0),\quad
 a_\ell(0)=0,\qquad
 J_\ell(u)=\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}a_\ell(k)\cos(ku).
\]
The function $a_\ell$ is convex and nonnegative on $[0,n]$,
by its positive power series in odd powers. Put
$w_k=(a_\ell(k)+a_\ell(n-k))/2$ for $0\leq k\leq n$.
This sequence is convex, symmetric, and nonnegative, with
$w_0=w_n=a_\ell(n)/2$. On the cyclic indices $0,\ldots,n-1$,
the negative second difference of $w$ is nonpositive away from
zero and sums to zero. Its Fourier transform at each nonzero
frequency is nonnegative: subtract its zero sum and use
$\cos v-1\leq0$ on the off-zero terms. Dividing by the strictly
positive negative-Laplacian multiplier gives nonnegativity of
the Fourier transform of $w$; the zero frequency is also
nonnegative because $w\geq0$. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6-radial-grid-sign}
 J_\ell(2\pi b/n)\geq-a_\ell(n)/2\qquad(b\in\mathbb Z).
\end{equation}

Set $A=\sum_{j\in D}a_{\ell_j}(n)$ and
$J_0^*(u)=\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\cos(ku)/k$.
The real top moment, with
$c=1-\max|s_i|^2/2\geq3/4$, gives
$t\geq c(1+A)$. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6-top-mass-budget}
 t\geq3/4,\qquad A\leq2t,\qquad t-A/2\geq t/3.
\end{equation}
These inequalities control every auxiliary exponential without
bounding the individual depths.

Use the signed Dirichlet test
\[
 D_n(w)=\Re\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}w^k,\qquad
 I=\sum_{h\in D}\sum_{i\in S}\lambda_iD_n(x_i/x_h).
\]
For distinct labels, the reference chord is at least
$4m(i,h)/n$. Every chord along the relative angular perturbation
is at least $3m(i,h)/n$, and
$|1-(x_i/x_h)^n|\leq|s_i-s_h|$. The geometric sum yields
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6-grid-upper}
 |I|\leq(n/3)tB_D.
\end{equation}

Expand the stationary moments in $I$. For each hole the result is
$t$ plus the sum of $J_0^*$ over all projected directions plus
the sum of $J_{\ell_j}$ over auxiliary directions. The reference
sum of $J_0^*$ is zero. Its derivative is bounded by
$2/|1-e^{iu}|$, so its total change over all holes is at most
$(2/3)dB_P$. Also the coefficients
$k a_\ell(k)=\cosh(k\ell)-1$ are increasing; Abel summation
gives $|J_\ell'(u)|\leq2n a_\ell(n)/|1-e^{iu}|$.
The diagonal auxiliary term does not move. Summing the remaining
changes by auxiliary columns and applying
\eqref{F:eq:r6-radial-grid-sign} gives
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6-grid-lower}
 I\geq d(t-A/2)-(2/3)dB_P-(2/3)nAB_D.
\end{equation}
Under the stated budgets and \eqref{F:eq:r6-top-mass-budget},
the two error terms in \eqref{F:eq:r6-grid-lower}, together with
the upper bound in \eqref{F:eq:r6-grid-upper}, are at most
\[
 dt\left(\frac2{45}+\frac1{15}+\frac1{60}\right)
 =\frac{23}{180}dt<\frac13dt.
\]
This contradicts \eqref{F:eq:r6-top-mass-budget} and proves the theorem.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Explicit independent jitter, including degree nine]
\label{F:cor:r6-n9-grid-tube}
With $H_r=\sum_{k=1}^r1/k$ and $r=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, the
closed tube
\[
 |s_i|\leq\frac{d}{80nH_r}\quad\hbox{for every }i
\]
is excluded. At degree nine this is the angular halfwidth
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6-n9-grid-jitter}
 |\arg(x_i/\zeta_i)|\leq\frac{d}{13500}
       \qquad(d=9-N).
\end{equation}
The displacement of each label is independent, and every depth
$\ell_j>0$ is admitted in the excluded input family.
\end{corollary}

Indeed each cyclic inverse-distance sum is at most $2H_r$;
the budgets follow from $|s_i-s_h|\leq2\max|s_i|$ and $d<n$.
At $n=9$, $H_4=25/12$ and $80n^2H_4=13500$.
The theorem concerns a matching of both physical and auxiliary
projections. It does not assert that arbitrary physical support
lies near such a grid, or that an arbitrary auxiliary phase list
has the matching required here.

\section{Larger physical cyclic grids and a degree-nine consequence}\label{col:F:28}
\label{F:sec:r6-larger-grid}

The following consequence of Keio R20 has different hypotheses
from the projected full-grid theorem: it constrains the physical
support alone and leaves all auxiliary phases unrestricted.
Suppose the $N$ physical directions form a subset of a rotated
regular $M$-grid, with $M\geq N$, and let $m=M-N$ be the number
of omitted reference vertices. Keep $d=n-N\geq1$ and put
\[
 k_0=\max(1,M-n),\qquad k_1=\min(M-1,n),\qquad L=4d+2m.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Complementary-moment recurrence exclusion]
\label{F:thm:r6-larger-grid}
If $k_1-k_0+1\geq L$, no positive physical masses and nonzero
off-circle auxiliary roots can satisfy the stationary moment system
on such a physical grid. For $M=n$, the endpoint moments improve
the sufficient condition to $n+1\geq6d$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Normalize the reference grid to the $M$th roots of unity. Write
$D_k$ for the power sum of its omitted vertices and
$C_k=\tfrac12\sum_{\gamma\in\mathcal A}\gamma^k$, where
$\mathcal A$ is the multiset of $2d$ auxiliary reciprocal-conjugate
roots. Thus $C_0=d$ and $C_{-k}=\overline{C_k}$.
The stationary equations are $kM_k=p_k+C_k$.
Physical grid support gives $M_{M-k}=\overline{M_k}$ and
$p_{M-k}=p_{-k}=-D_{-k}$ for $1\leq k<M$.
Using both available moment indices proves
\[
 E_k:=kC_{M-k}-(M-k)C_{-k}+(M-2k)D_{-k}=0,
       \qquad k_0\leq k\leq k_1.
\]
Extend this definition to every integer. Direct expansion gives
\[
 E_k=\frac12\sum_{\gamma\in\mathcal A}
       [k(\gamma^M+1)-M](\gamma^{-1})^k
       +\sum_{\beta\text{ omitted}}(M-2k)(\beta^{-1})^k.
\]
Its annihilating recurrence has order $L$ and characteristic
polynomial
\[
\prod_{\gamma\in\mathcal A}(z-\gamma^{-1})^2
 \prod_{\beta\text{ omitted}}(z-\beta^{-1})^2.
\]
Its constant coefficient is nonzero, so $L$ consecutive zero
values propagate in both directions to all integers.
For $M\ne n$ this contradicts $E_0=M(M-n)\ne0$.
For $M=n$, the two endpoint values are already zero, giving
a zero block of length $n+1$. The identically zero sequence
is again impossible: after equal bases are grouped, every
nonunit auxiliary base has a nonzero constant coefficient
$-M/2$ times its multiplicity, and hence a genuine simple or
double pole in the generating function. Distinct bases have
distinct poles, and unit omitted bases cannot cancel them.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{A new physical-support slice at degree nine.}
For $n=9$, $N=8$ and $M=10$, one has $d=1$, $m=2$,
$k_0=1$, $k_1=9$, and $L=8$. Consequently every eight-point
subset of every rotated regular decagon is excluded, regardless
of the positive masses and auxiliary phase or depth.
This is a continuous family under common rotation, not a
finite list of remaining solution boxes. Its exact-support
hypothesis does not close all eight-atom geometry.

\section{Spectral interpolation and joint derivative mass filters}\label{col:F:29}
\label{F:sec:r6geometry}
Two geometry-sensitive consequences of the stationary equation are
credited to the supplied Taisho R18 and R22.  Their proofs below use only
the stationary reduction already established in this paper.  They apply
in arbitrary degree and at arbitrary support defect.

Throughout this section $n\ge2$.  The points
$\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_N$ denote the physical poles on the
unit circle. Choose the outer spectral factor $Q$ of degree $n$, so that
$h=|Q|^2$ has exactly double circle zeros at those poles. Write
\[
 Q(z)=C\prod_{j=1}^N(z-\zeta_j)
          \prod_{\ell=1}^{n-N}(1-\overline{\omega_\ell}z),
 \qquad |\omega_\ell|<1.
\]
Thus $\omega_\ell$ are the reciprocal-conjugate representatives of the
off-circle roots of this chosen outer factor, with multiplicities.
This explicit convention avoids confusing them with zeros of the
Cayley Blaschke map.

\begin{theorem}[Finite Gram and centered derivative filters]
\label{F:thm:r6geometry}
Define the spectral cardinal polynomial
\[
 \ell_j(z)=\frac{Q(z)}{(z-\zeta_j)Q'(\zeta_j)}.
\]
For any subset $S$ of the physical supports containing $j$, put
\[
 K_S=\left(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(\zeta_i\overline{\zeta_r})^k
                                      \right)_{i,r\in S}.
\]
Then $K_S$ is positive definite and
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6gram}
 \lambda_j=\|\ell_j\|_{H^2}^2\ge[K_S^{-1}]_{jj},
 \qquad t\ge\operatorname{tr}K_{\{1,\ldots,N\}}^{-1}.
\end{equation}
Set
\[
 S_j=\sum_{\ell=1}^{n-N}
       \frac{1-|\omega_\ell|^2}{|\zeta_j-\omega_\ell|^2},\qquad
 F_j=\sum_{\beta\in\mathcal B_j}
       \frac{2\Im(\overline\beta\zeta_j)}{|\zeta_j-\beta|^2},
\]
where $\mathcal B_j$ contains the other physical poles and all
$\omega_\ell$, with multiplicities.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6derivative}
 \boxed{\lambda_j\ge\frac1n+
         \frac{3(S_j^2+F_j^2)}{n(n^2-1)}},\qquad
 t\ge\frac Nn+\frac{3}{n(n^2-1)}\sum_j(S_j^2+F_j^2).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
At $\zeta_j$ the stationary equation $(D+\Phi)h=nh$ and its difference
kernel give
\[
 Dh(\zeta_j)=-2\int\frac{|Q(z)|^2}{|z-\zeta_j|^2}\,dm(z),
 \qquad (\Phi h)(\zeta_j)=2\lambda_j|Q'(\zeta_j)|^2.
\]
The integrand is bounded because the zero is simple.  Since
$h(\zeta_j)=0$, this proves the cardinal norm identity.
Evaluation on the distinct nodes of $S$ from the polynomials of degree
at most $n-1$ is onto by Lagrange interpolation. Its Gram matrix is
$K_S$, so the minimum squared norm for values $e_j$ is
$[K_S^{-1}]_{jj}$. The actual $\ell_j$ is feasible for these constraints.
This proves \eqref{F:eq:r6gram}, including its trace consequence.

Let $p(z)=\ell_j(\zeta_j z)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}c_kz^k$, so $p(1)=1$.
The vectors $(1)_{k=0}^{n-1}$ and $(k-(n-1)/2)_{k=0}^{n-1}$ are
orthogonal, with squared norms $n$ and $n(n^2-1)/12$.
Bessel's inequality yields
\[
 \|p\|_2^2\ge\frac1n+\frac{12}{n(n^2-1)}
                      |p'(1)-(n-1)/2|^2.
\]
For each normalized root factor, put $w=\overline\beta\zeta_j$.
Its logarithmic derivative is $-w/(1-w)$, whose real and imaginary
parts are respectively
\[
 \frac12\left(1-\frac{1-|\beta|^2}{|\zeta_j-\beta|^2}\right),
 \qquad-\frac{\Im(\overline\beta\zeta_j)}{|\zeta_j-\beta|^2}.
\]
Summing the $n-1$ factors gives
$p'(1)-(n-1)/2=-(S_j+iF_j)/2$ and proves
\eqref{F:eq:r6derivative}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Uniform reference-map budget]
\label{F:cor:r6reference}
Put
\[
 H_0(z)=\frac1N\sum_j\frac{\zeta_j+z}{\zeta_j-z},\qquad
 J_0(z)=\frac{H_0(z)-1}{H_0(z)+1}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6reference}
 t\ge\frac Nn+\frac{3N}{n(n^2-1)}
 \left|\sum_{\ell=1}^{n-N}
       \frac{1+J_0(\omega_\ell)}{1-J_0(\omega_\ell)}\right|^2.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The inverse Cayley term is $H_0(\omega_\ell)$.
Its real part is the averaged Poisson value and its imaginary part
is minus the averaged auxiliary force.  The physical pair forces
cancel in their uniform sum.  Hence the sum inside the modulus equals
$N^{-1}\sum_j(S_j-iF_j)$.  Cauchy--Schwarz in
\eqref{F:eq:r6derivative} proves the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Pair separation under a mass cap]
\label{F:cor:r6pair}
If $N\ge2$ and $t<T$, every two distinct physical poles with smaller angular
separation $\theta>0$ satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6pair}
 \theta^2>\frac{24}{n(n^2-1)(T-(N-2)/n)}.
\end{equation}
At $n=9$, the mass cap $T=13/4$ therefore implies
\[
 \theta^2>\frac{6}{5(125-4N)}\qquad(N=5,6,7,8).
\]
For the same cap, the reference-map test becomes
\[
 \left|\sum_{\ell=1}^{9-N}H_0(\omega_\ell)\right|^2
 <\frac{780}{N}-\frac{80}{3}.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For two nodes the Gram inverse diagonal is
$n/(n^2-|\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}e^{ik\theta}|^2)$.
Since $1-\cos u\le u^2/2$, its denominator is at most
$n^2(n^2-1)\theta^2/12$. Thus both masses are at least
$12/[n(n^2-1)\theta^2]$. The other $N-2$ masses are at
least $1/n$ each. Sum and use $t<T$ to obtain
\eqref{F:eq:r6pair}.  The last inequality is
\eqref{F:eq:r6reference} with $n=9,t<13/4$.
\end{proof}

These inequalities exclude all configurations that violate them,
with no assumption of equal masses, auxiliary symmetry, or bounded
defect.  They leave configurations that pass every displayed filter;
no complete support stratum is declared empty on this basis.

\section{Projected coefficient energy closes a further radial region}\label{col:F:30}
\label{F:sec:r6projectedenergy}
The projected spectrum in this section is different from the low Cayley
coefficient energy used earlier.  We reproduce the singleton cancellation
of Heisei R19, include its polar entropy input, and sharpen its rational
thresholds.  No grid matching or angular separation is assumed.

Let $\zeta_i$ be the physical unit poles, and write the auxiliary pairs
as $(e^{-\ell_j}\xi_j,e^{\ell_j}\xi_j)$, $|\xi_j|=1$ and $\ell_j>0$.
Define
\[
 P(z)=\prod_{i=1}^N(1-\overline{\zeta_i}z)
             \prod_{j=1}^{n-N}(1-\overline{\xi_j}z)
       =\sum_{k=0}^n p_kz^k,\quad Z=\|P\|_2^2,
\]
\[
 A=n\max_j\ell_j,\qquad
 D_r=\frac1Z\sum_{k=0}^n|1-2k/n|^r|p_k|^2\quad(r=2,4).
\]
For an auxiliary index put $P_j=P/(1-\overline{\xi_j}z)$,
$Z_j=\|P_j\|_2^2$, and $\mathcal Q=(n^2Z)^{-1}\sum_jZ_j$.

\begin{theorem}[Singleton energy bound and explicit excluded regions]
\label{F:thm:r6projectedenergy}
Every stationary tuple of positive defect satisfies
\begin{align}
 -\log a_n-(1-\log2)\ge{}&\frac{1-3D_2}{4}
 -\frac{\mathcal Q}{2}\cosh(A/n)T(A)\notag\\
 &-\bigl(\cosh A-1-A^2/2\bigr)D_4,
 \qquad \mathcal Q\le D_2/2,\label{F:eq:r6energyentropy}\\
 T(A)={}&A^3/3+A\cosh A-\sinh A.\notag
\end{align}
In particular each of the following complete parameter regions is
strictly subcompetitive, uniformly in all root phases and defect sizes:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
\text{degree range}&A\text{ at most}&D_2\text{ at most}
 &-\log a_n-(1-\log2)\text{ greater than}\\\hline
n\ge9&2&3/40&1/100\\
n\ge10&3&1/52&1/1000\\
n\ge10&4&1/190&1/400.
\end{array}
\]
The last two rows improve the supplied R19 values $1/60$ and $1/200$.
The first row also applies to the ninth coefficient.
\end{theorem}

\subsection{The polar entropy input with its contraction proof}
For any all-circle degree-$n$ polynomial, set
$\Gamma=\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}k(n-k)|p_k|^2/n^2$; thus
$\Gamma/Z=(1-D_2)/4$.
We need the reinforced inequality
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6polarbonus}
 \operatorname{Ent}(|P|^2/Z)
 \ge1-\log2+\max\{0,3\Gamma/Z-1/2\}.
\end{equation}
Here is the polar argument, following Lei--Zhang's construction
\cite{F:lei} and the extra Fej\'er test in Heisei R15.
First take simple unit roots and multiply by a unit phase so $P=P^*$,
where reflection is in degree $n$.  Put $q=P-zP'/n$ and $v=q^*/q$.
One has $q+q^*=P$.  In the disk
$\Re(zP'/P)<n/2$, by summing
$\Re(z/(z-\zeta))=1/2-(1-|z|^2)/(2|z-\zeta|^2)$.
Thus $q$ has no interior zero.  A boundary zero of $q$ would also
annihilate $q^*$ and hence both $P$ and $P'$, contradicting simplicity.
Consequently $v$ is inner and $v(0)=0$.

For $F(0)=0$ write
$S_n(F)=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(n-j)|[z^j]F|^2/j$.
Multiplication by a Schur function contracts each finite $H^2$
coefficient prefix: truncate the input first, multiply, project, and
use the full $H^2$ contraction. Summation by parts with the decreasing
weights $(n-j)/j$ therefore gives $S_n(\phi F)\le S_n(F)$.
For $F_k=v^kq=v^{k-1}q^*$ this implies $S_n(F_k)\le\Gamma$.
Weighted Cauchy--Schwarz and $q_j=(n-j)p_j/n$ give
\[
 M_k:=\int|q|^2v^k\,dm=\langle F_k,q\rangle,\quad
 |M_k|\le\Gamma\ (k\ge1),\quad
 M_1=\Gamma,\quad M_0=Z/2-\Gamma.
\]
Indeed the second weighted factor is
$\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}j|q_j|^2/(n-j)=\Gamma$.

The absolutely convergent Fourier series obtained by multiplying the
radial limit of $\log|1+w|^2$ by $|1+w|^2$ has constant coefficient
$2$, first coefficients $3/2$, and $k$th coefficients
$2(-1)^k/[k(k^2-1)]$ for $k\ge2$.
With $e_k=\Gamma+(-1)^k\Re M_k\ge0$, it follows that
\[
 J-Z=4\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}\frac{e_k}{k(k^2-1)},
 \qquad J=\int|P|^2\log|P/q|^2\,dm.
\]
The positive Fej\'er polynomial
$1-(4/3)\Re v+(2/3)\Re v^2$ gives
$0\le M_0-2\Gamma+(2/3)e_2$.
Keeping the $k=2$ summand shows $J-Z\ge\max(0,2\Gamma-M_0)$.
Finally $|1+v|^2dm/2$ is a probability measure, and Jensen applied
to $x\log x$ gives
$\int|P|^2\log|q|^2\,dm\ge Z\log(Z/2)$.
Adding proves \eqref{F:eq:r6polarbonus}.
Approximation by distinct unit roots extends the statement to repeated
roots, since the entropy integral of $|P|^2$ is continuous under uniform
convergence by continuity of $x\log x$ at zero.
In particular its excess over $1-\log2$ is at least $(1-3D_2)/4$.

\subsection{Cancelling the actual singleton normalizer}
Make $F(\theta)=e^{-in\theta/2}P(e^{i\theta})$ real by a constant
phase. Differentiating its sine factors and then extending through
zeros gives
\[
 \sum_{\alpha\text{ projected}}\left|\frac{P(z)}{1-\bar\alpha z}\right|^2
     =F'^2-FF'',\qquad
 \sum_{\alpha\text{ projected}}\left\|\frac{P}{1-\bar\alpha z}\right\|_2^2
     =2\|F'\|_2^2=\frac{n^2ZD_2}{2}.
\]
The product $FF'$ is periodic also when $n$ is odd.
Restricting the nonnegative sum to auxiliary indices proves
$\mathcal Q\le D_2/2$.

Put $C_j=2(\cosh\ell_j-1)$.  The actual radial normalizer is
\[
 Z'=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n-N\}}
  \left\|\frac{P}{\prod_{j\in S}(1-\bar\xi_jz)}\right\|_2^2
          \prod_{j\in S}C_j,\qquad a_n=e^{-t}Z'.
\]
The unit phase in the reciprocal factorization is $+1$ because the
physical density $h$ is nonnegative and nonzero; its circle mean is
therefore exactly $a_n=e^{-t}Z'$. Every term is nonnegative.
Inflate every projected factor, including
physical factors, to logarithmic radius $L=A/n$. By self-inversive
symmetry the resulting mean is
$\sum_k|p_k|^2\cosh((n-2k)L)$, bounded above by
\[
 Z\{1+A^2D_2/2+(\cosh A-1-A^2/2)D_4\}.
\]
This follows term by term from the positive cosh series and
$|1-2k/n|\le1$.  The fully inflated singleton sum is
$2(\cosh L-1)n^2ZD_2/2\ge ZA^2D_2/2$.
The true terms of order at least two are bounded by the fully inflated
terms of order at least two.  Hence $\log x\le x-1$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6normalizercancel}
 \log(Z'/Z)-\sum_j C_jZ_j/Z
 \le(\cosh A-1-A^2/2)D_4.
\end{equation}

The stationary finite logarithmic jet paired against $|P|^2$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6projectedpairing}
 -\log a_n=\operatorname{Ent}(|P|^2/Z)
       +\sum_j L_j(\ell_j)/Z-\log(Z'/Z),
\end{equation}
where
$L_j(u)=-2\sum_{k=1}^n(\cosh(ku)-1)
\Re(\widehat{|P|^2}(k)\xi_j^k)/k$.
To see the pairing, the formal log of $R$ agrees with $\log f$
through degree $n$, while its real pairing with $|P|^2$ vanishes
because $P$ is zero at every physical Herglotz pole.  Subtract the
projected logarithm $-t+2\log P$; the displayed finite correction
is precisely the remaining reciprocal-pair Fourier sum.
Boundary logarithms of unit factors are integrable, so radial
approximation justifies this finite pairing even at repeated roots.

Let $x_j$ be the coefficient vector of $P_j(\xi_jz)$, of length $n$.
Taking the second difference of its autocorrelations to form $|P|^2$
and differentiating the last finite sum gives
\[
 L_j(\ell_j)-C_jZ_j
 =2\int_0^{\ell_j}(\cosh u-1)x_j^*K_ux_j\,du,
 \qquad(K_u)_{ab}=\sinh(u|a-b|).
\]
For explicit verification of the sign, the derivative's constant
part is $2Z_j\sinh u$, and its remaining part is
$2(\cosh u-1)x_j^*K_ux_j$.
Writing centered vectors
$c_a=\cosh(u(a-(n-1)/2))$ and $s_a=\sinh(u(a-(n-1)/2))$,
one has $K_u=cc^{\mathsf T}-ss^{\mathsf T}-E_u$ with
$(E_u)_{ab}=e^{-u|a-b|}$.
The row sums bound $\|E_u\|\le n$, and midpoint convexity yields
\[
 \|s\|^2\le\int_{-n/2}^{n/2}\sinh^2(ux)\,dx
               =\frac{\sinh(nu)}{2u}-\frac n2.
\]
Discarding the positive rank-one term and using
$\cosh u-1\le u^2\cosh(A/n)/2$ gives
\[
 L_j(\ell_j)-C_jZ_j
 \ge-\frac{Z_j\cosh(A/n)}{2n^2}
      \int_0^A(v^2+v\sinh v)\,dv
 =-\frac{Z_j\cosh(A/n)}{2n^2}T(A).
\]
Sum, use \eqref{F:eq:r6normalizercancel},
\eqref{F:eq:r6projectedpairing} and \eqref{F:eq:r6polarbonus} to prove
\eqref{F:eq:r6energyentropy}.

Since $D_4\le D_2$, the lower gap is at least
\[
 \frac14-D_2\left\{\frac34+\frac14\cosh(A/n)T(A)
                       +\cosh A-1-A^2/2\right\}.
\]
All terms inside braces increase with $A\ge0$ and decrease with $n$.
The accompanying exact checker bounds the cosh and sinh values by
positive exponential Taylor sums and rational tails at the three
worst endpoints $(n,A)=(9,2),(10,3),(10,4)$.
It proves the strict rational gap margins in the table without
floating-point acceptance.

\paragraph{What the combination does and does not cover.}
Heisei R20--R22 approach the opposite projected spectral end, where
$P=1+U+p_nz^n$ has tiny intermediate coefficient norm and $D_2$ is
close to one.  The present theorem treats $D_2$ close to zero.
These conditions do not exhaust the interval $0\le D_2\le1$.
For example the projected two-grid family
$P=(1-a z^M)(1-b z^M)$, $|a|=|b|=1$, has
$D_2=2/(2+|a+b|^2)\in[1/3,1]$; bounds for that special motif
cannot be applied to an arbitrary polynomial of the same spread.
Thus no whole band $A\le4$ is declared closed.  Nevertheless the
regions in the table are independent of grid matching and give
valid additional exclusions for unbounded degree and defect.

\section{The full-support case, with equality, inside this paper}\label{col:F:31}
\label{F:sec:r6-full-support}
The polar proof in Section~\ref{F:sec:r6projectedenergy} also supplies
the full-support entropy step without an external intermediate lemma.
This is an internal proof of the already known full-support result,
not a new deficient-support exclusion.

\begin{proposition}[A strict all-circle entropy gap away from a binomial]
\label{F:prop:r6-all-circle-gap}
For any all-circle polynomial $P(z)=\sum_{j=0}^n p_jz^j$ of degree
$n\ge2$, use $Z$ and $\Gamma$ from Section~\ref{F:sec:r6projectedenergy}.
Then
\[
 \operatorname{Ent}(|P|^2/Z)
 \ge 1-\log2+\frac{2\Gamma}{n(n-1)Z}.
\]
Consequently equality in the basic bound $1-\log2$ holds precisely
for a nonzero constant multiple of $1+\eta z^n$, $|\eta|=1$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
First assume simple circle roots. In the preceding polar construction,
$q=P-zP'/n$ has degree at most $n-1$, whereas $v^kq$ has a zero of
order at least $k$ at the origin. Hence
$M_k=\langle v^kq,q\rangle=0$ for $k\ge n$.
The nonnegative series already proved there therefore gives
\[
 J-Z=4\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}\frac{e_k}{k(k^2-1)}
 \ge4\Gamma\sum_{k=n}^{\infty}\frac1{k(k^2-1)}
 =\frac{2\Gamma}{n(n-1)}.
\]
The sum telescopes since its partial sum from $n$ through $m$ equals
$1/[2n(n-1)]-1/[2m(m+1)]$.
The same Jensen inequality gives the displayed entropy bound.
Approximation extends it to repeated roots with the same fixed $n$.
If entropy equals $1-\log2$, then $\Gamma=0$, so every interior
coefficient $p_1,\ldots,p_{n-1}$ vanishes. The two endpoint
coefficients have equal modulus for an all-circle polynomial.
Conversely, for $P=1+\eta z^n$ one has $Z=2$, $q$ constant of
unit modulus, $J=Z$, and the entropy is $1-\log2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Full support and its canonical equality case]
\label{F:thm:r6-full-support}
Every normalized stationary tuple with $N=n$ satisfies $a_n\le2/e$.
After restoring rotations and constant phases, equality gives exactly
the canonical exponentials
\[
 f(z)=\xi\exp\!\left(-\frac{1+\eta z^n}{1-\eta z^n}\right),
 \qquad |\xi|=|\eta|=1.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
There are no auxiliary factors. The finite stationary logarithmic
pairing of Section~\ref{F:sec:r6projectedenergy} reduces to
$tZ=\int|P|^2\log|P|^2\,dm$ and $a_n=e^{-t}Z$.
Thus $-\log a_n=\operatorname{Ent}(|P|^2/Z)$.
For $n\ge2$ the proposition proves the sharp inequality and forces
$P$ to be a binomial in equality. Its physical moment directions
form a rotated regular $n$-grid. They all have the same $n$th power,
so the top stationary moment gives $nt-n=0$, hence $t=1$.
The lower $n-1$ moments and invertibility of the discrete Fourier
matrix then give every mass equal to $1/n$. Their Herglotz function
is $(1+\eta z^n)/(1-\eta z^n)$ after rotation, proving the formula.
For $n=1$, the single top stationary moment directly gives $t=1$,
with the same conclusion. Restoring the constant phase gives $\xi$.
\end{proof}

At degree nine this treats $N=9$ and retains its equality functions.
It does not remove the deficient support sizes left in the revised
ledger, and it is not counted as another newly closed residual stratum.

\section{A calibrated energy identity and a stronger signed angular sieve}\label{col:F:32}
\label{F:sec:r6calibrated}
The construction in Reiwa R13, R20, R29 and R30 admits a self-contained
stationary derivation.  Keeping both the zero constant mode and the missing
$n$th mode improves its final angular exclusion.  In this section $R$ is the
matching reciprocal polynomial of the stationary reduction and $a_n>0$;
there is no additional competitiveness assumption.

\subsection{The inverse coordinate and its exact energy}
Write $f=e^{-H}=\sum_{j\ge0}a_jz^j$, $H(0)=t>0$, and
\[
 R(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}a_jz^j+
             \sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\overline{a_j}z^{2n-j},\qquad
 h(z)=z^{-n}R(z).
\]
Set
\[
 B(z)=\sum_{j=1}^n j\overline{a_{n-j}}z^{j-1},\qquad
 A_1=\sum_{j=1}^n j|a_{n-j}|^2,\qquad \sigma=A_1/n.
\]
The stationary identity $(n-D)h=\Phi h$, with $D$ the absolute
Fourier multiplier, implies
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6volterra}
 (R/f)'(z)=2z^ne^{H(z)}B(z).
\end{equation}
Indeed, on the physical circle away from the poles, $zH'(z)=-\Phi(z)$,
while $zR'=z^n(nh+\widetilde D h)$ with signed multiplier
$\widetilde D$.  Thus
$zR'+zH'R=z^n(D+\widetilde D)h
=2\sum_{j=1}^n j\overline{a_{n-j}}z^{n+j}$.
Double zeros of $R$ at each support pole cancel the possible poles of
$H'R$, so this is also a holomorphic identity in the disk.

Put $J(z)=ze^{H(z)/n}$ and
$\Omega=\{z\in\mathbb D:|J(z)|<1\}$.
This entire sublevel is one domain, and $J:\Omega\to\mathbb D$ is
conformal.  To check this without a boundary smoothness assumption, every
preimage of $|w|\le r<1$ lies in $|z|\le r$, since $\Re H\ge0$.
Consequently $J$ restricted to each component is proper onto the disk:
its image is open and closed, and limits over a compact target stay in
the same open component.  Each component must contain a zero of $J$.
There is exactly one zero, namely $0$, and it is simple.  The proper map
therefore has degree one, by its preimage count at zero.  Let
$\varphi:\mathbb D\to\Omega$ be its conformal inverse.

As $R/f=1+O(z^{n+1})$, write
\[
 (R/f)(\varphi(w))=1+w^nV(w),\qquad
 V(w)=\sum_{j\ge1}v_jw^j.
\]
Equation~\eqref{F:eq:r6volterra} and $J(\varphi(w))=w$ give
\[
 nV+wV'=2w\varphi'(w)B(\varphi(w)).
\]
Dividing by $w$, taking the normalized Bergman norm, and changing variables
through the conformal map prove
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6energy}
 \sum_{j\ge1}\frac{(n+j)^2}{j}|v_j|^2
 =4\int_\Omega |B(z)|^2\frac{dA(z)}\pi
 \le4A_1.
\end{equation}
All identities follow first on compact subdisks and then by monotone
convergence of the nonnegative coefficient sum and the conformal area
integral.  In particular they do not require a regular boundary for
$\Omega$.

An integration by parts in the residue after $w=J(z)$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6pin}
 v_j=\frac{2}{n+j}[z^{j-1}]B(z)e^{-jH(z)/n},\qquad v_n=\sigma.
\end{equation}
For clarity, the first formula is the Lagrange residue
$(n+j)^{-1}[z^{n+j-1}](R/f)'e^{-(n+j)H/n}$ followed by
\eqref{F:eq:r6volterra}.  At $j=n$ the remaining coefficient is
$[z^{n-1}]Bf=A_1$, which proves the second formula.
Let $W=V-\sigma w^n$.  Since $(n+j)^2/j\ge4n$, equations
\eqref{F:eq:r6energy}--\eqref{F:eq:r6pin} imply
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6W}
 [w^0]W=[w^n]W=0,\quad
 \|W\|_{H^2}^2\le\sigma(1-\sigma),\quad 0<\sigma\le1.
\end{equation}
Here $\sigma>0$ follows from $a_0=e^{-t}>0$; the upper bound is
already forced by the pinned term in the nonnegative energy sum.
No lower estimate for the physical phase slope has been used.
Finally $f(\varphi(w))/\varphi(w)^n=w^{-n}$, so
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6htransport}
 h(\varphi(w))=w^{-n}+\sigma w^n+W(w).
\end{equation}
The right side has boundary values almost everywhere, with square-integrable
real part.  These boundary values are used below.

\subsection{A phase-free one-root test and a degree-nine consequence}
An interior auxiliary zero $w_*$ of $R$ with
\[
 \delta_*=n\log(1/|w_*|)-\Re H(w_*)>0
\]
is in $\Omega$.  Its calibrated image is
$\beta=J(w_*)$, of modulus $r=e^{-\delta_*/n}<1$.
Since $R(w_*)=0$, equation~\eqref{F:eq:r6htransport} implies
$W(\beta)=-\beta^{-n}-\sigma\beta^n$.
Retaining the weights in \eqref{F:eq:r6energy} gives the evaluation kernel
\[
 G_n(r)=\sum_{\substack{j\ge1\\j\ne n}}
                 \frac{j r^{2j}}{(n+j)^2},
 \qquad
 |W(\beta)|^2\le4n\sigma(1-\sigma)G_n(r).
\]
The series converges for $r<1$.  Here $0<\sigma<1$, as also follows
from $\sigma\le\sum_{j<n}|a_j|^2\le1-a_n^2<1$.
For $a=r^{-n}$ and $b=r^n=a^{-1}$, the reverse triangle inequality
and the exact square identity
\[
 (a-b\sigma)^2-4a(a-b)\sigma(1-\sigma)
       =\bigl(a-(2a-b)\sigma\bigr)^2
\]
yield a phase-free necessary condition:
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6oneroot}
 \boxed{nG_n(e^{-\delta_*/n})\ge e^{2\delta_*}-1.}
\end{equation}
This uses the actual value of the Herglotz potential at the root;
it imposes no separation or phase-matching assumption.
The left side decreases and the right side increases with
$\delta_*>0$, so any strictly certified failed threshold excludes all
larger adjusted depths.

\begin{corollary}[Every degree-nine auxiliary root is shallow after calibration]
\label{F:cor:r6ninecalibrated}
For $n=9$, every interior auxiliary root of a stationary tuple satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6ninecalibrated}
 \boxed{9\log(1/|w_*|)-\Re H(w_*)<\frac12.}
\end{equation}
In particular this is a necessary inequality in each of the support
strata $N=5,6,7,8$, for every auxiliary root including multiplicities.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Suppose the left side is at least $1/2$.  Then
$r^2\le e^{-1/9}<q=162/181$, using the first three terms of
$e^{1/9}$.  Since $j/(9+j)^2\le1/(9+j)$, the exact rational bound is
\[
 9G_9(r)\le
 9\sum_{\substack{1\le j\le99\\j\ne9}}
       \frac{j q^j}{(9+j)^2}
       +\frac{9q^{100}}{109(1-q)}
 <\frac53.
\]
The strict comparison is checked by integer rational arithmetic in the
attached verifier.  On the other hand
$e^{2\delta_*}-1\ge e-1>5/3$, using the first four terms of $e$ and
its positive remainder.  This contradicts \eqref{F:eq:r6oneroot}.
\end{proof}
The calibrated inequality does not say that every root has positive
adjusted depth, and it supplies no common lower bound on its physical
radius independent of $H$.  Those distinctions are essential when it
is inserted in the residual catalogue.

\subsection{Two necessary signed-size inequalities}
Use normalized angular measure $dm=d\alpha/(2\pi)$ in the calibrated
coordinate, and define
\[
 c(\alpha)=\cos(n\alpha),\qquad
 E=\{\alpha:\Re h(\varphi(e^{i\alpha}))<0\}.
\]
Measure in this coordinate is harmonic measure from zero in $\Omega$.
\begin{theorem}[Strengthened calibrated sign obstruction]
\label{F:thm:r6sign}
Every stationary tuple in the preceding setting satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6signconclusion}
 \boxed{\int_{E\cap\{c<0\}}c^2\,dm\ge\frac7{36}},\qquad
 \boxed{|E|>\frac14}.
\end{equation}
Thus either $|E|\le1/4$ or a negative-half weighted integral below $7/36$
is a strict exclusion certificate.  The supplied R30 thresholds were
$3/16$ and $5/24$, respectively.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Put $u=\Re W$ and $v=u/(1+\sigma)$.  The zero constant and $n$th mode
in \eqref{F:eq:r6W}, together with orthogonality of Fourier modes, give
\begin{equation}\label{F:eq:r6orth}
 \int v\,dm=\int vc\,dm=0,\qquad
 \|v\|_2^2\le
 \frac{\sigma(1-\sigma)}{2(1+\sigma)^2}\le\frac1{16}.
\end{equation}
The last inequality is equivalent to $(1-3\sigma)^2\ge0$.
Also $E=\{c+v<0\}$ by \eqref{F:eq:r6htransport}.

Let $F=E^c\cap\{c<0\}$ and $a=\int_Fc^2\,dm$.
On $F$ one has $v\ge-c>0$.  If $a>0$, set
$I=-\int_Fvc\,dm\ge a$.
Since $\int vc=0$, Cauchy--Schwarz on $F$ and $F^c$ separately yields
\[
 \|v\|_2^2\ge\frac{I^2}{a}
                +\frac{I^2}{1/2-a}
 \ge\frac{a}{1-2a}.
\]
This also yields the conclusion at $a=0$ by continuity.
Using \eqref{F:eq:r6orth}, $a\le1/18$.  The total cosine-square integral
on the negative half-period is $1/4$, so the first assertion is
$1/4-1/18=7/36$.

For the second assertion suppose, to the contrary, that $|E|\le1/4$.
Set $a_0=1/7$, $b_0=9/8$ and
$w=-a_0+(b_0-1)c$.
The two orthogonality conditions in \eqref{F:eq:r6orth} give
\[
 \|v\|_2^2=\|v-w\|_2^2-\|w\|_2^2.
\]
On $F$, $v-w\ge a_0-b_0c>0$.  Among all subsets of
$\{c<0\}$ of measure at most $1/4$, removal of the quarter-period
centered at the negative peak removes the largest integral of
$(a_0-b_0c)^2$, because this function increases as $c$ decreases.
The $n$-fold phase winding preserves this distribution.  Hence
\[
 \|v\|_2^2\ge
 \frac1\pi\int_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/4}(a_0-b_0\cos x)^2\,dx
       -a_0^2-\frac{(b_0-1)^2}{2}.
\]
The integral evaluates to
\[
 L=-\frac{3a_0^2}{4}-\frac{(b_0-1)^2}{2}+
   \frac{b_0^2}{8}
  +\frac{2a_0b_0(1-\sqrt2/2)-b_0^2/4}{\pi}.
\]
Use $\sqrt2<99/70$ and $\pi>157/50$.  The bracket multiplying
$1/\pi$ is negative.  These rational enclosures give the strictly
valid lower bound
\[
 L>\frac{36179}{562688}
   =\frac1{16}+\frac{1011}{562688}>\frac1{16},
\]
contradicting \eqref{F:eq:r6orth}.  This proves $|E|>1/4$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A finite-root expression for the excluded geometry}
Choose one root from each reciprocal pair, with the physical unit roots
counted once, and write
\[
 h(z)=C\prod_{j=1}^n(1-\overline{\gamma_j}z)(1-\gamma_j/z),
 \quad C>0,\quad \gamma_j=e^{-L_j+i\theta_j},\quad L_j\ge0.
\]
For almost every calibrated boundary point write
$\varphi(e^{i\alpha})=e^{-S+i\theta}$ and $v_j=\theta-\theta_j$.
The inverse cannot have boundary limit zero, since continuity of $J$ at
zero would contradict $J(\varphi(re^{i\alpha}))=re^{i\alpha}$.
Define
\[
 F_j(S)=\cosh L_j-\cosh S\cos v_j+i\sinh S\sin v_j.
\]
Each reciprocal factor is $2e^{-L_j}F_j(S)$, so
\[
 E=\left\{\alpha:\Re\prod_{j=1}^n F_j(S)<0\right\}
\]
up to null sets.  This avoids any choice of an argument branch.  If no
factor vanishes, it is equivalently the set where
$\cos(\sum_j\arg F_j(S))<0$.
The sign tests in Theorem~\ref{F:thm:r6sign} are therefore explicit
conditions on the reciprocal root geometry in its actual calibrated
coordinate.  They keep the signs of the individual root contributions;
replacing their sum by a sum of absolute values would lose the proved
criterion.  For $n=9$ the same thresholds apply to every
$N=5,6,7,8$ support stratum.  No argument here forces an arbitrary
stationary tuple to violate them, so no entire one of those four strata
is declared closed by this theorem.

\section{Exclusion of the five-atom stationary stratum at degree nine}\label{col:F:33}
\label{F:sec:r6-n9-five-atom-join}

\begin{theorem}[Degree-nine five-atom closure]
\label{F:thm:r6-n9-five-atom}
No competitive stationary candidate at degree $n=9$ has exactly
five physical atoms.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The exact Rayleigh witness in Theorem~\ref{F:thm:r6ninemass} forces
$t>T_0:=228091/100000$ in this support stratum. The support-free
ninth-row certificate excludes every $t\geq13/4$. It remains to
treat the closed band $T_0\leq t\leq13/4$; including its endpoints
makes the overlap explicit.

The stationary cardinal identity gives $\lambda_i\geq1/9$ for
each of the five atoms. Relabel the atoms so the masses are
nondecreasing. Every relevant mass tuple therefore belongs to
\[
 \mathcal P=\left\{\boldsymbol\lambda\in\mathbb R^5:
 \frac19\leq\lambda_1\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_5,
 \quad T_0\leq\sum_{i=1}^5\lambda_i\leq\frac{13}{4}\right\}.
\]
The completed finite verifier covers all of $\mathcal P$ and all
five support angles, after one common rotation removes one angle.
It begins with a containing rectangle and contracts only by the
displayed order and total-mass constraints. Every retained box is
either bisected into two closed children or accepted by a strict
continuum upper bound. Each accepted bound is the largest of
certified four-angle vertex bounds plus the five-coordinate Hardy
mass remainder. The coarse grid has 40 points per full angle and
the fine grid has 64; each individually bounds the entire angular
continuum by the interpolation and arithmetic error estimates of
Section~\ref{F:sec:r6-five-atom-errors}. The optional coarse rejection
heuristic only requests further subdivision and never removes a box.

The matching completed run, source hashes and terminal record in
the completion ledger show that the stack became empty and every
accepted box satisfied
\[
 \sup|a_9|<\frac{2943}{4000}<\frac2e.
\]
All estimates allow coincident support angles, so they also bound
the required subdomain of distinct physical atoms. Thus the entire
middle band is subcompetitive. Together with the exact lower
mass exclusion and the support-free upper mass ray this excludes
the whole five-atom stationary stratum.
\end{proof}

This is a closure of the single pair $(n,N)=(9,5)$. It does not
extend to arbitrary $n$ with $N=5$, and it does not close the
degree-nine strata $N=6,7,8$. The full-support stratum $N=9$
retains the canonical equality case and is handled separately by
the entropy theorem.

The search stack was empty at completion, the terminal record was

 <\frac{2943}{4000}<\frac2e.
